Competition|Good-Natured and Positive.ask: How seriously are you actually taking this?

Competition|Grounded.recognize: You know your own worth independently of the standings, which is why a bad season does not unmake you the way it unmakes most competitive people. The rigidity is that being settled and wanting to win together mean you rarely change your approach, even when the field has moved past it.
Competition|Grounded.ask: Has your method aged past the field you are in?

Competition|Hands-on and Observant.recognize: You move on an opening the moment it appears, and in a close race that reflex is usually the whole difference. The gap is that moving to hold position leaves out the question of whether the position was worth defending.
Competition|Hands-on and Observant.ask: What are you fighting for out of reflex?

Competition|Handy and Resourceful.recognize: You find a way to come out ahead with less than everyone else had, which is why you win from behind more often than the odds should allow. The trap is that a scrappy advantage is temporary, and you can win a round on something that leaves you worse positioned afterward.
Competition|Handy and Resourceful.ask: What did winning that one cost you structurally?

Competition|Hardworking.recognize: You outwork the field because being second is worse to you than being tired, and that trade has produced most of what you have. The danger is that there is no amount of labour that settles the question permanently, and the standings reset every year.

Competition|Honest.recognize: You own a defeat plainly rather than explaining it away, which is why your account of your own record can be trusted. The imbalance is that you are hardest on yourself in exactly the moments when the loss was not about you at all.
Competition|Honest.ask: How much of that outcome was actually in your hands?

Competition|Honest and Direct.recognize: You state where you stand and where others do, which gives people real information instead of the polite fog most groups operate in. The impact is that being told plainly you are behind is hard to hear, and not everyone was in the race you were scoring.

Competition|Idealistic.recognize: You want to be best at something that deserves to have a best, which is why your ambition points at worthwhile things rather than merely winnable ones. The ache is that a high standard plus a ranking instinct means you are never at the top of your own scale.
Competition|Idealistic.ask: Who is ahead of you on a measure only you use?

Competition|Imaginative.recognize: You can see yourself winning in vivid detail, and that image is genuinely part of how you get there rather than being idle daydreaming. The risk is that you also rehearse the version where someone beats you, and that plays just as clearly.
Competition|Imaginative.ask: Which defeat do you keep watching in your head?

Competition|Independent.recognize: You set your own bar and race against it, which means you are not at the mercy of whatever the group happens to value this year. The narrowing is that competing alone means nobody sees your effort, and you can end up striving hard in a place where winning changes nothing.
Competition|Independent.ask: Who would notice if you came first at this?

Competition|Informed.recognize: You know exactly where everyone stands because you follow it closely, which is why you are rarely surprised by a rival's move. The cost is that constant monitoring of other people's progress is a way of spending your attention on their work instead of yours.
Competition|Informed.ask: How much time went into watching rather than doing?

Competition|Insightful.recognize: You see what actually decides the outcome, so you play the thing that matters while others work hard on things that do not. The exposure is that seeing the game quickly can leave you dismissive of people still playing it the slow way.
Competition|Insightful.ask: Who have you written off as not getting it?

Competition|Kind and Encouraging.recognize: You lift people up genuinely while wanting to finish ahead of them, and both of those are true at once rather than one being a cover for the other. The strain is that you know exactly how much you meant each piece of encouragement, and some of it you are not sure about.
Competition|Kind and Encouraging.ask: Which compliment did you give with something else running underneath?

Competition|Knowledgeable.recognize: You have gone deep partly because being out-known is unbearable, and that pressure has built something real rather than merely defensive. The rigidity is that being put right by someone else registers as a loss, and you will argue a small point past where it was worth arguing.
Competition|Knowledgeable.ask: Which minor point did you fight for far too long?

Competition|Loyal, Patient, and Reliable.recognize: You remain in a race for years after the fast starters have quit, which is how you have taken things that were never supposed to be yours. The bind is that neither instinct concedes, so a pursuit that stopped making sense a decade ago still has your name on it.
Competition|Loyal, Patient, and Reliable.ask: What are you still trying to win from an earlier version of your life?

Competition|Observant.recognize: You see what the people ahead of you are doing differently, and that noticing is why you close gaps rather than merely resenting them. The bind is that studying others closely means your attention sits on their run rather than your own.
Competition|Observant.ask: What would you be doing if you could not see anyone else?

Competition|Open-Minded.recognize: You will take an approach from someone who is beating you, which is rarer than it sounds and is most of why you improve. The cost is that adopting whatever is winning can leave you without a method of your own.
Competition|Open-Minded.ask: What is yours here that you did not take from someone else?

Competition|Organized and Effective.recognize: You work out the route to first place and then follow it, which is why your results look inevitable rather than lucky. The rigidity is that a route aimed at one form of winning does not adapt, and you can execute perfectly toward a prize that has moved.
Competition|Organized and Effective.ask: Is the finish line still where it was when you set out?

Competition|Original.recognize: You go your own way partly because it is the one place nobody is ahead of you, and that instinct has produced things that would not otherwise exist. The bind is that choosing the unoccupied ground means you win uncontested, and part of you knows the win was easier for that reason.
Competition|Original.ask: Did you pick that path because it was right or because it was empty?

Competition|Passionate.recognize: You care enormously and you want to be first, which is why your intensity produces results rather than only heat. The danger is that losing at something you love this much is genuinely devastating, and you have not built anywhere for that to go.
Competition|Passionate.ask: What happened inside you the last time you came second?

Competition|Perceptive.recognize: You sense a rival's weakness or a shift in the field before it is visible, which is why you are positioned early. The risk is that a competitive eye takes ordinary behaviour for manoeuvring, and you can find opponents in people who were not playing.
Competition|Perceptive.ask: Who did you decide was against you without evidence?

Competition|Positive and Enthusiastic.recognize: You stay up even when you are behind, which is why you are still in things long after the mood should have taken you out of them. The cost is that both instincts avoid dwelling, and a defeat that had something to teach you gets bounced past rather than examined.
Competition|Positive and Enthusiastic.ask: What did the last loss have to tell you?

Competition|Principled.recognize: You will not win by means you consider wrong, which is why your record is clean in a way many high performers' quietly is not. Where it turns is that your restraint becomes a scoreboard of its own, and someone who cut a corner gets judged rather than understood.
Competition|Principled.ask: What corners were they cutting to survive?

Competition|Proactive Initiative.recognize: You go first because being first is the point, so you are underway while the field is still deciding whether to enter. The overreach is that both instincts push forward, and you can claim ground that someone else had a better right to.

Competition|Quick Thinkers.recognize: You are faster than the people around you and you know it, which is why you take the openings that close in seconds. The blind spot is that being quickest in the room is a low bar you keep clearing, and it can stand in for being right.
Competition|Quick Thinkers.ask: When were you last the slowest person in a room?

Competition|Rational.recognize: You can tell the difference between a real advantage and a story you would like to believe, which is why your read on your own position is trustworthy. The blind spot is that reducing everything to who is ahead leaves out most of what a relationship or a piece of work actually is.
Competition|Rational.ask: What here has no ranking and still matters?

Competition|Rational and Practical.recognize: You put your effort where it changes your standing, so nothing you do is decorative, and your time converts into position. The narrowing is that both instincts test by advantage, and anything that yields none gets cut before it can prove itself.
Competition|Rational and Practical.ask: What did you stop doing because it did not get you anywhere?

Competition|Receptive.recognize: You will hear coaching from anyone who is better than you, which is why you improve at a rate that surprises people who have been at it longer. The strain is that being open and wanting to be first pull against each other, and taking advice can feel like admitting a gap.
Competition|Receptive.ask: Whose help have you turned down because accepting it stung?

Competition|Reliable.recognize: You perform to the same level every time rather than only when it matters, which is why your record does not have the gaps most competitive people's do. The pressure is that consistency becomes another thing you must not lose at, and an ordinary bad day starts to feel like a failure.
Competition|Reliable.ask: What happens in you when you have an average week?

Competition|Research-Oriented.recognize: You establish where you actually stand rather than guessing, which is why you are neither falsely confident nor needlessly discouraged. The tension is that one half wants more data and the other has already entered, and you can be running while still checking whether you should have.
Competition|Research-Oriented.ask: How much of your effort goes into confirming your position?

Competition|Results Oriented.recognize: Your drive to come first and your drive to complete are one instinct twice over, so what you take on lands, and it lands ahead of the field. What is absent is any question about worth - neither half asks whether the result was worth having, only whether you got there first.
Competition|Results Oriented.ask: Which of your wins do you not actually value?

Competition|Sensitive and Warm.recognize: You are tender with people and you still want to beat them, and holding both is harder than either alone would be. The friction is that you can pull your effort to spare someone, and then be quietly resentful about a result you chose.
Competition|Sensitive and Warm.ask: Where did you hold back and then mind about it?

Competition|Sensitive to Others.recognize: You notice what winning costs the other person, and that awareness keeps your drive from leaving damage behind it. The bind is that you will scale down your own ambition to protect someone's feelings and then carry the loss privately.
Competition|Sensitive to Others.ask: What did you give up so someone else would not feel bad?

Competition|Sociable.recognize: You like being around people and you like being the one they notice, which is why you are usually near the centre of a room rather than at its edge. The cost is that a room you are scoring by attention is a room you can never simply be in.
Competition|Sociable.ask: When did you last enjoy a gathering without registering how you were doing in it?

Competition|Spontaneous.recognize: You take an opening the instant it appears, which is why you get things that go to whoever moves first. The friction is that a chance grabbed for the sake of getting there ahead of someone can leave you holding something you never wanted.
Competition|Spontaneous.ask: What did you win that you had no use for?

Competition|Strong Practical Skills.recognize: You are good at the work and you want to be best at it, which is why your skill keeps climbing instead of settling. The load is that ability plus a drive to lead the field makes you take on far too much, because handing it off means someone else gets the credit.
Competition|Strong Practical Skills.ask: What are you refusing to delegate because of who would be praised?

Competition|Strong Sense of Duty.recognize: You take on what is yours and you want to carry it better than anyone else would, which is why your responsibilities are met to a standard nobody asked for. The danger is that both instincts add weight, and you accept more in order to be the one carrying most.
Competition|Strong Sense of Duty.ask: How much of your load did you take on to prove something?

Competition|Strong-willed.recognize: You want to win and you will not be pushed off, which is why you are still there in situations where the pressure removed everyone else. The rigidity is that not yielding and not losing feel like the same thing to you, so a sensible retreat is unavailable.
Competition|Strong-willed.ask: When did you last walk away from something on purpose?

Competition|Supportive.recognize: You get behind people and you want them to come first, which is why your help is real rather than the kind that quietly hopes for something modest. The strain is that you can only fully cheer someone whose success does not touch your own, and you know which relationships those are.
Competition|Supportive.ask: Who can you not entirely celebrate?

Competition|Very Loyal.recognize: You stand by your people and you want your side on top, which is why the ones with you have someone genuinely fighting for them. The blind spot is that a rivalry turns a disagreement into a side to be beaten, and you may be at war with someone who was only ever a colleague.
Competition|Very Loyal.ask: Who did you turn into an opponent?

Competition|Very Responsible.recognize: You own where you finished rather than reaching for the conditions, which is why your self-assessment can be believed. The pressure is that taking the result personally means every outcome becomes a statement about you, and no season is ever just a season.
Competition|Very Responsible.ask: Can a bad season be just a bad season for you?

Maximizer|Altruistic.recognize: You give people your best rather than your leftovers, and what you hand over is genuinely finished. The cost is that you will pour hours into someone whose situation only needed something adequate, and the person with a plain ordinary need waits while you perfect the last one.
Maximizer|Altruistic.ask: Who needed ordinary help while you were perfecting something for someone else?

Maximizer|Analytical.recognize: You find the underlying structure of what makes something work and then push that part until it is exceptional, which is rarer than either skill alone. What gets thin is your patience for the pieces that will never be more than functional, and most of any system is functional pieces.
Maximizer|Analytical.ask: Which working piece have you starved of care because it could not become remarkable?

Maximizer|Bold.recognize: You will bet on the strongest option instead of the safest one, and you commit hard enough that the bet usually pays. The exposure is that you scrap a merely decent path the moment a brilliant one appears, and brilliant paths are not always as good as they look from a distance.
Maximizer|Bold.ask: What did you walk away from that would have worked?

Maximizer|Calm and Practical.recognize: You take something good and quietly make it better without any drama about it, so improvements land before anyone notices they were needed. What hides in that steadiness is how much you have already rejected. People think you are easy to please because you never made a scene about the version you threw out.
Maximizer|Calm and Practical.ask: What have you quietly thrown out that nobody knew you had judged?

Maximizer|Charismatic.recognize: You draw people toward the best version of a thing, and your appetite for quality is itself persuasive. The risk is that people adopt your standard without owning it, so when you move on to the next thing they cannot hold what you built.
Maximizer|Charismatic.ask: Which of your standards would collapse the week you left?

Maximizer|Charming.recognize: You get people to accept a raised bar without feeling criticised, which is the hardest part of holding a standard at all. The cost is that the pleasantness can obscure how absolute you are, and people agree to something more demanding than they realised they were agreeing to.
Maximizer|Charming.ask: Who signed up for your standard without knowing what it would cost them?

Maximizer|Clear Communication.recognize: You can say exactly what good looks like, in words anyone can act on, which turns a vague instinct for quality into something a team can actually hit. The gap is that the version you describe is the finished one, and people hear a demand where you meant a direction.
Maximizer|Clear Communication.ask: Does your team hear a target or a verdict?

Maximizer|Creative.recognize: You are not satisfied with a workable idea when a beautiful one is available, and you have the taste to tell the difference. What suffers is finishing. There is always one more pass, and the work sits at ninety percent for months while you chase the last piece of it.
Maximizer|Creative.ask: What is sitting unfinished right now because it is not yet beautiful?

Maximizer|Curious.recognize: You dig into what makes the good ones good, so your questions go past how something works to why it beats the alternatives. The cost is that the investigation can outlast its usefulness, and you keep studying a thing you already do better than the people you are studying.
Maximizer|Curious.ask: Which of your investigations has outlived its purpose?

Maximizer|Decisive Action.recognize: You will choose the strongest option quickly rather than surveying every option slowly, and that speed keeps your standards from turning into paralysis. The exposure is that a fast call on what counts as best locks in your first read of quality, and first reads are the ones most shaped by taste.
Maximizer|Decisive Action.ask: Was that the best one, or the one that looked best first?

Maximizer|Dedicated.recognize: You stay with a thing long enough to take it from good to genuinely rare, which almost nobody does because it takes years. The risk is that the years themselves become the reason to continue, and you keep polishing something the world stopped needing a while ago.
Maximizer|Dedicated.ask: Is this still worth being the best at?

Maximizer|Determined.recognize: You will not stop at competent, and you have the endurance to close the distance between competent and outstanding. What that hides is the toll. The last increment of quality costs more than everything before it, and you pay it without checking whether anyone wanted it.
Maximizer|Determined.ask: Who asked for that final increment?

Maximizer|Diligent and Observant.recognize: You spot the small flaw that keeps a good thing from being a great one, and you spot it early enough for it to matter. The cost is that the same eye finds flaws in things that are finished, and a team can feel permanently one correction away from your approval.
Maximizer|Diligent and Observant.ask: Whose work have you signed off on without a correction?

Maximizer|Direct.recognize: You say plainly that something is not good enough, which saves months of polite drifting. What you underrate is that a judgement about the work sounds like a judgement about the person when it comes from someone whose bar everyone already knows is high.
Maximizer|Direct.ask: Who heard your verdict on the work as a verdict on them?

Maximizer|Direct and Authentic.recognize: You will admit which parts of your own work fall short before anyone else names them, and that honesty makes your high bar bearable to be around. The risk is that public self-criticism from you sets a tone where nobody feels permitted to be satisfied with theirs.
Maximizer|Direct and Authentic.ask: Has anyone on your team said they were proud of something lately?

Maximizer|Direct and Honest.recognize: You offer the assessment nobody asked for, it is usually accurate, and it usually improves the thing. What gets lost is that unrequested feedback on adequate work reads as a standing invitation to be measured, and people start bracing before they show you anything.
Maximizer|Direct and Honest.ask: Who shows you their work already flinching?

Maximizer|Disciplined.recognize: You build the habits that let quality repeat instead of depending on inspiration, so your best is reliable rather than occasional. The gap is that a routine tuned for one kind of strong output will keep producing it long after a different kind was needed.
Maximizer|Disciplined.ask: What is your routine still optimizing for?

Maximizer|Easygoing.recognize: You hold a very high bar without much visible tension about it, which makes you rare and pleasant to work near. What that conceals is the internal edit. People see the calm and not the constant quiet sorting of what is worth your effort and what is not.
Maximizer|Easygoing.ask: What did you rule out this week, and did you tell anyone you had?

Maximizer|Efficient Organizer.recognize: You take out whatever is not pulling weight so the strong parts get room, and the result runs cleaner than what most people build. The cost is that some of what looks like waste is slack, and a system with no slack in it performs beautifully until the first thing goes wrong.
Maximizer|Efficient Organizer.ask: Where is there room for something to go wrong?

Maximizer|Empathetic.recognize: You can tell what someone is already good at before they can name it themselves, and pointing at it changes people. The risk is that you invest where you see talent, and the person with ordinary gifts and genuine need reads your interest as a verdict on their ceiling.
Maximizer|Empathetic.ask: Who have you stopped investing in, and do they know why?

Maximizer|Energetic.recognize: You have the drive to keep going past the point where the thing was already acceptable, and that is where the distance between good and exceptional actually gets closed. What you miss is that your team hit their limit at acceptable, and they are still going because you are.
Maximizer|Energetic.ask: Who is still working because you have not stopped?

Maximizer|Enjoy Creating Order.recognize: You lay things out so the strong parts become obvious and the weak ones become easy to remove. The gap is that order achieved is order defended, and the structure that once showcased your best work becomes the reason a better idea does not fit.
Maximizer|Enjoy Creating Order.ask: What good idea did not fit your structure?

Maximizer|Enthusiastic.recognize: You get visibly excited about how good something could be, and that excitement is contagious enough to move people toward it. The cost is that your picture of the finished version is far more vivid than theirs, and they sign on to a level of work they cannot yet imagine.
Maximizer|Enthusiastic.ask: Do they know how far away finished is?

Maximizer|Excellent Brainstormers.recognize: You put out many options and then cut hard to the two that are actually strong, which is the half of idea work most people skip. The risk is that cutting early on instinct removes the odd option that needed a week before it would have looked good.
Maximizer|Excellent Brainstormers.ask: Which idea did you kill before it had time to prove itself?

Maximizer|Excellent Communicators.recognize: You can describe the difference between good work and outstanding work so vividly that people want the second one. The cost is that describing a standard is not the same as building it, and a room can leave persuaded while the actual gap sits exactly where it was.
Maximizer|Excellent Communicators.ask: What have you explained well and not yet built?

Maximizer|Excellent Organizers.recognize: You take a rough strength in a team and put scaffolding around it so it shows up every week rather than occasionally. The gap is that scaffolding built to protect quality gets elaborate, and at some point the machinery costs more than the improvement it was protecting.
Maximizer|Excellent Organizers.ask: How much of your setup exists to guard a bar nobody questions anymore?

Maximizer|Excellent People Skills.recognize: You get the best out of people because you can see their strongest edge and name it without embarrassing them. The risk is that your read of someone's ceiling forms fast and stays private, and they never learn which category you filed them into.
Maximizer|Excellent People Skills.ask: Who would be surprised by your private assessment of them?

Maximizer|Future Focused.recognize: You can see what a thing would be at its very best some years out, and you work backward from there rather than forward from now. The cost is that the version in your head is finished and the one in front of you is not, so the present one always looks like a letdown.
Maximizer|Future Focused.ask: When did you last let today's version be good?

Maximizer|Generous.recognize: You give away your best material rather than your spare material, and people can tell the difference immediately. What runs down is the supply. Giving at that level has a price you do not track, because tracking it would feel like withholding.
Maximizer|Generous.ask: What did the last thing you gave away actually cost you?

Maximizer|Good Practical Skills.recognize: You make things well with your hands and you can feel the difference between adequate and right, so what you produce lasts. The risk is the endless small correction. A finished object still has three things you would change, and you will go back to them.
Maximizer|Good Practical Skills.ask: What have you gone back to more than twice?

Maximizer|Good at Connecting with Others.recognize: You put the right two people together and something stronger comes out than either would have made alone, because you matched on ability rather than convenience. The gap is that people you cannot place stop hearing from you, and they notice.
Maximizer|Good at Connecting with Others.ask: Who have you not called since you ran out of uses for them?

Maximizer|Good-Natured and Positive.recognize: You keep the mood warm while holding a bar most people would find harsh, so correction from you lands as encouragement. The cost is that the warmth can make your dissatisfaction invisible, and people find out much later that you were never actually happy with it.
Maximizer|Good-Natured and Positive.ask: Who thinks you approved of something you did not?

Maximizer|Grounded.recognize: You are clear about what you are good at and you do not move off it when a fashion comes through, so your best work compounds instead of restarting. The gap is that the same steadiness makes you slow to notice when the thing you are best at has stopped being what is needed.
Maximizer|Grounded.ask: Is your strongest skill still the one that matters here?

Maximizer|Hands-on and Observant.recognize: You see what would make something better and your hands are already on it before the discussion has finished. The exposure is that a fix made at speed is a fix made from your taste alone, and the person whose work it was never got asked.
Maximizer|Hands-on and Observant.ask: Whose work did you improve without asking them?

Maximizer|Handy and Resourceful.recognize: You can get something to a high standard with whatever is on hand, so you rarely accept that constraints make good work impossible. The cost is that a clever workaround holding up strong output is still a workaround, and only you know where it is.
Maximizer|Handy and Resourceful.ask: What is your best work currently resting on?

Maximizer|Hardworking.recognize: You put in the hours, and unlike most people who do, you put them into the part that actually raises quality rather than the part that feels busy. The gap is that there is no natural stopping point in that work, because there is always a better version available.
Maximizer|Hardworking.ask: What tells you a piece of work is finished?

Maximizer|Honest.recognize: You will say out loud that something of yours is not good enough, which is rarer than saying it about someone else's. The risk is that the same honesty aimed outward has no volume control, and a passing observation from you gets treated as a ruling.
Maximizer|Honest.ask: What offhand comment of yours did someone take as final?

Maximizer|Honest and Direct.recognize: You say where the bar is and where the work currently sits, without softening the distance between the two. What you underestimate is that naming a gap out loud makes it the room's business, and the person now has an audience for their progress.
Maximizer|Honest and Direct.ask: Who is improving in public because of something you said?

Maximizer|Idealistic.recognize: You are chasing the finest possible version of things twice over, so nothing you touch is ever allowed to be merely fine. What is missing is any voice arguing for good enough. With both instincts pointing the same direction, the distance between what is and what could be never closes, and you live inside it.
Maximizer|Idealistic.ask: What would you have to accept for something to be finished?

Maximizer|Imaginative.recognize: You can see the better version in detail, which is exactly what lets you steer toward it rather than guess at it. The cost is that the vivid one in your head competes with the workable one in front of you, and the workable one usually loses.
Maximizer|Imaginative.ask: What did you abandon because you could see something better?

Maximizer|Independent.recognize: You set your own bar rather than taking the one on offer, and yours is higher, so you produce strong work without anyone having to demand it. The gap is that a bar nobody else agreed to is a bar nobody else is held to, and you end up carrying the quality alone.
Maximizer|Independent.ask: Who else is responsible for how good this is?

Maximizer|Informed.recognize: You follow what the best in your field are doing right now, so your sense of the bar comes from the frontier rather than from the room you are standing in. The cost is that the room you are standing in is where the work happens, and a standard set elsewhere can be impossible here.
Maximizer|Informed.ask: Is your bar set by this place or by somewhere else?

Maximizer|Insightful.recognize: You get to the one change that would most improve a situation while others are still listing ten. The risk is that the single change you name is so obviously right that it makes the other nine feel worthless, including to the people who offered them.
Maximizer|Insightful.ask: Whose contribution did you make irrelevant this week?

Maximizer|Kind and Encouraging.recognize: You tell people what their strongest quality is and they believe you, because you are not someone who hands out praise loosely. The gap is that praise from a high bar is scarce by design, and the people who never hear it conclude something you did not mean.
Maximizer|Kind and Encouraging.ask: Who has never heard you say anything good about them?

Maximizer|Knowledgeable.recognize: You have deep command of your subject and can tell a strong argument from a merely plausible one immediately. The cost is that the same discrimination applied to people sorts them fast, and a sorting done at first contact rarely gets revisited.
Maximizer|Knowledgeable.ask: Who did you write off in the first conversation?

Maximizer|Loyal, Patient, and Reliable.recognize: You will remain with a person or a project for years to bring it to its best, and that patience is what makes the difference achievable at all. The risk is that the same patience keeps you inside something whose ceiling you privately recognized a long time ago.
Maximizer|Loyal, Patient, and Reliable.ask: What have you privately written off but not left?

Maximizer|Observant.recognize: You notice the difference between the good version and the very good one from across the room, without needing to be told what to look for. The gap is that noticing constantly is not free, and you are never quite off duty around anyone's work, including your own.
Maximizer|Observant.ask: When were you last around work you were not assessing?

Maximizer|Open-Minded.recognize: You will take a better idea from anywhere, including from people who outrank nobody, because what matters to you is whether it is strong. The cost is that a mind willing to be moved by quality gets moved often, and the team behind you experiences that as the target shifting again.
Maximizer|Open-Minded.ask: How many times has the target moved this quarter?

Maximizer|Organized and Effective.recognize: You have a repeatable way of getting things to a high level, so quality is not an accident of mood in your work. The gap is that a process built around your own taste produces your kind of good over and over, and a team following it cannot produce theirs.
Maximizer|Organized and Effective.ask: What would this look like if someone else set the criteria?

Maximizer|Original.recognize: You want the best version and you want it to be yours, so you rarely settle for the strongest option already on the table. The cost is that rejecting a proven approach in favor of your own means paying again for lessons other people already paid for.
Maximizer|Original.ask: What did you rebuild that already worked somewhere else?

Maximizer|Passionate.recognize: You care intensely about the distance between good and great, and that intensity is what carries a project through its unglamorous middle. The risk is that the same heat makes ordinary work feel like a personal affront, and people learn to keep their rough drafts away from you.
Maximizer|Passionate.ask: Who stopped showing you unfinished work?

Maximizer|Perceptive.recognize: You can tell what someone is capable of at their best from very little evidence, and you are usually correct. The gap is that a fast estimate of potential also produces a fast estimate of limit, and the second one is much harder for anyone to escape.
Maximizer|Perceptive.ask: Whose ceiling did you assign, and when?

Maximizer|Positive and Enthusiastic.recognize: You make the climb toward a higher bar feel exciting rather than punishing, so people go further with you than they would have alone. The cost is that your optimism about how good this could get can outrun their sense of how much work that actually is.
Maximizer|Positive and Enthusiastic.ask: Do they know what you are asking of them?

Maximizer|Principled.recognize: You hold a high bar as a matter of principle, so quality and rightness have fused into one thing for you. What goes missing is the middle. Work that is acceptable without being the best does not just dissatisfy you, it feels wrong, which is a heavy thing to hand someone.
Maximizer|Principled.ask: Is ordinary work actually a moral failing?

Maximizer|Proactive Initiative.recognize: You start improving something before anyone asks, and by the time it comes up for discussion you have already taken it up a level. The exposure is that unrequested improvement changes what other people were planning around, and they find out after the fact.
Maximizer|Proactive Initiative.ask: Who had to replan because you got there first?

Maximizer|Quick Thinkers.recognize: You can tell almost instantly whether something is strong or merely adequate, and that judgement saves everyone weeks. The risk is that an instant verdict feels like a considered one from the inside, and you rarely go back to check the ones you made in a hurry.
Maximizer|Quick Thinkers.ask: Which snap judgement have you never revisited?

Maximizer|Rational.recognize: You can explain exactly why one version is better than another, so your preferences hold up as arguments rather than as taste. The gap is that a preference dressed as an argument is very hard to overturn, and people stop trying long before you would have been wrong.
Maximizer|Rational.ask: Has anyone ever won an argument with you about what is good?

Maximizer|Rational and Practical.recognize: You aim your improvement at the part that actually matters, so you do not gold-plate things nobody touches. The cost is that what counts as mattering is your call, and a detail that is invisible to you can be the whole thing to whoever relies on it.
Maximizer|Rational and Practical.ask: What looked like waste to you and was not?

Maximizer|Receptive.recognize: You will let a better idea in from anywhere, which is unusual in someone with strong opinions about quality. The gap is that being persuadable about the how while immovable about the bar means people can influence your methods and never your expectations.
Maximizer|Receptive.ask: Has anyone ever talked you down from a bar you had set?

Maximizer|Reliable.recognize: Your work lands consistently at the top of the range, so people plan around it being good rather than hoping it will be. The cost is that the promise is now to yourself as much as to them, and you will give up a weekend rather than hand over something ordinary.
Maximizer|Reliable.ask: What have you given up to avoid handing over something ordinary?

Maximizer|Research-Oriented.recognize: You find out what the best actually do before you set your own bar, so your target is calibrated rather than invented. The risk is that there is always one more example to study, and studying the best is a comfortable substitute for competing with them.
Maximizer|Research-Oriented.ask: How long have you been studying instead of starting?

Maximizer|Results Oriented.recognize: You care about the end product being genuinely strong, not merely delivered, so your work holds up after the deadline passes. The gap is that the last stretch of quality and the deadline are usually in direct conflict, and you have a habit of choosing quality and paying for it privately.
Maximizer|Results Oriented.ask: What did that last piece of polish cost you?

Maximizer|Sensitive and Warm.recognize: You can hold someone to a high bar while making it obvious you are on their side, which is the only way a demanding standard ever gets accepted. The cost is that people work hard for you personally, and when you leave the bar leaves with you.
Maximizer|Sensitive and Warm.ask: Are they doing this for the work or for you?

Maximizer|Sensitive to Others.recognize: You notice when a correction is going to land badly and you time it accordingly, so your feedback gets heard instead of deflected. The gap is that timing a hard thing well can slide into never quite finding the right moment, and some assessments go unsaid for years.
Maximizer|Sensitive to Others.ask: What have you been waiting for the right moment to say?

Maximizer|Sociable.recognize: You are around a lot of people and you naturally sort them by what they are exceptional at, so you always know who to call. The risk is that a network organized by ability is a network where being ordinary means falling out of contact.
Maximizer|Sociable.ask: Who used to be in your circle and quietly is not?

Maximizer|Spontaneous.recognize: You will drop the plan when a better opportunity shows itself, and your instinct for which one is better is good. The cost is that everyone else was building on the plan, and the upgrade you grabbed cost them work they had already done.
Maximizer|Spontaneous.ask: Whose work did your last change throw away?

Maximizer|Strong Practical Skills.recognize: You can take a job all the way to a high finish yourself, so you rarely have to accept someone else's version of good enough. The gap is that doing it yourself is also how you avoid the harder work of getting somebody else up to that level.
Maximizer|Strong Practical Skills.ask: Who have you never trusted to do this well?

Maximizer|Strong Sense of Duty.recognize: You treat getting something to its best as a responsibility rather than a preference, so you will not quietly let a bar slip when nobody is looking. The cost is that duty and appetite feel identical from the inside, and you cannot tell which one is keeping you up.
Maximizer|Strong Sense of Duty.ask: Is this a requirement or a want?

Maximizer|Strong-willed.recognize: You hold your bar under pressure from people who would rather have it done than done well, and you usually win those arguments. The risk is that winning them repeatedly teaches you that opposition to your bar is always weakness, and sometimes it is information.

Maximizer|Supportive.recognize: You get behind what someone is strongest at rather than what they asked for help with, and that redirection is often the most useful thing anyone does for them. The gap is that it is still your read of their strength, and they may have wanted the other thing.
Maximizer|Supportive.ask: What did they ask you for that you did not give them?

Maximizer|Very Loyal.recognize: You are committed to the people and the work you rate highly, and that commitment is durable because it was earned rather than assumed. The cost is that regard granted on merit can be withdrawn on merit, and the people around you sense that the assessment is ongoing.
Maximizer|Very Loyal.ask: Does anyone close to you believe your regard is unconditional?

Maximizer|Very Responsible.recognize: You own the quality of what leaves your hands, so nothing goes out with your name on it that you are unwilling to be judged for. The gap is that owning your own quality quietly becomes owning everyone's, and you start rewriting work that was theirs to get wrong.
Maximizer|Very Responsible.ask: Whose mistake did you erase before anyone saw it?

Self-Assurance|Altruistic.recognize: You help people without needing them to confirm you were right to, so your generosity never arrives with a bill attached. The cost is that you also do not check, and help given out of your own certainty can be the help you wanted to give rather than the help they needed.
Self-Assurance|Altruistic.ask: When did you last ask someone what they actually wanted from you?

Self-Assurance|Analytical.recognize: You take a situation apart and then trust your own read of it, so you arrive at a position while others are still hedging. The gap is that the analysis and the certainty land together, so you never quite experience the moment where you could have been talked out of it.
Self-Assurance|Analytical.ask: What would it take for someone to move you off a position?

Self-Assurance|Bold.recognize: You back yourself and you act on it, both instincts pointing the same direction, so you take risks that would keep other people awake at night. What is absent is hesitation of any kind. Nothing in you argues for waiting, and the only brake available is an outcome that has already happened.
Self-Assurance|Bold.ask: What has ever made you slow down?

Self-Assurance|Calm and Practical.recognize: You stay level in a crisis because you trust your own judgment about what matters, so a room organizes itself around you without being asked to. The risk is that your composure reads as proof you are right, and nobody offers the correction they would have offered a visibly uncertain person.
Self-Assurance|Calm and Practical.ask: Whose correction have you not had in a long time?

Self-Assurance|Charismatic.recognize: You are believed before you have made your case, because certainty is more persuasive than argument. The cost is that you get agreement you did not earn, and you have no reliable way of telling which of your calls were actually good ones.
Self-Assurance|Charismatic.ask: Which of your recent calls has been genuinely tested?

Self-Assurance|Charming.recognize: You can hold an unpopular position without making enemies, which is a rare combination and it keeps rooms open to you. The gap is that pleasantness plus certainty means disagreement never quite reaches you, and you leave conversations believing you persuaded people who simply gave up.
Self-Assurance|Charming.ask: Who stopped arguing with you instead of agreeing with you?

Self-Assurance|Clear Communication.recognize: You say where you stand in terms nobody has to interpret, so no one is left guessing at your position or reading your mood for it. The risk is that an unhedged position from a certain person sounds like settled fact, and people build on it as though it were.
Self-Assurance|Clear Communication.ask: What have people treated as settled that was only your opinion?

Self-Assurance|Creative.recognize: You make what you think should exist rather than what you were told the market wanted, and you can sustain that through the years when nobody agrees. The cost is that the same self-trust turns feedback into noise, and some of it was signal.
Self-Assurance|Creative.ask: What criticism did you wave off that turned out to be accurate?

Self-Assurance|Curious.recognize: You ask questions freely because you are not worried about looking like you do not already have the answer, and that security lets you learn in public. The gap is that you take in what you find and still arrive where you were going, so the inquiry rarely changes the destination.
Self-Assurance|Curious.ask: When did something you found out actually change your mind?

Self-Assurance|Decisive Action.recognize: You trust your judgment and you act on it at once, doubled up, so a call that would take a group a month takes you a morning. What is absent is the pause between being sure and moving, and that pause is where most people discover they were wrong.
Self-Assurance|Decisive Action.ask: What usually lives in the gap between being sure and acting?

Self-Assurance|Dedicated.recognize: You stay with something for years on your own belief in it, without needing the encouragement most people require to keep going. The risk is that self-sustaining belief has no external check, and the quality that carries you through a hard patch also carries you through a dead end.
Self-Assurance|Dedicated.ask: Who would tell you if this was over?

Self-Assurance|Determined.recognize: You are sure you are right and you will not stop, and those two things reinforce each other into something close to immovable. What is missing is any inward argument. Certainty supplies the direction and stamina supplies the distance, and neither one asks whether the direction was good.
Self-Assurance|Determined.ask: Does anything exist that could turn you around?

Self-Assurance|Diligent and Observant.recognize: You spot the detail that matters and act on your own read of it rather than escalating for a second opinion. The gap is that small calls made alone accumulate, and by the time anyone reviews the work your judgment is baked into all of it.
Self-Assurance|Diligent and Observant.ask: Which small call of yours has nobody ever reviewed?

Self-Assurance|Direct.recognize: You state your position without hedging because you are not managing how it lands, and people always know where you are. The cost is that certainty plus a refusal to soften leaves no visible opening, and the person with a better idea reads the room and keeps it.
Self-Assurance|Direct.ask: How would somebody with a better idea get it to you?

Self-Assurance|Direct and Authentic.recognize: You will say what you actually think and stand behind it, so there is no daylight between the private and the public version of you. The risk is that openness from somebody this sure is not an invitation to respond, it is an announcement, and people receive it that way.
Self-Assurance|Direct and Authentic.ask: Was that a conversation or a statement?

Self-Assurance|Direct and Honest.recognize: You offer your assessment before being asked, and you are willing to be the only person in the room holding it. The gap is that an unrequested verdict from someone who does not doubt themselves closes a topic rather than opening one.
Self-Assurance|Direct and Honest.ask: What discussion did you end this week?

Self-Assurance|Disciplined.recognize: You built your own way of working and you keep to it regardless of what anyone around you does, which makes you productive and hard to disrupt. The cost is that a routine you chose and trust is one you will never audit, and it can outlive the conditions it was built for.
Self-Assurance|Disciplined.ask: What part of your routine has never been questioned?

Self-Assurance|Easygoing.recognize: You are unbothered by most things because you already trust how you will handle them, so pressure that flattens other people slides off you. The gap is that low anxiety plus high self-trust removes the discomfort that usually prompts a person to take a second look.
Self-Assurance|Easygoing.ask: What are you untroubled by that probably deserves a check?

Self-Assurance|Efficient Organizer.recognize: You cut a process down to what you judge necessary and you do it without convening anyone, so things get faster around you. The risk is that necessity was assessed by one person, and the step you removed was load-bearing for somebody whose job you have not done.
Self-Assurance|Efficient Organizer.ask: Whose work rests on the step you removed?

Self-Assurance|Empathetic.recognize: You read what someone is feeling and you trust that read enough to act on it, so you step in while others are still wondering whether they should. The cost is that a confident read of another person is still a read, and you rarely check it against what they would have said.
Self-Assurance|Empathetic.ask: When did you last ask instead of already knowing?

Self-Assurance|Energetic.recognize: You have both the certainty and the stamina to carry an idea a long way on your own steam, and you do not run out when the enthusiasm around you does. The gap is that a group that stopped believing can keep moving on your energy alone, and nobody has to admit it.
Self-Assurance|Energetic.ask: Is your team still with you, or just still moving?

Self-Assurance|Enjoy Creating Order.recognize: You put things in the order that makes sense to you and you do not negotiate it, so your environment works and works quickly. The risk is that a setup built from one person's certainty is legible to that person only, and everyone else is guessing at your logic.
Self-Assurance|Enjoy Creating Order.ask: Could anyone else run your setup tomorrow?

Self-Assurance|Enthusiastic.recognize: You are excited about what you are sure of, and that combination pulls people in hard because it looks like evidence. The cost is that your certainty and your excitement are indistinguishable from outside, so people cannot tell what you have tested from what you merely want.
Self-Assurance|Enthusiastic.ask: Which part of this have you actually tested?

Self-Assurance|Excellent Brainstormers.recognize: You put out ideas without worrying about which ones make you look foolish, so you produce far more of them than a cautious person would. The gap is that you also pick the winner yourself, immediately, and the selection is exactly where a second opinion would have paid.
Self-Assurance|Excellent Brainstormers.ask: Who chose the idea you are working on?

Self-Assurance|Excellent Communicators.recognize: You speak with an authority that comes from actually believing what you are saying, so audiences follow you further than the argument alone would take them. The cost is that fluency and certainty together are almost impossible to interrupt, and the room's best objection dies in somebody's throat.
Self-Assurance|Excellent Communicators.ask: When did someone last interrupt you with a good point?

Self-Assurance|Excellent Organizers.recognize: You set up how the work will run and you commit to it without a long consultation, so a team has a shape to operate in on day one. The gap is that a design nobody debated is a design nobody owns, and they will follow it without ever telling you where it fails.
Self-Assurance|Excellent Organizers.ask: Where is your setup failing that nobody has mentioned?

Self-Assurance|Excellent People Skills.recognize: You handle people well and you trust your instincts about them, so you can move through a difficult room without preparing for it. The risk is that a confident read of a person, formed quickly and never checked, becomes the version of them you deal with for years.
Self-Assurance|Excellent People Skills.ask: Who are you still treating as the person you first met?

Self-Assurance|Future Focused.recognize: You are sure about where things are heading and you act on that now rather than waiting for confirmation, which is why you are early to almost everything. The cost is that a forecast held with certainty stops behaving like a forecast, and you will not notice the moment it stops matching events.
Self-Assurance|Future Focused.ask: What would tell you your picture of the future is wrong?

Self-Assurance|Generous.recognize: You give freely because you are not anxious about running short, and that absence of fear makes you more generous than more careful people manage to be. The gap is that confidence about your own resources is not the same as having them, and you tend to find the floor by hitting it.
Self-Assurance|Generous.ask: Do you know what is actually left?

Self-Assurance|Good Practical Skills.recognize: You can make the thing yourself and you have no doubt that you can, so you start where other people would hire someone. The risk is that certainty about your own ability is hardest to correct in exactly the areas where nobody has ever formally checked your work.
Self-Assurance|Good Practical Skills.ask: Where has your work never been inspected by someone who knew better?

Self-Assurance|Good at Connecting with O.recognize: You put people together on your own judgment about who should meet, and you are right often enough that a name from you carries weight. The cost is that your verdict on a person travels with them, and a quiet reservation of yours can follow someone into rooms they never enter.
Self-Assurance|Good at Connecting with O.ask: Whose reputation are you carrying without their knowledge?

Self-Assurance|Good-Natured and Positive.recognize: You are warm and sure of yourself at the same time, so people find you easy to be around and easy to believe. The gap is that good humor plus certainty can make a serious disagreement feel like a mood problem, and the person raising it ends up apologizing to you.
Self-Assurance|Good-Natured and Positive.ask: Who apologized for disagreeing with you?

Self-Assurance|Grounded.recognize: You are settled in yourself and immovable under pressure, both at once, so almost nothing from outside can shift you. What is missing is any inward wobble. With no counterweight, being unshakeable feels exactly the same whether you are standing on something solid or merely standing.
Self-Assurance|Grounded.ask: Is the ground under you solid, or only familiar?

Self-Assurance|Hands-on and Observant.recognize: You see it and your hands are on it, with no interval for a second opinion, because you already trust the judgment behind the reflex. The risk is that speed and certainty together remove both of the places where an error usually gets caught.
Self-Assurance|Hands-on and Observant.ask: What did you do before anyone could question it?

Self-Assurance|Handy and Resourceful.recognize: You will invent a way through with whatever is around, because it does not occur to you that there might not be one. The cost is that a workaround built on self-belief gets treated as solved, and nobody ever goes back to check whether it held.
Self-Assurance|Handy and Resourceful.ask: What did you get around that you never actually fixed?

Self-Assurance|Hardworking.recognize: You will put in the hours without needing anyone to notice, because your sense of whether it was worth it comes from inside you. The gap is that no external measure means no external stop, and you can spend years on something only you have ever evaluated.
Self-Assurance|Hardworking.ask: Who besides you has ever judged this worth doing?

Self-Assurance|Honest.recognize: You will own a mistake plainly, without the long defensive preamble, because being wrong once does not shake your sense of yourself. The risk is that recovering from error so easily means the error costs you nothing, and lessons that cost nothing rarely stick.
Self-Assurance|Honest.ask: What has a mistake of yours actually changed about how you work?

Self-Assurance|Honest and Direct.recognize: You say the hard thing outright and you carry the weight of having said it without needing reassurance afterward. The cost is that the other person is left holding all of the discomfort, because none of it stayed with you.
Self-Assurance|Honest and Direct.ask: Who is still carrying something you said and put down?

Self-Assurance|Idealistic.recognize: You are certain about how things ought to be, and that certainty is what lets you pursue a vision through years of indifference. The gap is that a picture held this firmly stops being a goal and becomes a measure, and the people around you are being measured against something they never agreed to.
Self-Assurance|Idealistic.ask: Did anyone else sign up for your version of how this ought to go?

Self-Assurance|Imaginative.recognize: You can see something that does not exist and treat it as achievable, which is the combination that actually gets new things made. The cost is that certainty about an imagined thing feels identical to certainty about a proven one, and only one of them has evidence behind it.
Self-Assurance|Imaginative.ask: Which of these are you sure of because it worked, and which because you can see it?

Self-Assurance|Independent.recognize: You trust your own judgment and you answer to nobody about it, which is the same instinct twice, so you are unaccountable by design rather than by accident. What is missing is anyone with the standing to check you, and you did not remove them, you simply never appointed one.
Self-Assurance|Independent.ask: Who has ever had the right to overrule you?

Self-Assurance|Informed.recognize: You keep up with what is happening and you form your own view of it rather than adopting whatever reading is going around. The gap is that a private interpretation, held confidently and never argued out loud, can drift a long way from the facts without you noticing.
Self-Assurance|Informed.ask: When did you last say your read of things to someone who might push back?

Self-Assurance|Insightful.recognize: You get to the heart of something quickly and you trust the conclusion enough to act, so you are useful in exactly the moments where other people stall. The risk is that a fast insight and a wrong one feel the same from inside, and your confidence does not distinguish between them.
Self-Assurance|Insightful.ask: How do you tell a good instinct from a fast one?

Self-Assurance|Kind and Encouraging.recognize: You tell people they can do it and they believe you, because your certainty about them sounds like information rather than comfort. The cost is that your belief in someone can carry them past where they were ready to go, and the fall is longer for having been urged on.
Self-Assurance|Kind and Encouraging.ask: Who did you send further than they were ready to go?

Self-Assurance|Knowledgeable.recognize: You have real depth in your subject and you trust what you have learned, so you will hold a position against a whole room. The gap is that expertise and certainty compound, and the territory next to your subject feels just as clear to you when it is not.
Self-Assurance|Knowledgeable.ask: How far past your subject does your certainty travel?

Self-Assurance|Loyal, Patient, and Relia.recognize: You commit to people and to work for the long run, and your certainty is what makes that possible when there is no evidence yet that it will pay. The risk is that the same firmness applied to a person who has changed means you are loyal to a version of them that is gone.
Self-Assurance|Loyal, Patient, and Relia.ask: Are you committed to who they are or who they were?

Self-Assurance|Observant.recognize: You take in what is happening around you and reach your own verdict on it without needing to compare notes with anyone. The cost is that a conclusion formed alone and never spoken cannot be corrected, and you can be the only person in the building with the wrong picture.
Self-Assurance|Observant.ask: When did you last check your picture against somebody else's?

Self-Assurance|Open-Minded.recognize: You will consider an idea from anywhere without feeling threatened by it, because nothing anyone says destabilizes you. The gap is that being unthreatened is not the same as being movable, and people mistake your willingness to listen for a willingness to change.
Self-Assurance|Open-Minded.ask: When did listening last lead you to change something?

Self-Assurance|Organized and Effective.recognize: You have a way of running things that you settled on long ago and do not revisit, so almost nothing in your week is improvised. The gap is that a system you trust completely is a system you stopped testing, and it will fail quietly rather than obviously.
Self-Assurance|Organized and Effective.ask: What in your setup has not been examined in years?

Self-Assurance|Original.recognize: You take positions nobody else holds and you are comfortable being alone in them, which is where genuinely original work comes from. The cost is that comfort with isolation removes the signal isolation usually sends, and being the only one who thinks this stops meaning anything to you.
Self-Assurance|Original.ask: Does it ever concern you that nobody agrees?

Self-Assurance|Passionate.recognize: You care intensely and you are sure you are right to, so your commitment has none of the wobble that usually accompanies strong feeling. The risk is that certainty makes intensity permanent, and there is no natural point at which you would cool off and look again.
Self-Assurance|Passionate.ask: What would make you feel less strongly about this?

Self-Assurance|Perceptive.recognize: You pick up what is going on beneath the surface and you back your interpretation of it without second-guessing. The gap is that an unverified interpretation held confidently hardens into a fact about that person, and they never get told what they were accused of.
Self-Assurance|Perceptive.ask: What have you concluded about someone that you have never said to them?

Self-Assurance|Positive and Enthusiastic.recognize: You are optimistic and certain at once, so a group under strain will borrow your steadiness rather than sink. The cost is that people cannot separate your assessment from your temperament, and they take your confidence as evidence about the situation when it is evidence about you.
Self-Assurance|Positive and Enthusiastic.ask: Is it going well, or are you simply not worried?

Self-Assurance|Principled.recognize: You are sure of what is right and you will hold that line without needing anyone to agree, which makes you genuinely incorruptible. The risk is that certainty about a principle and certainty about your reading of a situation feel identical from inside, and only the first one has earned that weight.
Self-Assurance|Principled.ask: Is this a principle, or is this your reading of the facts?

Self-Assurance|Proactive Initiative.recognize: You start before you are asked because you already trust your judgment about what needs doing, so things are underway while others are still coordinating. The gap is that acting first also settles the question first, and the discussion that would have happened does not.
Self-Assurance|Proactive Initiative.ask: What conversation did your head start prevent?

Self-Assurance|Quick Thinkers.recognize: You form a view fast and you are willing to say it immediately, which makes you formidable in a live argument. The cost is that a position you arrive at in three seconds is one you will defend for three years, because you have never had cause to distrust the process.
Self-Assurance|Quick Thinkers.ask: Which of your positions was formed in under a minute?

Self-Assurance|Rational.recognize: You work things out for yourself and you trust the conclusion because you can see exactly how you got there. The gap is that a chain you built alone has no independent check, and one wrong premise early produces a very confident answer at the end.
Self-Assurance|Rational.ask: What early assumption is all of this resting on?

Self-Assurance|Rational and Practical.recognize: You cut to what will actually work and you back your own call about it rather than convening a group. The risk is that what works is judged against your picture of the problem, and that picture has never been challenged by somebody living inside it.
Self-Assurance|Rational and Practical.ask: Who experiences this problem differently than you do?

Self-Assurance|Receptive.recognize: You will hear anyone out without feeling any pressure from what they say, so people find you approachable in a way certain people usually are not. The gap is that listening with no risk of being changed is not quite listening, and eventually people work that out.
Self-Assurance|Receptive.ask: What did somebody tell you recently that cost you something to hear?

Self-Assurance|Reliable.recognize: You do what you said you would without the reassurance most people need along the way, so your word holds under conditions where others would renegotiate. The cost is that you will honor a commitment long past the point where it made sense, because reopening it would feel like wavering.
Self-Assurance|Reliable.ask: Which promise are you honoring that should have been renegotiated?

Self-Assurance|Research-Oriented.recognize: You will look into something properly and then commit to what you found, without the endless hedging that usually follows research. The risk is that you stop looking at the point where the answer matched what you already thought, and that point arrives early.
Self-Assurance|Research-Oriented.ask: What did you stop researching once it started agreeing with you?

Self-Assurance|Results Oriented.recognize: You are certain what success looks like here and you drive at it without renegotiating the definition halfway, which is why things actually complete around you. The gap is that the definition was yours from the start, and a result nobody else chose can be delivered perfectly and still be the wrong one.
Self-Assurance|Results Oriented.ask: Who else agreed on what winning looks like here?

Self-Assurance|Sensitive and Warm.recognize: You are personally warm and internally certain, so people feel cared for by somebody who is clearly not going to fall apart. The cost is that your care and your verdicts come from the same place, and a person who has your affection cannot easily tell when you have quietly judged them.
Self-Assurance|Sensitive and Warm.ask: Who is closest to you and least sure where they stand?

Self-Assurance|Sensitive to Others.recognize: You notice how things land on people and you factor that in, but you do it without letting it move what you actually think. The gap is that adapting the delivery while never adapting the position teaches people that being heard by you and being answered by you are two separate events.
Self-Assurance|Sensitive to Others.ask: Do people leave you feeling answered or just heard?

Self-Assurance|Sociable.recognize: You are at ease in any room because you do not need it to like you, which is exactly why rooms tend to. The risk is that not needing approval also means not registering disapproval, and you can lose somebody's regard without ever noticing it go.
Self-Assurance|Sociable.ask: Who cooled on you, and when did you find out?

Self-Assurance|Spontaneous.recognize: You act in the moment because you trust yourself to handle whatever follows, so opportunities that require an instant answer come to you. The cost is that self-trust converts a gamble into a certainty in your own memory, and you rarely account for how much of the good outcome was luck.
Self-Assurance|Spontaneous.ask: How much of that was actually luck?

Self-Assurance|Strong Practical Skills.recognize: You take on almost anything practical without pausing, because you have never yet found the edge of what you can do. The gap is that not having found the edge is not the same as there not being one, and you will discover it while something heavy is already in the air.
Self-Assurance|Strong Practical Skills.ask: What are you assuming you could take on that you have never actually done?

Self-Assurance|Strong Sense of Duty.recognize: You take on what is yours to do and you need nobody checking that you are doing it, which makes you unusually trustworthy with things nobody is watching. The cost is that you also define what is yours, and that definition has never been negotiated with the people it lands on.
Self-Assurance|Strong Sense of Duty.ask: Whose call was it that this belongs to you?

Self-Assurance|Strong-willed.recognize: You are certain and you are unyielding, which is the same instinct arriving twice, so pressure that would redirect most people simply confirms you instead. What is absent is any inward brake. Nothing in this pairing generates doubt, and doubt is the only thing that ever makes a person look again.
Self-Assurance|Strong-willed.ask: What was the last thing you doubted?

Self-Assurance|Supportive.recognize: You get behind people with a certainty about them that they often do not have about themselves, and that transfers. The cost is that your assessment of somebody becomes the thing they rely on, and if you are wrong about them they will find out much later than they should have.
Self-Assurance|Supportive.ask: Whose confidence in themselves is actually just yours?

Self-Assurance|Very Loyal.recognize: You commit to people completely and you do not waver when others do, so the people you are for have something rare. The risk is that certainty about a person makes evidence about them hard to take in, and you will be the last one told.
Self-Assurance|Very Loyal.ask: What do others know about someone close to you that you would refuse to hear?

Self-Assurance|Very Responsible.recognize: You take on what you commit to and carry it without supervision, because your own judgment is enough of a check for you. The gap is that a person who supervises themselves has set both the task and the passing mark, and nobody else has ever seen either one.
Self-Assurance|Very Responsible.ask: Who else has ever seen the mark you hold yourself to?

Significance|Altruistic.recognize: You want your life to count for something, and you have chosen to make it count by giving, which is a better answer than most people arrive at. The cost is that generosity aimed partly at mattering needs a witness, and the help nobody sees is the help you find hardest to keep offering.
Significance|Altruistic.ask: Which of your good deeds has no witness?

Significance|Analytical.recognize: You want your work taken seriously, so you make sure it can survive being pulled apart, which is why your arguments hold up. The gap is that rigor pursued for standing rather than for truth stops early, right at the point where the case has already become persuasive.
Significance|Analytical.ask: What have you left unexamined because the argument already worked?

Significance|Bold.recognize: You take on things at a scale most people would not attempt, and the size of the attempt is part of the point for you. The cost is that a smaller, quieter version of the same work would have helped just as many people, and you would not have wanted it.
Significance|Bold.ask: Would you still do this if it were small?

Significance|Calm and Practical.recognize: You want to matter and you carry that without any visible hunger, so people experience you as substantial rather than striving. The gap is that the wanting is still there, running quietly beneath everything, and nobody around you can help with something they cannot see.
Significance|Calm and Practical.ask: Where does the wanting go when you keep it out of sight?

Significance|Charismatic.recognize: You draw a room and you want the room, and that combination puts you in front of people early and often. The risk is that being compelling and being right get rewarded identically in a room, so you receive no feedback on which of the two you brought.
Significance|Charismatic.ask: When were you last told you were wrong by someone who admired you?

Significance|Charming.recognize: You can make an ambitious move look like a favor to everyone involved, which is why your rise has been smoother than most. The cost is that a want you never state cannot be refused, and the people helping you have not been told what they are helping with.
Significance|Charming.ask: Do the people around you know what you are aiming at?

Significance|Clear Communication.recognize: You can make what you are doing sound consequential in a single sentence, so your work gets notice that better work often does not. The gap is that the sentence is much easier to improve than the work, and you will feel the pull to keep improving the sentence.
Significance|Clear Communication.ask: Which is further along, the project or the way you describe it?

Significance|Creative.recognize: You make things you want to be known for, and that ambition is what keeps you at the difficult part long after the enjoyable part ended. The cost is that an audience in your head during the making changes what gets made, usually toward whatever you expect to be admired.
Significance|Creative.ask: What would you make if it could never be shown to anyone?

Significance|Curious.recognize: You are drawn to questions that matter rather than ones that merely interest you, so your attention lands on things with consequence attached. The gap is that a question's importance and your appetite for it get tangled, and you can lose track of which one is pulling.
Significance|Curious.ask: Would this still fascinate you if it were unimportant?

Significance|Decisive Action.recognize: You sign on fast to the things you judge worth being associated with, so you are in position before an opportunity is obvious to anyone else. The risk is that the speed is partly a fear of missing the important one, and fear chooses differently than judgment does.
Significance|Decisive Action.ask: Was that a choice, or a fear of being left out of it?

Significance|Dedicated.recognize: You will stay with something for a decade because you want it to amount to something lasting, and that horizon is the reason it might. The cost is that work tied to a legacy is very hard to abandon, even once you can see it will not turn out to be the thing.
Significance|Dedicated.ask: What would it take for you to walk away from this?

Significance|Determined.recognize: You want to matter and you have the stamina to keep going until you do, which is why you outlast people who wanted it just as badly. The gap is that a goal defined by recognition has no finish line inside it, and stamina without a finish line is only a longer road.
Significance|Determined.ask: How will you know when you have arrived?

Significance|Diligent and Observant.recognize: You do the small things properly because you understand that credibility gets built out of details nobody thanks you for. The risk is that the same care aimed at how you are perceived becomes constant monitoring, and you register every small shift in how a room treats you.
Significance|Diligent and Observant.ask: How much of your day goes to tracking how you are seen?

Significance|Direct.recognize: You say your piece plainly and you want it on the record, so your contributions are hard to overlook or reassign to someone else. The cost is that candor in the service of being noticed sounds different from candor in the service of the truth, and people hear the difference before you do.
Significance|Direct.ask: Did that need to be said, or did it need to be said by you?

Significance|Direct and Authentic.recognize: You share the unpolished version of yourself, and that openness makes people trust you far faster than they otherwise would. The gap is that vulnerability offered in front of an audience is still a performance, and you may not be able to tell from inside which one you are doing.
Significance|Direct and Authentic.ask: Would you have said that with nobody watching?

Significance|Direct and Honest.recognize: You offer the honest assessment before anyone asks, and being the person who says it is part of what you are after. The cost is that truth-teller is a role in a room, and holding a role changes what you find yourself saying.
Significance|Direct and Honest.ask: What have you said mainly because it was yours to say?

Significance|Disciplined.recognize: You have built the habits that make a large ambition survivable, so your output is steady rather than dependent on how inspired you feel. The gap is that a routine designed around a distant goal makes today permanently instrumental, and you have not had an ordinary week in years.
Significance|Disciplined.ask: When did you last do something that was not for anything?

Significance|Easygoing.recognize: You want a large life and you carry that lightly, which spares you the grinding anxiety usually attached to it. The risk is that ambition without urgency can sit unexamined for a very long time, and you may be waiting to be discovered rather than working.
Significance|Easygoing.ask: Are you building toward this or waiting for it?

Significance|Efficient Organizer.recognize: You cut out whatever does not take you toward something consequential, so very little of your time goes to the merely pleasant. The cost is that some of what you removed was the part of a life that was never supposed to be productive.
Significance|Efficient Organizer.ask: What did you cut out because it led nowhere?

Significance|Empathetic.recognize: You can feel what people need and you want to be the one who provides it, which makes you far more motivated to actually help than to sympathize. The gap is that help given partly in order to matter to someone creates a debt neither of you will name.
Significance|Empathetic.ask: Who owes you something you would never admit to wanting?

Significance|Energetic.recognize: You have the drive to pursue something large and the stamina to sustain the pursuit, so you cover ground that would flatten other people. The risk is that the energy is partly borrowed from the wanting, and the wanting does not stop when your body needs it to.
Significance|Energetic.ask: What are the quiet stretches like for you?

Significance|Enjoy Creating Order.recognize: You put your surroundings in order because someone doing consequential work ought to look like it, and the order genuinely does help. The cost is that the appearance and the substance get maintained by the same effort, and only one of them is the actual work.
Significance|Enjoy Creating Order.ask: Which parts of this exist for an audience?
