Connectedness|Direct and Honest.recognize: You will name what you think a situation actually means, unprompted, and often you are right in a way that changes the room. The gap is that an unrequested interpretation of somebody's life is a large thing to hand them, and they may not have been asking what it meant.
Connectedness|Direct and Honest.ask: Who wanted help and got an interpretation?

Connectedness|Disciplined.recognize: You have practices that keep you alert to the larger picture, so your sense of it is tended rather than occasional. The cost is that a discipline built around meaning will keep producing meaning, including in the weeks when nothing much was happening.
Connectedness|Disciplined.ask: What did you find significance in during a week that was only a week?

Connectedness|Easygoing.recognize: You are unworried about outcomes because you trust that things resolve the way they are supposed to, which spares you a great deal of the anxiety other people carry. The gap is that the same trust removes urgency, and some things do not resolve unless somebody is urgent about them.
Connectedness|Easygoing.ask: What is waiting on somebody to be urgent?

Connectedness|Efficient Organizer.recognize: You can see which parts of a system genuinely depend on each other, so what you remove is truly surplus rather than merely invisible to you. The cost is that seeing everything as interdependent makes removing anything feel consequential, and you may leave things in place out of a sense of relatedness rather than need.
Connectedness|Efficient Organizer.ask: What are you keeping because it is attached to something?

Connectedness|Empathetic.recognize: You feel what other people feel and you understand that as part of something shared rather than as an intrusion, so being affected by others does not distress you. The gap is that somebody who experiences separateness as an illusion has very little defense, and other people's states arrive without a border.
Connectedness|Empathetic.ask: Where do you end and they begin?

Connectedness|Energetic.recognize: You have real drive and it is fed by a sense that the work belongs to something larger, so your energy does not depend on visible progress. The cost is that energy sourced from meaning does not respond to tiredness, and your body is not part of the framework.
Connectedness|Energetic.ask: What is your body saying that you have been reading as something else?

Connectedness|Enjoy Creating Order.recognize: You lay things out so the relationships between them become visible, which is a rarer kind of order than mere neatness. The gap is that a layout expressing how you see things fit becomes hard to alter, because altering it would mean the picture was wrong.
Connectedness|Enjoy Creating Order.ask: What would you have to admit if this were done differently?

Connectedness|Enthusiastic.recognize: You get excited about how things come together, and that excitement carries because it is about something bigger than the project itself. The cost is that enthusiasm rooted in meaning does not survive the meaning being questioned, and a practical objection can feel like an attack on the whole picture.
Connectedness|Enthusiastic.ask: How do you take it when somebody says this is only a project?

Connectedness|Excellent Brainstormers.recognize: You come up with ideas by seeing how distant things relate, so what you offer is unlike what a linear thinker would suggest. The gap is that a mind joining anything to anything will join some things that should stay apart, and the odd idea and the bad one look identical on arrival.
Connectedness|Excellent Brainstormers.ask: Which joins have you made that went nowhere?

Connectedness|Excellent Communicators.recognize: You can put a large pattern into words people are able to hold, which is why what you see does not stay locked inside you. The cost is that a well-told framework spreads faster than it can be checked, and you may hear your own reading come back to you as established fact.
Connectedness|Excellent Communicators.ask: Where did that idea come from before you said it?

Connectedness|Excellent Organizers.recognize: You can see how the parts of an enterprise actually relate and you can put that into a working shape, so what you set up reflects real dependencies. The gap is that a design expressing a deeper order is hard to revise, because changing it means the order was misread.
Connectedness|Excellent Organizers.ask: What in your design has never been revised?

Connectedness|Excellent People Skills.recognize: You are good with people and you see each of them as part of a larger picture, so nobody in your orbit gets treated as incidental. The cost is that a person given a place in your picture is hard to release from it, and they may have outgrown the role you see them in.
Connectedness|Excellent People Skills.ask: Has anyone outgrown the place you gave them?

Connectedness|Future Focused.recognize: You sense where things are heading because you can feel how the pieces are moving together, so your reading of what comes rests on relationships rather than on extrapolation. The gap is that a felt sense of direction cannot be disproved, and being wrong about it does not register as being wrong.
Connectedness|Future Focused.ask: When was your sense of where this was going mistaken?

Connectedness|Generous.recognize: You give without keeping accounts, because you do not experience your resources as separate from anybody else's. The cost is that a person who cannot see the boundary cannot see the bottom either, and you will find your limit only by going past it.
Connectedness|Generous.ask: How would you know you had given too much?

Connectedness|Good Practical Skills.recognize: You work with your hands and you understand what you make as part of something larger, so the object and its purpose stay joined for you. The gap is that meaning invested in an object makes it hard to release, and you keep things long past their use because of what they stand for.
Connectedness|Good Practical Skills.ask: What are you holding onto for what it represents?

Connectedness|Good at Connecting with Ot.recognize: You bring people together and you understand those meetings as part of something already in motion, so your matchmaking carries a sense of rightness. What is absent is any test. Both halves treat a joining as meant, so a pairing that fails looks like a mystery rather than a mistake.
Connectedness|Good at Connecting with Ot.ask: Which of your matches simply did not work?

Connectedness|Good-Natured and Positive.recognize: You are warm and you carry a settled sense that things fit together, so people find being near you steadying rather than merely pleasant. The cost is that somebody who reads every event as part of a good design has trouble sitting with a person who has concluded otherwise.
Connectedness|Good-Natured and Positive.ask: Can you sit with somebody who has decided there is no design?

Connectedness|Grounded.recognize: You are rooted in something larger than your circumstances, so a bad year does not shake your sense of who you are. The gap is that meaning which survives everything also absorbs everything, and a genuinely wrong situation can be turned into part of the story instead of being left.
Connectedness|Grounded.ask: What did you make sense of instead of leaving?

Connectedness|Hands-on and Observant.recognize: You see what needs doing and you also see what it belongs to, so your practical help is never merely transactional. The cost is that moving quickly on a felt significance means you can step into something that was not yours to be part of.
Connectedness|Hands-on and Observant.ask: Whose situation did you enter because it felt meant?

Connectedness|Handy and Resourceful.recognize: You find a way through by seeing how the available pieces relate, which is why solutions occur to you that nobody was hunting for. The gap is that an unexpected resource turning up feels like confirmation, and you can read ordinary luck as a sign you are on the right road.
Connectedness|Handy and Resourceful.ask: What have you taken as confirmation that was only luck?

Connectedness|Hardworking.recognize: You work hard because you understand the labor as part of something that matters, so the hours have never felt like a sacrifice to you. The cost is that meaningful work has no natural ceiling, and nobody around you can tell your devotion apart from your exhaustion.
Connectedness|Hardworking.ask: Who could tell if this stopped being good for you?

Connectedness|Honest.recognize: You are candid about what you sense is going on beneath things, including when it does not reflect well on you. The gap is that an honest report of an intuition is still an intuition, and the honesty of the delivery lends it weight the content has not earned.
Connectedness|Honest.ask: How much of that was evidence?

Connectedness|Honest and Direct.recognize: You say what you believe a situation means without softening it, so people around you get your reading rather than a hedged version of it. The cost is that a firm word about what something means can settle a question for somebody who was still living inside it.

Connectedness|Idealistic.recognize: You believe things are moving toward something better and you can say why, so your hope has a shape rather than being merely temperamental. The gap is that a framework in which everything is heading somewhere good has no place to put an event that was simply bad.

Connectedness|Imaginative.recognize: You can see how things might join up in ways that do not exist yet, which is where genuinely new arrangements come from. The cost is that imagining a relationship and perceiving one feel identical from inside, and you cannot always tell which of the two you have done.
Connectedness|Imaginative.ask: Did you see that, or did you make it?

Connectedness|Independent.recognize: You go your own way while feeling part of something larger, so your independence has never made you lonely the way it makes other people. The gap is that a sense of belonging to everything can substitute for belonging to somebody, and you may have far fewer actual ties than you feel you do.
Connectedness|Independent.ask: Who would notice first if you disappeared?

Connectedness|Informed.recognize: You follow what is happening across a wide field and you see how the pieces bear on each other, so your picture is joined rather than a list of headlines. The cost is that a mind assembling everything into one picture fits new information into the existing shape, and the shape rarely gets rebuilt.
Connectedness|Informed.ask: When did new information last change your whole picture?

Connectedness|Insightful.recognize: You get to what a situation is really about by seeing what it belongs to, which is why your read goes deeper than the available facts. The gap is that depth arrived at this way cannot be shown to anybody, and people either accept it or you have nothing further to offer them.
Connectedness|Insightful.ask: What would you say to somebody who does not accept it?

Connectedness|Kind and Encouraging.recognize: You tell people their difficulty is part of something, and they find that steadying, because coming from you it is not a platitude. The cost is that meaning offered early can arrive well before somebody is ready to have their suffering explained to them.
Connectedness|Kind and Encouraging.ask: Who needed you to say nothing about why?

Connectedness|Knowledgeable.recognize: You have real depth and you can see how your field sits inside everything else, so what you have learned does not stay walled off from the rest. The gap is that a framework joining your subject to everything makes you feel qualified a good deal further out than you are.
Connectedness|Knowledgeable.ask: How far from your subject do you still speak with authority?

Connectedness|Loyal, Patient, and Reliab.recognize: You remain with people through a great deal, because you understand the relationship as something more than an arrangement. The cost is that a bond understood as meant is a bond you will not end, and you can outlast a situation that stopped being good for either of you.
Connectedness|Loyal, Patient, and Reliab.ask: Which relationship has outlasted its usefulness to both of you?

Connectedness|Observant.recognize: You notice what is happening and you notice what it echoes, so very little passes you as merely an event. The gap is that somebody who sees echoes everywhere will hear one in random noise, and you cannot tell the difference at the moment of noticing.
Connectedness|Observant.ask: What did you notice this week that was only noise?

Connectedness|Open-Minded.recognize: You will take in any account of how things fit, which is why your way of seeing has grown rather than hardened. The cost is that a mind willing to accommodate every explanation ends up with one that can absorb anything, and an idea explaining everything predicts nothing.
Connectedness|Open-Minded.ask: What could your way of seeing not explain?

Connectedness|Organized and Effective.recognize: You order your life around what you understand to be its larger purpose, so your calendar and your convictions are not separate documents. The gap is that a schedule built to serve a meaning is very hard to question, because questioning it means questioning the meaning.
Connectedness|Organized and Effective.ask: Which commitment would you hold even if the reason stopped applying?

Connectedness|Original.recognize: You see joins nobody else sees, so what you propose is unlike the standard answer and occasionally far better than it. The cost is that unusual and correct are separate things, and the same faculty in you produces both of them.
Connectedness|Original.ask: How do you tell your good unusual ideas from the rest?

Connectedness|Passionate.recognize: You care intensely because you experience what you are doing as part of something that matters beyond it, so your commitment has a depth other people's lacks. The gap is that intensity fused with meaning cannot be moderated, because moderating it would feel like caring less about the thing itself.
Connectedness|Passionate.ask: Could you care less about this without betraying it?

Connectedness|Perceptive.recognize: You sense what is beneath a situation and you sense what it is part of, the same faculty twice over, so almost nothing arrives at you as ordinary. What is missing is anything saying no. Neither half doubts a perception, so an impression becomes a fact without ever being examined.
Connectedness|Perceptive.ask: What have you perceived that was never checked?

Connectedness|Positive and Enthusiastic.recognize: You are hopeful because you trust the shape of things, so your optimism is not naive and people can feel it rests on something. The cost is that a hope grounded in meaning does not adjust to evidence, and it can carry you cheerfully through a situation that was deteriorating.
Connectedness|Positive and Enthusiastic.ask: What got worse while you stayed hopeful?

Connectedness|Principled.recognize: You hold your convictions as part of a larger order rather than as personal preferences, which is why they do not bend under social pressure. The gap is that a principle understood as woven into how things are cannot be revised, and some of yours were formed a very long time ago.
Connectedness|Principled.ask: Which of your convictions came from your twenties?

Connectedness|Proactive Initiative.recognize: You act when you sense the moment belongs to you, so you begin things other people are still waiting for permission on. The cost is that a felt sense of rightness about timing is not information, and you can start something at genuinely the wrong time with total confidence.
Connectedness|Proactive Initiative.ask: Is a sense of rightness about timing the same as good timing?

Connectedness|Quick Thinkers.recognize: You make the join fast, so you arrive at what something means while other people are still gathering the details. The gap is that a quick join is a join made on partial material, and arriving fast makes the conclusion feel more certain rather than less.
Connectedness|Quick Thinkers.ask: Which of your fast conclusions rested on very little?

Connectedness|Rational.recognize: You want your sense of how things fit to hold up under argument, so you do not simply assert what you feel. The cost is that a framework can be made internally consistent without being true, and rigor applied inward does not test it against anything outside.
Connectedness|Rational.ask: What outside your framework could show it wrong?

Connectedness|Rational and Practical.recognize: You keep your sense of the larger picture tied to what actually has to get done this week, so your meaning never floats free. The gap is that treating a purpose as practical makes it operational, and an operational purpose stops being examined and starts being executed.
Connectedness|Rational and Practical.ask: When did you last examine why you are doing this?

Connectedness|Receptive.recognize: You take in what comes and you understand it as having arrived for a reason, so nothing that happens to you is wasted. The cost is that an event understood as meant is an event you will not resist, and some of what arrives should be turned away.
Connectedness|Receptive.ask: Does everything that happens to you have to mean something?

Connectedness|Reliable.recognize: You do what you said because a promise belongs to a fabric rather than to a transaction, so your word holds without needing enforcement. The gap is that a commitment understood that way cannot be renegotiated, and you will carry an arrangement long after it became unreasonable.

Connectedness|Research-Oriented.recognize: You look for how findings relate to each other rather than collecting them, which is why you notice things that specialists miss. The cost is that a search for how things join will keep going until it finds one, and that search has no stopping rule built into it.
Connectedness|Research-Oriented.ask: When do you stop looking for the join?

Connectedness|Results Oriented.recognize: You get things done and you understand the work as serving something beyond the result, which spares you the emptiness that follows a delivered project. The gap is that a purpose this large cannot be completed, so nothing you deliver ever fully counts.
Connectedness|Results Oriented.ask: What have you completed that felt like enough?

Connectedness|Sensitive and Warm.recognize: You are tender with people and you carry a sense that their situation belongs to something bigger, so your comfort has substance rather than only good feeling. The cost is that placing somebody's pain inside a larger design is a claim about their life, and it is not always welcome.
Connectedness|Sensitive and Warm.ask: Who did not want their situation explained?

Connectedness|Sensitive to Others.recognize: You are careful with people because you feel how what you do travels outward well past them. The gap is that seeing every action as having far effects makes small decisions heavy, and you can be paralyzed by a choice that genuinely did not matter.
Connectedness|Sensitive to Others.ask: Which small decision are you making too large?

Connectedness|Sociable.recognize: You are among people often and you experience those gatherings as more than pleasant, so an ordinary evening can feel significant to you. The cost is that expecting significance from other people means a night that was only a night registers as a letdown.
Connectedness|Sociable.ask: When was an ordinary evening enough?

Connectedness|Spontaneous.recognize: You follow what arises because you trust it arose for a reason, so you take chances a more calculating person would let pass. The gap is that treating a sudden urge as a sign removes the one check you had, and nothing is left standing between wanting to and doing it.
Connectedness|Spontaneous.ask: What have you done because it felt meant?

Connectedness|Strong Practical Skills.recognize: You can take on a great deal and you understand the load as part of your place in something, so you rarely resent it. The cost is that a burden understood as yours by design will not be questioned, and nobody reassigns work that somebody has accepted as their purpose.
Connectedness|Strong Practical Skills.ask: What are you shouldering that was never actually assigned?

Connectedness|Strong Sense of Duty.recognize: You take what you owe seriously because you understand yourself as answerable to a larger whole, not merely to the person asking. The gap is that a duty owed to something abstract can never be discharged or renegotiated, and there is nobody with the authority to release you from it.
Connectedness|Strong Sense of Duty.ask: Who could ever tell you that you had done enough?

Connectedness|Strong-willed.recognize: You are immovable about what you believe because you experience it as more than an opinion, so pressure that shifts other people does not touch you. The cost is that a conviction held as part of how things are cannot lose an argument, and you may not have lost one in years.
Connectedness|Strong-willed.ask: When did you last genuinely lose an argument?

Connectedness|Supportive.recognize: You get behind people because you see their work as part of something you also serve, so your support does not depend on whether you like them. The gap is that help given for the sake of the larger thing can continue long after the person stopped deserving it.
Connectedness|Supportive.ask: Who are you supporting for the cause rather than for themselves?

Connectedness|Very Loyal.recognize: You are bound to your people in a way that has never needed a reason, because the bond itself is the reason. The cost is that a tie understood as given rather than chosen cannot be reconsidered, and you have never asked whether you would choose it now.
Connectedness|Very Loyal.ask: Would you choose these people again today?

Connectedness|Very Responsible.recognize: You take ownership of your part because you can see how much depends on it, so nothing gets dropped where you are standing. The gap is that seeing how everything depends on everything makes your part look infinite, and you end up responsible for outcomes far past what you touch.
Connectedness|Very Responsible.ask: How far past your own work does your sense of fault extend?

Developer|Altruistic.recognize: You see what someone could become and you spend yourself getting them there, so the people around you grow on your time and your energy. The cost is that giving and growing draw from the same account, and you rarely check the balance until you have nothing left for anyone.
Developer|Altruistic.ask: Who is drawing on you right now that you have not counted?

Developer|Analytical.recognize: You can see the growth in a person and also explain the mechanism behind it, which makes your encouragement specific enough to act on. The gap is that studying how someone develops can replace the slower work of walking beside them while they do it.
Developer|Analytical.ask: Which person have you diagnosed instead of accompanied?

Developer|Bold.recognize: You will tell someone to their face that they are capable of far more than they are attempting, and you will say it before they are ready to hear it. The cost is that a person can be talked into a room they have no skills for yet.
Developer|Bold.ask: Who did you promote in your head before they were ready?

Developer|Calm and Practical.recognize: You grow people at a steady temperature, never rushing them and never panicking when they stall, which is why slow starters do well with you. The gap is that some people need alarm to move, and your steadiness reads to them as permission to stay where they are.
Developer|Calm and Practical.ask: Who needed you to sound worried and never heard it?

Developer|Charismatic.recognize: You draw people in and then you actually invest in them, so the pull you have is not empty; it leads somewhere. The cost is that people come to you for the feeling of being believed in, and some of them will never do the work that belief was supposed to fund.
Developer|Charismatic.ask: Who enjoys your confidence in them without acting on it?

Developer|Charming.recognize: You make growth feel unthreatening, so people let you near the parts of themselves they are embarrassed about. The gap is that a comfortable conversation can substitute for a hard one, and the thing they most need to change is often the thing neither of you brings up.
Developer|Charming.ask: What have you never said to someone you are developing?

Developer|Clear Communication.recognize: You tell people exactly what you see in them, in words they can repeat back, which is why your feedback tends to stick. The cost is that a clean sentence about someone's growth can flatten a complicated person into a single storyline they then feel obliged to live out.
Developer|Clear Communication.ask: Who is living up to a description you gave them?

Developer|Creative.recognize: You find unusual ways to bring someone along, inventing the assignment or the challenge that fits this particular person rather than reaching for a standard plan. The gap is that a custom approach is hard to hand off, and your people grow attached to you rather than to the growing itself.
Developer|Creative.ask: Which of your people could keep developing without you?

Developer|Curious.recognize: You ask people questions about themselves that they have not been asked before, and the asking itself moves them forward. The cost is that your interest can outrun their readiness, and you go three layers deep with someone who came in for something small.
Developer|Curious.ask: Whose small question did you turn into a large one?

Developer|Decisive Action.recognize: You decide quickly that someone is worth backing and then you back them, which means your people feel chosen rather than evaluated. The gap is that an early call is still a call, and the person you did not pick in the first month rarely gets a second look.
Developer|Decisive Action.ask: Which first impression has never been updated?

Developer|Dedicated.recognize: You stay with people long past the point where others would have moved on, and some of your best stories are about someone who took years. The cost is that loyalty to a person's growth can outlast the evidence, and you keep pouring into someone who stopped showing up for it.
Developer|Dedicated.ask: Who have you kept investing in against the evidence?

Developer|Determined.recognize: You will not let someone quit on themselves, and your unwillingness to accept their low estimate of their own capacity is often what carries them. The gap is that determination applied to another person's life can become a contest you are trying to win rather than a gift you are giving.
Developer|Determined.ask: Whose growth have you turned into your own scoreboard?

Developer|Diligent and Observant.recognize: You notice the small improvement nobody else registered and you name it out loud, which is why people feel seen working for you. The cost is that the same eye finds every small failure, and a person can end up managed at a level of detail that shrinks them.
Developer|Diligent and Observant.ask: What have you corrected that you should have let go?

Developer|Direct.recognize: You tell people the hard thing about themselves because you believe they can handle it and grow from it, and most of them can. The gap is that you calibrate the delivery to what you would want, and some people need the same information arriving much more slowly.
Developer|Direct.ask: Who shut down after a conversation you thought went well?

Developer|Direct and Authentic.recognize: You use your own failures as teaching material, so the people you develop get the unedited version rather than a polished one. The cost is that your story becomes the template, and someone whose path looks nothing like yours may quietly conclude they are doing it wrong.
Developer|Direct and Authentic.ask: Who is trying to grow the way you grew?

Developer|Direct and Honest.recognize: You offer feedback nobody asked for because you would rather someone hear it from you than never hear it at all. The gap is that unrequested honesty about a person's capacity lands differently than unrequested honesty about their work, and the second kind is much easier to receive.
Developer|Direct and Honest.ask: Whose character did you assess when they only asked about their work?

Developer|Disciplined.recognize: You build growth into a routine, with regular check-ins that happen whether or not anyone feels like it, and that reliability is why progress actually accumulates. The cost is that development on a schedule can miss the moment someone was ready, which rarely arrives on the calendar.
Developer|Disciplined.ask: When did someone open up at the wrong time for you?

Developer|Easygoing.recognize: You let people grow at their own speed without pressure, which is exactly what some of them needed after years of being pushed. The gap is that low pressure and low expectation look identical from the outside, and a person can spend a long time comfortable with you and not much further along.
Developer|Easygoing.ask: Who has been comfortable with you for a year without changing?

Developer|Efficient Organizer.recognize: You find the shortest route to someone's next level and remove everything that is not moving them there, which saves people years. The cost is that some growth only happens in the wasted time, and the detours you cut out were where a person figured out who they were.
Developer|Efficient Organizer.ask: What have you optimized out of someone's development?

Developer|Empathetic.recognize: You feel where a person is before they say it, so you know when to press and when to wait, and that timing is most of the skill. The gap is that carrying their fear as your own makes you protect them from the discomfort that was going to be the growth.
Developer|Empathetic.ask: Who did you spare from something they needed?

Developer|Energetic.recognize: You bring so much drive to another person's growth that they borrow it, and people leave conversations with you willing to attempt things they were not willing to attempt an hour before. The cost is that borrowed drive runs out, and you are not always there when it does.
Developer|Energetic.ask: Who only moves when you are in the room?

Developer|Enjoy Creating Order.recognize: You give people a clear path with stages and milestones, which turns a vague ambition into something they can actually start on Monday. The gap is that a person is not a project, and the messiest, least sequential part of their growth is usually the part that matters.
Developer|Enjoy Creating Order.ask: What in their life does not fit your plan for them?

Developer|Enthusiastic.recognize: You get visibly excited about what someone could do, and that excitement is often the first time anyone has been enthusiastic about their future. The cost is that your intensity sets a pace, and a person can start performing growth for you rather than pursuing it for themselves.
Developer|Enthusiastic.ask: Who is growing to keep you happy?

Developer|Excellent Brainstormers.recognize: You can produce a dozen different ways forward for someone in a single sitting, so nobody leaves your office without options. The gap is that a person with twelve paths often takes none of them, and choosing was the hard part you just made harder.
Developer|Excellent Brainstormers.ask: Which option should you have taken off their table?

Developer|Excellent Communicators.recognize: You can describe someone's future back to them so vividly that they start believing it, and belief is truly most of what they were missing. The cost is that a compelling speaker fills the room, and the person whose life is being discussed may never get to say what they want.
Developer|Excellent Communicators.ask: When did they last describe their own future to you?

Developer|Excellent Organizers.recognize: You build the whole apparatus around a person's development, the mentor and the reading and the assignment, and it works because you actually maintain it. The gap is that a heavy system takes credit for the growth, and neither of you learns whether they would have made it alone.
Developer|Excellent Organizers.ask: How much of their progress is the scaffolding?

Developer|Excellent People Skills.recognize: You are easy to be developed by, because you make the whole thing feel like a friendship rather than an evaluation. The cost is that warmth makes the hard sentence harder to say, and you may have been putting off one specific conversation for months.
Developer|Excellent People Skills.ask: Which conversation have you been postponing?

Developer|Future Focused.recognize: You see where a person ends up in ten years and you start preparing them for it now, which is why your people are ready early. The gap is that they have not agreed to that future, and may want a much smaller life than the one you are building them for.
Developer|Future Focused.ask: Have they told you what they actually want?

Developer|Generous.recognize: You give away your time, your contacts, and your credit to people earlier in the journey than you, and you do it without keeping a ledger. The cost is that no ledger means no limit, and the people who ask most often are not always the people who would use it best.
Developer|Generous.ask: Who gets your time because they ask, not because it helps?

Developer|Good Practical Skills.recognize: You teach by handing someone the actual task and standing beside them while they do it badly the first time, which is how most skill is truly transferred. The gap is that you develop what can be demonstrated, and the parts of a person that cannot be practiced get less of your attention.
Developer|Good Practical Skills.ask: Which part of this job cannot be shown, only said?

Developer|Good at Connecting with Others.recognize: You grow people by putting them in front of the right person at the right time, and a single connection you made has changed several careers. The cost is that a network can substitute for the slower work, and being known by everyone is not the same as being ready.
Developer|Good at Connecting with Others.ask: Who did you put in front of someone before they were prepared?

Developer|Good-Natured and Positive.recognize: You make growing feel survivable, because you find the encouraging read on a setback faster than anyone. The gap is that a person needs to sit in a failure long enough to learn from it, and you tend to rescue them out of it within the hour.
Developer|Good-Natured and Positive.ask: What failure did you talk someone out of feeling?

Developer|Grounded.recognize: You keep a person steady while they grow, so they can take a serious risk knowing the floor stays where it is. The cost is that stability can become the ceiling too, and someone who needed to leave your orbit entirely may stay because staying is comfortable.
Developer|Grounded.ask: Who should have outgrown you by now?

Developer|Hands-on and Observant.recognize: You spot what someone needs and give it to them the same day, no meeting scheduled, no plan drafted, and that speed is why your feedback ever lands. The gap is that you respond to what is visible right now, and a slow-building problem in someone rarely announces itself in a moment.
Developer|Hands-on and Observant.ask: What has been quietly true about them for a year?

Developer|Handy and Resourceful.recognize: You develop people with whatever is available, turning a spare hour or an odd assignment into the thing that moves them. The cost is that growth assembled this way is uneven, and a person can end up with a strange collection of strengths and a gap nobody planned for.
Developer|Handy and Resourceful.ask: What obvious thing has this person never been taught?

Developer|Hardworking.recognize: You put in more hours on other people's growth than most put into their own, and it shows in how far your people get. The gap is that the hours you spend on them are hours not spent on you, and the person with the least development plan around here may be you.
Developer|Hardworking.ask: When did anyone last develop you?

Developer|Honest.recognize: You will tell someone the truth about their ceiling, which is rare and often kinder than the encouragement everyone else offers. The cost is that a ceiling you can see at this moment is not permanent, and a person told about theirs may stop testing it.
Developer|Honest.ask: Whose limit did you name too early?

Developer|Honest and Direct.recognize: You say plainly what someone must change, without softening it into a question, and people who want to grow find that a relief. The gap is that a plain statement about a person is heavier than one about a project, and it can be carried for years.
Developer|Honest and Direct.ask: Which sentence of yours is someone still carrying?

Developer|Idealistic.recognize: You hold a picture of who someone could be at their very best, and holding it is often the reason they reach for it. The cost is that the distance between that picture and the actual person is a distance they can feel, and some of them experience your hope as a standing verdict.
Developer|Idealistic.ask: Who feels measured against your version of them?

Developer|Imaginative.recognize: You can see a version of someone's life that does not exist yet and describe it well enough that they can see it too. The gap is that imagining a future costs nothing, and the unglamorous next step is the part that neither of you has scheduled.
Developer|Imaginative.ask: What is the very next thing they should do?

Developer|Independent.recognize: You grow people by giving them room and refusing to hover, which produces adults rather than dependents. The cost is that room and absence are hard to tell apart, and someone who was struggling may have read your restraint as a lack of interest.
Developer|Independent.ask: Who read your restraint as indifference?

Developer|Informed.recognize: You retain what each of your people is working on, what they struggled with last month, and what they said they wanted a year ago. The gap is that holding that much about someone can feel like surveillance to them, however kindly it is meant.
Developer|Informed.ask: What do you understand about them that they never told you?

Developer|Insightful.recognize: You see what is holding a person back faster than they do, sometimes in a first conversation, and naming it correctly can save them years. The cost is that arriving before they do means they never did the finding, and a conclusion handed over is easier to argue with.
Developer|Insightful.ask: What did you tell them that they needed to discover?

Developer|Kind and Encouraging.recognize: You are the voice people replay when they are about to give up, because you told them something true about themselves at a moment they could not see it. The gap is that protection is a habit, and there are hard facts about their situation you have decided they cannot handle yet.
Developer|Kind and Encouraging.ask: What are you keeping from them for their own good?

Developer|Knowledgeable.recognize: You have the reference, the example, and the person who solved this before, so nobody you develop has to start from nothing. The cost is that expertise wants to be dispensed, and a mentoring conversation can turn into a lecture with the other person nodding.
Developer|Knowledgeable.ask: How much of your last coaching conversation did you talk?

Developer|Loyal, Patient, and Reliable.recognize: You are still checking on people you stopped being responsible for a decade ago, and that consistency is why they still answer. The gap is that patience with someone's pace can quietly become tolerance of it, and there is a difference between waiting for growth and waiting instead of it.
Developer|Loyal, Patient, and Reliable.ask: Who have you been waiting on for too long?

Developer|Observant.recognize: You gather a lot about a person before you say anything, so when you finally speak it is accurate and it carries weight. The cost is that the gathering has no natural end, and someone can go a long stretch without hearing the thing you decided about them months ago.
Developer|Observant.ask: What conclusion have you reached and not shared?

Developer|Open-Minded.recognize: You take seriously the possibility that someone will grow in a direction you did not expect, which is why unusual people thrive near you. The gap is that holding every path as equally plausible gives a person no signal, and sometimes what they need is your opinion.
Developer|Open-Minded.ask: What do you actually think they should do?

Developer|Organized and Effective.recognize: You have a repeatable process for bringing someone along and it works, which is why you can develop many people at once instead of a favorite few. The cost is that a process assumes a starting point, and the person who arrives at an unusual angle gets fitted to it anyway.
Developer|Organized and Effective.ask: Who does not fit the way you usually do this?

Developer|Original.recognize: You develop people toward what is distinct about them rather than the standard version of the role, so your people do not resemble each other. The gap is that being unlike everyone else is expensive to maintain, and you may be asking someone to carry an identity they did not choose.
Developer|Original.ask: Whose uniqueness are you more invested in than they are?

Developer|Passionate.recognize: You care about someone's growth with an intensity that is uncomfortable to be near and impossible to fake, and people can tell the difference. The cost is that caring that hard about an outcome you do not control is a way to get hurt, and you have been hurt this way before.
Developer|Passionate.ask: Whose choices have cost you the most?

Developer|Perceptive.recognize: You pick up what a person is not saying about their own ambition, and you develop the thing they actually want rather than the thing they announced. The gap is that filling in what someone leaves unsaid means you are supplying it, and sometimes what you sense in them started in you.
Developer|Perceptive.ask: What did you want at their age?

Developer|Positive and Enthusiastic.recognize: You lift people into believing they can do the thing, and for many of them that belief was the only missing piece. The cost is that an upward push is your default response, and a person who came to tell you something is going badly may leave without having said it.
Developer|Positive and Enthusiastic.ask: Who tried to tell you bad news and got encouraged instead?

Developer|Principled.recognize: You develop character alongside capability, so the people you bring up are not just more skilled but more trustworthy. The gap is that a moral failing reads to you as a different category of problem than a skill gap, and the person who fell short that way may not get a second season with you.
Developer|Principled.ask: Who lost your investment over a failure of character?

Developer|Proactive Initiative.recognize: You start developing someone before anyone asks you to, often before they realize they are being developed, and by the time it is official you are a year in. The cost is that unasked-for investment creates an obligation the other person never agreed to carry.
Developer|Proactive Initiative.ask: Who owes you something they never agreed to?

Developer|Quick Thinkers.recognize: You can turn an offhand comment into a growth conversation in the moment it happens, which means you catch people while they are still open. The gap is that a quick answer is a first answer, and your instinct about what someone needs has not been checked against anything.
Developer|Quick Thinkers.ask: Which of your reads on someone has never been tested?

Developer|Rational.recognize: You can lay out exactly why a person should make a particular move, and the argument is usually right. The cost is that people do not grow because the case is sound; they grow when something in them shifts, and you have less patience for that part.
Developer|Rational.ask: Where did being right fail to move anyone?

Developer|Rational and Practical.recognize: You develop people toward what will actually be needed, not toward an abstract profile, so your investment tends to pay off visibly. The gap is that a person is being formed for more than what the organization requires from them, and that part gets less of your attention.
Developer|Rational and Practical.ask: What in them is worth growing even if it never pays off?

Developer|Receptive.recognize: You are willing to be wrong about someone, which means people can correct your picture of them and you will actually update it. The cost is that a person's own account of themselves is not always the most accurate one, and you tend to defer to it.

Developer|Reliable.recognize: You show up for the standing conversation every time, and that predictability is what lets someone bring you the thing they are ashamed of. The gap is that the number of people you have promised this to grows every year, and you have never once told anyone you were at capacity.
Developer|Reliable.ask: How many of these commitments can you actually hold?

Developer|Research-Oriented.recognize: You look for proof that an approach to developing someone actually works rather than repeating what was done to you, and your people benefit from that rigor. The cost is that a person in front of you is a sample of one, and waiting for certainty can cost them the season they needed you in.
Developer|Research-Oriented.ask: What are you still deciding about someone who needed you last month?

Developer|Results Oriented.recognize: You measure your investment in people by what they go on to accomplish, which keeps your mentoring honest and stops it becoming a nice conversation that changes nothing. The gap is that some people you pour into will not produce anything visible, and their growth was true anyway.
Developer|Results Oriented.ask: Who grew in a way you cannot point to?

Developer|Sensitive and Warm.recognize: You create the conditions where someone will admit what they are afraid of, and almost nobody else gets that admission out of them. The cost is that comfort is what you are best at providing, and there are people who will only move when they are made uncomfortable.
Developer|Sensitive and Warm.ask: Who have you kept comfortable for too long?

Developer|Sensitive to Others.recognize: You tailor how you develop each person to what they can absorb, and nobody gets the version of you that would have crushed them. The gap is that softening it every time means the message keeps getting smaller, and by the third attempt the hard thing has been sanded down to nothing.
Developer|Sensitive to Others.ask: What have you toned down so often it disappeared?

Developer|Sociable.recognize: You develop people in groups and in passing, over meals and in hallways, which means far more people get something from you than would fit in a formal schedule. The cost is that everyone gets a little and nobody gets much, and the person who needed an hour got six minutes.
Developer|Sociable.ask: Who needed an hour from you this month?

Developer|Spontaneous.recognize: You act on a hunch about someone the moment you have it, handing them an opportunity that was not planned and would not have survived a process. The gap is that a hunch-driven pattern of investment is invisible to everyone else, and it can look like favoritism to the people who were not chosen.
Developer|Spontaneous.ask: How would you explain who you invest in?

Developer|Strong Practical Skills.recognize: You give people true work with true stakes rather than exercises, and that is why the growth sticks. The cost is that when they start to fail you can do it yourself faster, and taking the task back is the exact moment their development stops.

Developer|Strong Sense of Duty.recognize: You treat someone's growth as a debt you owe rather than a favor you offer, which means you follow through long after the enthusiasm has worn off. The gap is that a debt like that does not know how to end, and you are still carrying responsibility for people who no longer need you to.
Developer|Strong Sense of Duty.ask: Whose growth is no longer yours to carry?

Developer|Strong-willed.recognize: You will hold your read on a person against everyone else's opinion, and more than once you have been the only one who was right. The cost is that the same firmness applies when you are wrong, and a person you have decided about has a long way to travel to change your mind.
Developer|Strong-willed.ask: Who have you been wrong about and not admitted it?

Developer|Supportive.recognize: You put your own reputation behind people before they have earned it, which is often the thing that gets them the chance. The gap is that support with no conditions attached teaches nothing, and someone who never feels a consequence from you has no reason to change.
Developer|Supportive.ask: What consequence have you absorbed on their behalf?

Developer|Very Loyal.recognize: You will speak for a person you are developing in a room where they are being criticized, and they may never learn you did it. The cost is that loyalty can seal someone off from accurate feedback, and the criticism you absorbed might have been the most useful thing they never heard.
Developer|Very Loyal.ask: What criticism did you shield them from?

Developer|Very Responsible.recognize: You take a person's failure to grow as your own failure to develop them, and that ownership is why you keep improving at this. The gap is that their choices are theirs, and carrying results you never controlled is a reliable way to burn out of the work you are best at.
Developer|Very Responsible.ask: Which of their failures did you file as yours?

Empathy|Altruistic.recognize: You feel what someone is carrying and then you do something about it, so your care never stays at the level of sympathy. The cost is that both instincts spend the same reserve, and you can arrive at the end of a week with nothing left for the people who live with you.
Empathy|Altruistic.ask: Who gets the version of you that has nothing left?

Empathy|Analytical.recognize: You feel a room accurately and you can also say why it is the way it is, which makes you unusually useful when something is wrong and nobody can name it. The gap is that explaining a feeling is a way of stepping outside it, and you may be doing that to yourself constantly.
Empathy|Analytical.ask: When did you last let yourself simply feel something?

Empathy|Bold.recognize: You will name out loud what everyone in the room is feeling and no one will say, which takes more courage than most people realize. The cost is that a feeling made public cannot be taken back, and sometimes the person you named it for was not ready to be seen.
Empathy|Bold.ask: Whose privacy did your honesty cost?

Empathy|Calm and Practical.recognize: You take on what others are feeling without letting it show, so you can sit with a person in crisis and be the steadiest thing in the room. The gap is that calm on the outside is not the same as calm, and nobody checks on the one who never seems shaken.
Empathy|Calm and Practical.ask: Who has any idea what this costs you?

Empathy|Charismatic.recognize: You draw people to you and then you truly feel what they bring, which is why strangers tell you things within minutes. The cost is that the pull does not have an off switch, and you end up holding the private material of people you barely have room for.
Empathy|Charismatic.ask: Whose story are you holding that you did not ask for?

Empathy|Charming.recognize: You perceive what a person needs and give them exactly that, which is why they relax so quickly around you. The gap is that meeting someone where they are can shade into telling them what they want to hear, and the two feel identical from the inside.
Empathy|Charming.ask: When did you agree with someone you did not agree with?

Empathy|Clear Communication.recognize: You can put a person's own feeling into words they recognize immediately, and being described accurately is a relief most people rarely get. The cost is that a clean summary of a complicated inner life can close the subject before the person had finished having it.
Empathy|Clear Communication.ask: Who stopped talking once you named it for them?

Empathy|Creative.recognize: You turn what you pick up from others into something they can look at, a story or an image that says it better than a direct sentence would. The gap is that making something out of a feeling is also a way of keeping a small distance from it.
Empathy|Creative.ask: What have you made instead of said?

Empathy|Curious.recognize: You ask the question underneath the question, and because people can tell you already know the answer, they tell you the truth. The cost is that curiosity plus feeling means you go deep with almost anyone, including people who should have stayed acquaintances.
Empathy|Curious.ask: Who did you get close to by accident?

Empathy|Decisive Action.recognize: You register how a decision will land on people and you make it anyway, which is the rarer combination and the reason your calls hold. The gap is that feeling the cost in advance can convince you that you have already accounted for it, when the people affected have not been asked.
Empathy|Decisive Action.ask: Whose reaction did you predict instead of hear?

Empathy|Dedicated.recognize: You stay present to someone's pain long past the point where others get tired, and that endurance is why people in a hard season call you first. The cost is that there is no natural end, and you have been the one still carrying a situation everyone else has moved on from.
Empathy|Dedicated.ask: What are you still carrying alone?

Empathy|Determined.recognize: You feel how much a person is struggling and you keep going with them anyway rather than letting the difficulty end the attempt. The gap is that your insistence can override what their exhaustion is telling you, and you may be dragging someone who wanted to stop.
Empathy|Determined.ask: Who has been asking to stop?

Empathy|Diligent and Observant.recognize: You notice the small shift in someone's face and you feel it at the same moment, so almost nothing gets past you. The cost is that a hundred small signals a day is a heavy load, and you may be reacting to things that meant nothing.
Empathy|Diligent and Observant.ask: What did you read into that was not there?

Empathy|Direct.recognize: You say the hard thing and you feel exactly how it lands, which means you can adjust in the moment rather than plowing ahead. The gap is that feeling the impact does not undo it, and you can spend days on a comment the other person forgot by lunch.
Empathy|Direct.ask: What did you say that only you remember?

Empathy|Direct and Authentic.recognize: You share what you are actually feeling rather than a managed version, and that honesty gives other people permission to stop performing. The cost is that your open state invites theirs, and you can find yourself in a depth of conversation neither of you scheduled.
Empathy|Direct and Authentic.ask: What did you share that you wish you had kept?

Empathy|Direct and Honest.recognize: You will tell someone the painful truth precisely because you feel what they are going through and think they deserve better than comfort. The gap is that your certainty about their inner life makes the delivery feel earned, and they may not agree that you have that standing.
Empathy|Direct and Honest.ask: Who did you speak to more intimately than they invited?

Empathy|Disciplined.recognize: You have built structure around your own sensitivity, with hours and habits that keep you functional in work that would flatten most people. The cost is that a system for managing feeling can become a way of not having it, and the discipline outlasts the reason for it.
Empathy|Disciplined.ask: What are you protecting yourself from that is no longer there?

Empathy|Easygoing.recognize: You feel what people are carrying and you never make a production of it, so being cared for by you costs nobody anything. The gap is that your lightness can read as not noticing, and someone in serious trouble may conclude you did not see it.
Empathy|Easygoing.ask: Who thinks you did not notice?

Empathy|Efficient Organizer.recognize: You can tell within a minute what a person actually needs and remove everything that is not that, which is why hard conversations with you are short and useful. The cost is that some feelings need the long way round, and a person can be helped quickly and still leave unheard.
Empathy|Efficient Organizer.ask: Who did you solve instead of listen to?

Empathy|Empathetic.recognize: You feel what others feel and you pick it up before they speak, the same instinct arriving twice, so there is almost no filter between another person's state and your own. What is absent is any part of you that stays separate. Nothing in you asks whose feeling this actually is.
Empathy|Empathetic.ask: Which of today's moods started in you?

Empathy|Energetic.recognize: You feel a group's mood and you can lift it by force of your own, which is why a room changes when you commit to it. The cost is that you are spending yourself to move other people's states, and that particular expense does not show up anywhere you can see it.
Empathy|Energetic.ask: Where does the energy you spend on rooms get replaced?

Empathy|Enjoy Creating Order.recognize: You feel the disorder in a group before it shows and you fix the conditions that caused it, so problems get solved before anyone names them. The gap is that not every difficult feeling is a problem in the environment, and some of them just have to be lived through.
Empathy|Enjoy Creating Order.ask: What are you trying to fix that only needs company?

Empathy|Enthusiastic.recognize: You feel what excites a person and you amplify it back to them, which is why people leave you more alive than they arrived. The cost is that the same channel carries everything, and a room's anxiety enters you as completely as its excitement does.
Empathy|Enthusiastic.ask: Whose anxiety are you carrying today?

Empathy|Excellent Brainstormers.recognize: You can imagine a dozen things a struggling person might need, because you are feeling their situation from the inside rather than guessing at it. The gap is that someone in pain cannot evaluate twelve options, and your abundance can land as pressure.
Empathy|Excellent Brainstormers.ask: What is the one thing they need from you?

Empathy|Excellent Communicators.recognize: You can say what a person is feeling more clearly than they can, and hearing it said well is often the thing that unlocks them. The cost is that your fluency fills the space, and the halting, unimpressive way they would have said it may have mattered more.
Empathy|Excellent Communicators.ask: Who needed to find their own words?

Empathy|Excellent Organizers.recognize: You build the arrangements that let a hurting person be supported by more than just you, bringing in the right people at the right time. The gap is that organizing care is easier than sitting in it, and you may be assembling a team so you do not have to stay in the room.
Empathy|Excellent Organizers.ask: What are you delegating that you should do yourself?

Empathy|Excellent People Skills.recognize: You feel what a person needs and you have the social skill to deliver it, which makes you the one everyone wants at a hard table. The cost is that skill and feeling can come apart, and you can perform care convincingly on a day you are not present at all.
Empathy|Excellent People Skills.ask: When did you go through the motions with someone?

Empathy|Future Focused.recognize: You feel where a person's current state is taking them and you respond to the version of them six months out. The gap is that they live today, and being cared for according to a forecast can leave someone feeling unmet in the only moment they actually occupy.
Empathy|Future Focused.ask: What do they need right now, not later?

Empathy|Generous.recognize: You feel a need and you meet it out of your own pocket, your own hours, your own margin, without waiting to be asked. The cost is that feeling need is a bottomless input and your resources are not, and you have gone past your limit more than once this year.
Empathy|Generous.ask: What came out of your own margin this month?

Empathy|Good Practical Skills.recognize: You feel what is wrong and then you fix something concrete, showing up with a meal or a repaired thing rather than words. The gap is that a task can stand in for a conversation, and the person may have needed you to sit down rather than be useful.
Empathy|Good Practical Skills.ask: When did you work instead of talk?

Empathy|Good at Connecting with Others.recognize: You feel who a person needs to meet and you make it happen, which is why your circle keeps widening and why so much of it depends on you. The cost is that every relationship you hold is one you feel, and a wide circle at your depth is a heavy thing to carry.
Empathy|Good at Connecting with Others.ask: Which of these relationships would survive you stepping back?

Empathy|Good-Natured and Positive.recognize: You feel the heaviness in a room and you carry some of it away by being warm inside it, which is a gift and not a trick. The gap is that raising a mood can be a way of ending a difficult moment early, before the person got to finish it.
Empathy|Good-Natured and Positive.ask: What conversation did you brighten too soon?

Empathy|Grounded.recognize: You absorb what others are feeling without being moved off your own ground, which is why people in chaos come and stand near you. The gap is that not being moved can look like not being reached, and someone may want evidence that their situation affected you.
Empathy|Grounded.ask: Who needs to see that this got to you?

Empathy|Hands-on and Observant.recognize: You feel it and respond in the same moment, no delay between noticing someone is struggling and being beside them. The gap is that responding that fast is responding to the surface, and the thing a person has been carrying for a year does not present itself in a moment you can see.
Empathy|Hands-on and Observant.ask: What have they been carrying since before you noticed?

Empathy|Handy and Resourceful.recognize: You feel what is needed and find a way to provide it with whatever is at hand, which is why you are useful in situations nobody prepared for. The cost is that a quick fix relieves the pressure that would have forced a permanent change, for them and for you.
Empathy|Handy and Resourceful.ask: Which recurring problem does your help keep rescuing?

Empathy|Hardworking.recognize: You feel what people need and you put in the hours to provide it, so your care has substance behind it rather than sentiment. The gap is that emotional labor is invisible labor, and you are working a second job that nobody has ever acknowledged.
Empathy|Hardworking.ask: What work of yours has nobody ever seen?

Empathy|Honest.recognize: You will say what you are feeling in a room, including the uncomfortable thing, because pretending costs you more than it costs most people. The cost is that a feeling voiced without a decision about whether to voice it is not always a gift to the person receiving it.
Empathy|Honest.ask: What did you say because you could not hold it?

Empathy|Honest and Direct.recognize: You tell people what you perceive in them without softening it, and because you are usually right it lands hard. The gap is that accuracy about someone's inner life is not permission to speak it, and being correctly read by someone can feel like being caught.
Empathy|Honest and Direct.ask: Who felt exposed by something you got right?

Empathy|Idealistic.recognize: You feel how far short the world falls from what it could be, and you feel it as a personal weight rather than an abstraction. The cost is that a heart calibrated to how things ought to be is a heart that grieves constantly, and you rarely let yourself rest in what is already good.
Empathy|Idealistic.ask: What is already good that you have not stopped to notice?

Empathy|Imaginative.recognize: You can inhabit another person's situation completely, which is why your grasp of what they are going through is so accurate. The gap is that you can also inhabit situations that have not happened, and you have grieved losses that never arrived.
Empathy|Imaginative.ask: What have you already mourned that has not happened?

Empathy|Independent.recognize: You feel everything around you and you process it alone, which is why you can stand in other people's storms without needing anything from them. The cost is that the processing never gets witnessed, and you have built a life where nobody has the job of asking about you.
Empathy|Independent.ask: Whose job is it to ask how you are?

Empathy|Informed.recognize: You hold what everyone is going through, who is struggling and who is barely holding on, and you carry that map without anyone assigning it to you. The gap is that the state of thirty people is thirty open files, and none of them ever close.
Empathy|Informed.ask: Which of these open files will ever close?

Empathy|Insightful.recognize: You feel your way to what is actually wrong with a person, arriving at the root while everyone else is still discussing the symptom. The cost is that feeling and concluding happen together for you, so a wrong conclusion arrives with the same certainty as a right one.
Empathy|Insightful.ask: What have you been certain about with no evidence?

Empathy|Kind and Encouraging.recognize: You feel where someone is fragile and you speak to exactly that place, which is why your encouragement works when generic praise does not. The gap is that you protect people from what you can feel would hurt them, and some of that was information they needed.
Empathy|Kind and Encouraging.ask: What are you withholding to spare someone?

Empathy|Knowledgeable.recognize: You pair what you feel with what you have learned, so your care comes with the right resource rather than only warmth. The cost is that information is easier to offer than presence, and a person in grief can end up with a reading list.
Empathy|Knowledgeable.ask: When did you reach for a resource instead of a chair?

Empathy|Loyal, Patient, and Reliable.recognize: You feel what someone is in and you remain there for as long as it takes, which is why the people in your life have never had to wonder about you. The cost is that remaining is your only setting, and you have been in situations far past the point they were doing you harm.
Empathy|Loyal, Patient, and Reliable.ask: What have you remained in too long?

Empathy|Observant.recognize: You take in the small signals and feel their weight at once, so you often know something is wrong before there is anything to point at. The cost is that certainty without proof is hard to act on, and you can spend weeks aware of a problem you never raised.
Empathy|Observant.ask: What have you been aware of and not said?

Empathy|Open-Minded.recognize: You can feel your way into a position you disagree with, which is why people with unpopular views trust you and why you rarely dismiss anyone. The gap is that inhabiting every side leaves you without ground of your own, and you can be moved by whoever is in front of you.
Empathy|Open-Minded.ask: What do you believe when nobody is arguing?

Empathy|Organized and Effective.recognize: You have a way of handling people in crisis that works repeatedly, so you can help many without losing the thread on any of them. The gap is that a person in pain is not a case, and a smooth process can leave someone feeling processed.
Empathy|Organized and Effective.ask: Who did you handle rather than meet?

Empathy|Original.recognize: You feel what nobody else in the room is registering, and you have learned to trust that reading even when everyone disagrees with you. The cost is that being alone in what you perceive is isolating, and over time you may have stopped saying it out loud.
Empathy|Original.ask: What have you felt lately and kept to yourself?

Empathy|Passionate.recognize: Your own cause is whatever you have felt from other people, which is why you fight for things that never happened to you. The gap is that intensity fed from outside has no natural limit, and you have taken on more than any one person's share of the world's weight.
Empathy|Passionate.ask: Which fight was never yours to take?

Empathy|Perceptive.recognize: You feel what people feel and you pick up what they do not say, two versions of the same instrument pointed at the same thing. What is absent is any check on the signal. Nothing in you asks whether what you perceived was theirs or a story you supplied.
Empathy|Perceptive.ask: What did you decide about someone with no confirmation?

Empathy|Positive and Enthusiastic.recognize: You feel the low point and you counter it, bringing energy to a person who has run out of their own. The cost is that turning toward the good is automatic for you, and a sad person may need you to stay down there with them for longer than you find bearable.
Empathy|Positive and Enthusiastic.ask: Whose sadness ran longer than your patience for it?

Empathy|Principled.recognize: You feel the harm in a situation before you can argue it, and your convictions come from having been in the room rather than from theory. The gap is that a conviction born in feeling is very hard to revise, and someone who caused harm may never get a second reading from you.

Empathy|Proactive Initiative.recognize: You feel that someone is in trouble and you are already at their door, often before they have decided to tell anyone. The cost is that arriving uninvited into a private difficulty takes a choice away from them, however welcome you turn out to be.
Empathy|Proactive Initiative.ask: Who did you show up for before they asked?

Empathy|Quick Thinkers.recognize: You feel a shift and answer it in the same breath, which is why people experience you as being right there with them. The gap is that fast feeling is unexamined feeling, and you can be three steps into comforting someone before checking what actually happened.
Empathy|Quick Thinkers.ask: What did you assume before they finished?

Empathy|Rational.recognize: You feel it fully and then examine whether the feeling is telling you the truth, which makes you far more accurate than either instinct alone. The cost is that the examining can become a verdict on the feeling, and you have talked yourself out of things you were right about.
Empathy|Rational.ask: What did you feel and then argue away?

Empathy|Rational and Practical.recognize: You feel what is happening and immediately look for what can be done about it, so your compassion produces outcomes rather than only comfort. The gap is that some pain has no action attached, and a person facing that may hear your search for a fix as a refusal to sit with them.
Empathy|Rational and Practical.ask: What can you do nothing about?

Empathy|Receptive.recognize: You take in what people bring without defending yourself against it, which is why they bring you the things they cannot say elsewhere. The cost is that having no barrier is not the same as choosing what enters, and you have absorbed things that were never yours.
Empathy|Receptive.ask: What is in you that somebody else put there?

Empathy|Reliable.recognize: You are the person who actually follows up two weeks later, because you never stopped feeling what they told you. The gap is that a memory that does not fade is also a load that does not lighten, and you are still carrying conversations from years ago.
Empathy|Reliable.ask: Which conversation from years ago is still with you?

Empathy|Research-Oriented.recognize: You check what you feel against what is actually true, asking rather than assuming, which makes your reads unusually trustworthy. The cost is that checking takes time a hurting person may not have, and you can be still confirming while the moment to help passes.
Empathy|Research-Oriented.ask: What did you check while someone waited?

Empathy|Results Oriented.recognize: You feel what people need and you make sure it actually arrives, so your compassion changes situations rather than only atmospheres. The gap is that not all care produces a result you can point to, and the hours you spent simply being present may have been the most valuable ones.
Empathy|Results Oriented.ask: What did you give that produced nothing visible?

Empathy|Sensitive and Warm.recognize: You feel what others feel and you radiate care outward, the same tenderness pointed both directions, so being near you is unmistakably safe. What is missing is any hardness at all. Nothing in you is willing to be the source of someone's discomfort, even when discomfort is what would help.
Empathy|Sensitive and Warm.ask: When did you last let someone be uncomfortable?

Empathy|Sensitive to Others.recognize: You feel what others feel and you shape yourself around it, the same responsiveness twice, so almost nothing you do lands badly on anyone. What is absent is a fixed point. Nothing in you holds still long enough for people to find out what you actually wanted.
Empathy|Sensitive to Others.ask: What did you want in that last meeting?

Empathy|Sociable.recognize: You enjoy being among people and you feel each of them individually, which is why a party leaves you both fed and wrecked. The gap is that the two cannot be separated, and you keep choosing the room without accounting for what the room takes.
Empathy|Sociable.ask: What does a full weekend actually cost you?

Empathy|Spontaneous.recognize: You act on what you feel the second you feel it, dropping everything for a person who needs you without weighing it first. The cost is that the people who get you are the ones whose need was loudest today, and quieter needs go unanswered for months.
Empathy|Spontaneous.ask: Whose quiet need have you been missing?

Empathy|Strong Practical Skills.recognize: You feel what is wrong and you are competent enough to take it off someone's plate entirely, which is why people in trouble hand you things. The gap is that taking it on is your reflex, and you have accepted burdens that belonged to people who could have grown by holding them.
Empathy|Strong Practical Skills.ask: What did you take on that was theirs to hold?

Empathy|Strong Sense of Duty.recognize: You convert what you feel into what you owe, so a need you have perceived turns into a duty you have accepted without any conversation taking place. The gap is that this happens silently and constantly, and your list of duties has grown far past anything anyone actually asked of you.
Empathy|Strong Sense of Duty.ask: Which of your duties did nobody request?

Empathy|Strong-willed.recognize: You feel deeply and you do not bend, which means your compassion has force behind it and people cannot talk you out of caring about someone. The cost is that the same firmness applies to what you feel about a person, and a first impression can harden into a permanent one.
Empathy|Strong-willed.ask: Who did you decide about years ago?

Empathy|Supportive.recognize: You feel where a person is weak and you position yourself under exactly that spot, which is why people who work with you stop being afraid to try. The gap is that steady help removes the pressure that produces change, and some of the people you hold up have stopped moving.
Empathy|Supportive.ask: Who has stopped trying because you are there?

Empathy|Very Loyal.recognize: You feel what your people feel and you take their side before you have the facts, which is why they never doubt where you are. The cost is that feeling with someone is not the same as seeing them clearly, and you may be the last person able to tell them they are wrong.
Empathy|Very Loyal.ask: Where have you been too close to see them clearly?

Empathy|Very Responsible.recognize: You feel the impact of your actions on other people acutely, which is why you are careful in ways most people are not. The gap is that feeling responsible and being responsible are not the same, and you apologize for weather you did not make.
Empathy|Very Responsible.ask: What have you apologized for that was not yours?

Harmony|Altruistic.recognize: You keep things calm and you put others first, so a group with you in it runs with less friction than it has any right to. The cost is that both instincts point away from you, and nobody in the room has any idea what you would have wanted.
Harmony|Altruistic.ask: When did you last state a preference?

Harmony|Analytical.recognize: You can spot where a disagreement is actually coming from and lower the temperature by naming the true issue rather than the loud one. The gap is that grasping a conflict thoroughly can become a substitute for entering it, and you may be studying a fight you should be in.
Harmony|Analytical.ask: Which conflict are you analyzing instead of joining?

Harmony|Bold.recognize: You will walk directly into a room where two people are at war and say the thing that de-escalates it, which most people would not attempt. The cost is that your comfort with intervening does not mean it was wanted, and some disputes needed to be had out fully.
Harmony|Bold.ask: Which argument did you end too early?

Harmony|Calm and Practical.recognize: You lower the temperature and you run at a low temperature yourself, the same instinct doubled, so almost nothing in a room can escalate past you. What is missing is any capacity for alarm. Nothing in you registers when a situation actually deserves to get loud.
Harmony|Calm and Practical.ask: What deserved more of a reaction than you gave it?

Harmony|Charismatic.recognize: You draw people toward you and things get easier when you arrive, which is why you are invited into rooms that have been difficult. The gap is that presence can paper over a problem for the length of a meeting, and it will be exactly where you left it next week.
Harmony|Charismatic.ask: What problem waits for you to leave the room?

Harmony|Charming.recognize: You take the edge off a room and you put people at rest, two versions of the same instinct, so friction rarely survives contact with you. What is absent is any willingness to be the difficulty. Nothing in you can be the reason a conversation gets uncomfortable.
Harmony|Charming.ask: When were you last the problem in a room on purpose?

Harmony|Clear Communication.recognize: You can say the calming thing in words nobody can misread, which is why heated conversations with you stop escalating on misunderstanding alone. The cost is that a tidy summary of a disagreement can flatten it, and both sides may accept a version neither of them meant.
Harmony|Clear Communication.ask: What did you smooth over that was not actually agreed?

Harmony|Creative.recognize: You find the third option nobody was arguing for, the one that lets both sides keep something, and you produce it under pressure. The gap is that an inventive compromise can be a way of avoiding the question of who was right, and sometimes that question matters.
Harmony|Creative.ask: Which disagreement had a right answer you talked around?

Harmony|Curious.recognize: You ask about the other side's view with sincere interest, and being asked that way is what usually takes the heat out of a person. The cost is that questions can go on indefinitely, and a group can spend an hour appreciating each other and still not decide anything.
