Harmony|Curious.ask: What decision has been postponed by more discussion?

Harmony|Decisive Action.recognize: You settle disputes rather than manage them, choosing an answer and getting everyone to it before the thing has time to fester. The gap is that a fast settlement is still a settlement someone lost, and the person who gave way may not have finished being upset.
Harmony|Decisive Action.ask: Who agreed to something they had not accepted?

Harmony|Dedicated.recognize: You keep working on a strained relationship long after both parties have given up on it, and more than one friendship in your life exists because you would not let it die. The cost is that some relationships should end, and your loyalty can keep a bad one alive for years.
Harmony|Dedicated.ask: Which relationship are you keeping alive by yourself?

Harmony|Determined.recognize: You will keep at a reconciliation through repeated failure, going back a fourth and fifth time when everyone else has written it off. The gap is that insisting on agreement becomes pressure, and the person still holding out may be the one who is right.
Harmony|Determined.ask: Who is holding out for a reason you have not heard?

Harmony|Diligent and Observant.recognize: You notice the small tension between two people weeks before it surfaces, and you have quietly defused more conflicts than anyone knows about. The cost is that constant low-level monitoring is draining, and you may be intervening in things that would have resolved themselves.
Harmony|Diligent and Observant.ask: Which tension would have settled itself?

Harmony|Direct.recognize: You will say plainly that a fight is not worth having, which is a form of directness people rarely expect from someone who avoids conflict. The gap is that declaring a disagreement pointless is itself a verdict, and you have delivered it in situations where you had not heard both sides.
Harmony|Direct.ask: Which argument did you dismiss without listening?

Harmony|Direct and Authentic.recognize: You will own your own part in a conflict first, which lowers the other person's guard faster than any argument could. The cost is that going first becomes automatic, and you have taken responsibility for things that were not yours in order to end an uncomfortable moment.
Harmony|Direct and Authentic.ask: Whose part in this did you take on as your own?

Harmony|Direct and Honest.recognize: You offer the honest read on a dispute when nobody asked, and because you clearly have no side in it, people accept it from you. The gap is that neutrality is a position too, and there are conflicts where declining to take a side is the wrong answer.
Harmony|Direct and Honest.ask: Which side should you have taken?

Harmony|Disciplined.recognize: You have habits that keep a group functioning, regular check-ins and clear agreements that stop small things becoming grievances. The cost is that a well-run system produces the appearance of agreement, and people learn to bring you the version of a problem that fits the process.
Harmony|Disciplined.ask: What are people not telling you because of how you run things?

Harmony|Easygoing.recognize: You avoid friction and you are unbothered by almost everything, the same instinct arriving twice, so you are the least demanding person most people know. What is missing is anything that would make you object. Nothing in you generates the pressure that gets a group to change.
Harmony|Easygoing.ask: What is worth making a fuss about?

Harmony|Efficient Organizer.recognize: You cut the parts of a disagreement that are not going anywhere and get people to the workable middle quickly, which saves everyone hours. The gap is that the discarded parts sometimes contained the actual issue, and it will come back with a different name.
Harmony|Efficient Organizer.ask: What keeps coming back under a new label?

Harmony|Empathetic.recognize: You feel the discomfort in a room and you act on it before anyone else has registered anything, so tension rarely gets far with you present. The cost is that you are responding to your own discomfort as much as theirs, and you may be ending conversations other people were fine having.
Harmony|Empathetic.ask: Whose discomfort were you actually relieving?

Harmony|Energetic.recognize: You put serious energy into keeping a group together, organizing the meal or the conversation that stops a rift widening. The gap is that the work of holding people together is constant and invisible, and you will run out long before anyone notices you were doing it.
Harmony|Energetic.ask: Who else is holding this group together?

Harmony|Enjoy Creating Order.recognize: You reduce conflict by removing its causes, clarifying who owns what so people stop colliding in the first place. The cost is that not all conflict comes from ambiguity, and a group can be perfectly run and still full of unspoken resentment.
Harmony|Enjoy Creating Order.ask: What resentment survives your best process?

Harmony|Enthusiastic.recognize: You are openly glad when a group is getting along, and that gladness makes agreement feel like an achievement rather than a compromise. The gap is that your visible delight when things go smoothly is a signal, and people learn not to raise the thing that would spoil it.
Harmony|Enthusiastic.ask: Who is protecting your mood by staying quiet?

Harmony|Excellent Brainstormers.recognize: You can produce a dozen ways two people might both get what they want, and one of them usually works. The cost is that offering alternatives is also a way of never saying which one you think is right, and a group needs that from someone.
Harmony|Excellent Brainstormers.ask: Which of those options do you actually prefer?

Harmony|Excellent Communicators.recognize: You can restate each side's position better than they put it themselves, and hearing yourself described fairly is what usually lowers a person's guard. The gap is that a skilled translator can make two incompatible positions sound compatible, and the disagreement goes underground rather than away.
Harmony|Excellent Communicators.ask: What disagreement went quiet without being settled?

Harmony|Excellent Organizers.recognize: You build the arrangements that keep people out of each other's way, and groups you run have noticeably fewer collisions than they should. The cost is that separation is not agreement, and two people can go years without conflict and also without ever working anything out.
Harmony|Excellent Organizers.ask: Which two people have you been keeping apart?

Harmony|Excellent People Skills.recognize: You can hold a relationship with both people in a feud, which is rare and is why you are often the only channel between them. The gap is that being liked by everyone requires never fully siding with anyone, and at some point that becomes its own kind of dishonesty.
Harmony|Excellent People Skills.ask: Where has being liked cost you your honesty?

Harmony|Future Focused.recognize: You see where a small friction ends up in two years and you deal with it now, which is why problems in your world rarely mature. The cost is that acting on a forecast means acting before there is evidence, and you have defused conflicts that were never going to happen.
Harmony|Future Focused.ask: What did you prevent that was not coming?

Harmony|Generous.recognize: You give up your portion to end a dispute, and you do it so readily that most people never realize a dispute was occurring. The gap is that a person who always gives way teaches everyone around them what to expect, and by now they expect it.
Harmony|Generous.ask: What have you given up so often that nobody asks anymore?

Harmony|Good Practical Skills.recognize: You end arguments by fixing the underlying practical problem, so what looked like a personality clash turns out to have been a broken process. The cost is that some clashes are actually about the people, and no amount of repairing the workflow will touch them.
Harmony|Good Practical Skills.ask: Which conflict is not about the process?

Harmony|Good at Connecting with Others.recognize: You put estranged people back in the same room and you do it so naturally that neither of them notices it was arranged. The gap is that proximity is not reconciliation, and two people can share a table for years while the original injury sits untouched.
Harmony|Good at Connecting with Others.ask: What injury has never been named out loud?

Harmony|Good-Natured and Positive.recognize: You take friction out of a room and you bring good humor into it, the same instinct twice, so people enjoy being around you and problems rarely feel urgent. What is absent is any weight. Nothing in you can make a group feel that something is serious.
Harmony|Good-Natured and Positive.ask: What needs to feel more serious than you have let it?

Harmony|Grounded.recognize: You stay put while a conflict rages, and your steadiness is often what keeps it from spreading, since a group takes its reading from whoever is least alarmed. The cost is that immovable and unresponsive look the same to someone who needs you to react.
Harmony|Grounded.ask: Who wanted proof that this affected you?

Harmony|Hands-on and Observant.recognize: You step in the moment a room turns, before anyone has decided whether to escalate, and that timing is why so little ever gets said in anger around you. The gap is that things said in anger are sometimes true, and you have prevented information from reaching people who needed it.
Harmony|Hands-on and Observant.ask: What true thing never got said because you intervened?

Harmony|Handy and Resourceful.recognize: You find the workaround that lets two people who cannot agree still get the thing done, assembled out of whatever is available. The cost is that a workaround leaves the disagreement exactly where it was, and you have been building around the same conflict for years.
Harmony|Handy and Resourceful.ask: Which conflict has your workaround been hiding?

Harmony|Hardworking.recognize: You will absorb extra work yourself rather than ask two people to sort out who should be doing it, and a lot of what you carry got to you that way. The gap is that every task you quietly take on removes the pressure that would have forced the conversation.
Harmony|Hardworking.ask: What are you doing that belongs to someone else?

Harmony|Honest.recognize: You will tell the truth in a conflict, but you will tell it in the least inflammatory order possible, which is why people can hear it from you. The cost is that arranging the truth carefully takes time, and by the time you are ready the moment has often closed.
Harmony|Honest.ask: What were you still composing when the moment closed?

Harmony|Honest and Direct.recognize: You state your position clearly and then immediately look for the common ground, which means people get your view without feeling attacked by it. The gap is that reaching for agreement right after speaking can read as taking it back, and your actual position gets lost.
Harmony|Honest and Direct.ask: What is your position, without the softening?

Harmony|Idealistic.recognize: You hold a picture of what this group could be when everyone is on the same side, and that picture is often what pulls people back toward each other. The cost is that reality never matches it, and you carry a low, constant grief about how things actually are.
Harmony|Idealistic.ask: What are you quietly grieving about this group?

Harmony|Imaginative.recognize: You can imagine your way into what both sides are protecting, which is why your read on a conflict is usually more generous and more accurate than anyone else's. The gap is that imagining a resolution is satisfying enough that you may never test whether it would hold.
Harmony|Imaginative.ask: Which compromise have you rehearsed but never proposed?

Harmony|Independent.recognize: You handle your own frictions without involving anyone, so you have almost no history of public conflict and no reputation for causing trouble. The cost is that private resolution means nobody learns anything, and a pattern that keeps recurring never becomes visible to the group.
Harmony|Independent.ask: What pattern have you absorbed so quietly that nobody sees it?

Harmony|Informed.recognize: You know exactly which people are not speaking, what started it, and who has taken which side, and you navigate around all of it without ever consulting a note. The gap is that holding the map is not the same as changing it, and you may be managing a situation you should be ending.
Harmony|Informed.ask: What situation are you managing that should be over?

Harmony|Insightful.recognize: You see what a conflict is truly about, usually something neither party has named, and you can steer the conversation toward it without embarrassing anyone. The cost is that arriving at the truth early means you may act on it before either person is ready to have it be true.
Harmony|Insightful.ask: What truth did you surface ahead of its moment?

Harmony|Kind and Encouraging.recognize: You keep the room gentle and you build people up inside it, two instincts pointing the same way, so almost nobody has ever felt small around you. What is missing is any source of pressure. Nothing in you produces the discomfort that makes a person change.
Harmony|Kind and Encouraging.ask: Who has never once felt challenged by you?

Harmony|Knowledgeable.recognize: You can settle a factual dispute instantly, which removes a whole category of argument before it starts. The gap is that most conflicts are not factual, and being the one with the answer can make you reach for facts in situations that were never about them.
Harmony|Knowledgeable.ask: Which argument did you try to win with information?

Harmony|Loyal, Patient, and Reliable.recognize: You remain in a strained situation for as long as it takes, and your presence over years is often the thing that eventually makes reconciliation possible. The cost is that this has no built-in limit, and you have absorbed a difficult dynamic for a decade rather than name it.
Harmony|Loyal, Patient, and Reliable.ask: What dynamic have you tolerated for a decade?

Harmony|Observant.recognize: You see a conflict forming days ahead and you are already adjusting to prevent it, usually without telling anyone that is what you are doing. The gap is that quiet prevention leaves no record, and the group has no idea how much of its calm is your work.
Harmony|Observant.ask: What have you prevented that nobody knows about?

Harmony|Open-Minded.recognize: You can hold both sides as reasonable, which is why people in a dispute will each accept you as fair. The cost is that treating every position as defensible leaves you unable to say a wrong one is wrong, and occasionally someone in a conflict simply is.
Harmony|Open-Minded.ask: Which position have you refused to call wrong?

Harmony|Organized and Effective.recognize: You have a reliable way of getting people through a disagreement, and it works often enough that groups hand you their hardest conversations. The gap is that a process gives everyone a script, and a person can complete every step without having changed their mind at all.
Harmony|Organized and Effective.ask: Who followed your process and still disagrees?

Harmony|Original.recognize: You bring an angle nobody had considered, which is often what breaks a deadlock where both sides have run out of arguments. The cost is that offering an unusual view is easier for you than defending it, and you tend to withdraw the idea the moment it meets resistance.
Harmony|Original.ask: Which idea did you drop as soon as it was questioned?

Harmony|Passionate.recognize: You care intensely about people being right with each other, which is why you will spend yourself on a reconciliation that has nothing in it for you. The gap is that intensity aimed at agreement is still pressure, and people can tell how much you need this to work out.
Harmony|Passionate.ask: Who agreed because they could tell you needed them to?

Harmony|Perceptive.recognize: You pick up a shift in the room before there is anything to point at, and you have already begun lowering the temperature while others are still talking. The cost is that you cannot always tell what you perceived from what you expected, and you have managed tension that existed only in you.
Harmony|Perceptive.ask: What tension did you handle that nobody else felt?

Harmony|Positive and Enthusiastic.recognize: You raise a room out of a bad moment, and your unwillingness to let a group sit in gloom has carried people through truly hard seasons. The gap is that both instincts move away from difficulty, and a group with you leading it may never sit with anything long enough to feel it.
Harmony|Positive and Enthusiastic.ask: What has this group never been allowed to sit with?

Harmony|Principled.recognize: You hold the line on how people treat each other, which is a form of conflict avoidance that has actual teeth to it. The cost is that a rule about conduct can end a conversation on procedural grounds, and the substance of what someone was trying to say gets lost in how they said it.
Harmony|Principled.ask: Whose point did you dismiss over their tone?

Harmony|Proactive Initiative.recognize: You are the first to reach out after something goes wrong, usually within hours, and that speed is why so few injuries in your world have time to set. The gap is that going first every time means you may be repairing things you did not break.
Harmony|Proactive Initiative.ask: Which apology belonged to somebody else?

Harmony|Quick Thinkers.recognize: You can defuse something in one sentence delivered at exactly the right second, which is a skill that cannot be taught. The cost is that a fast de-escalation is a decision made in a second, and you have shut down exchanges that were about to become useful.
Harmony|Quick Thinkers.ask: Which conversation was about to get somewhere when you ended it?

Harmony|Rational.recognize: You take the emotion out of a dispute by walking everyone back to the actual question, which works because it gives people a way to retreat without losing face. The gap is that some conflicts are entirely about feeling, and a sound argument is not an answer to being hurt.
Harmony|Rational.ask: Where did a sound argument fail to help?

Harmony|Rational and Practical.recognize: You steer people toward what will actually work rather than what either side wanted, and that pragmatism ends more arguments than persuasion ever does. The cost is that a workable answer can be the wrong one, and you have settled for functional in situations that called for right.
Harmony|Rational and Practical.ask: Where did you take workable over right?

Harmony|Receptive.recognize: You take in whatever someone brings and you smooth the space between you, the same yielding twice, so a disagreement with you barely counts as one. What is missing is any resistance at all. Nothing in you pushes back hard enough for the other person to find out where you are.
Harmony|Receptive.ask: Where do you actually stand on this?

Harmony|Reliable.recognize: You are the person everyone counts on to hold a group together, and you have never once failed to show up for that role. The gap is that a role nobody assigned can also be a role nobody can relieve you of, and you have been doing it for years without a break.
Harmony|Reliable.ask: Who could take this over from you?

Harmony|Research-Oriented.recognize: You find out what actually happened before responding to a conflict, which is why you almost never make one worse by acting on a wrong account. The cost is that fact-finding takes time, and a person who is upset now can experience your care as delay.
Harmony|Research-Oriented.ask: Who felt unsupported while you were getting the facts?

Harmony|Results Oriented.recognize: You push a disagreement to an actual conclusion rather than letting it hang, because an unresolved thing costs the work more than a hard conversation does. The gap is that closing something is not the same as healing it, and you may be counting settled matters that are still live for the people in them.
Harmony|Results Oriented.ask: What is settled for you and not for them?

Harmony|Sensitive and Warm.recognize: You take the sharpness out of a room and you bring tenderness into it, the same instinct twice, so people bring you things they would not risk saying anywhere else. What is absent is any hard edge. Nothing in you can deliver a message that would hurt to hear.
Harmony|Sensitive and Warm.ask: What message have you been unable to deliver?

Harmony|Sensitive to Others.recognize: You avoid friction and you bend around other people, the same instinct arriving twice, so you have almost never been the cause of anyone's difficult day. What is missing is a self that stays the same size. Nothing in you holds a shape when someone else needs the room.
Harmony|Sensitive to Others.ask: When did you last take up space?

Harmony|Sociable.recognize: You keep a large group comfortable, moving between people and making sure nobody is left in a bad conversation. The cost is that hosting is constant work and it looks like enjoyment, so nobody has ever offered to take a turn.
Harmony|Sociable.ask: When did you last attend something without working it?

Harmony|Spontaneous.recognize: You defuse things in the moment with whatever occurs to you, a joke or a change of subject that lands because it was not planned. The gap is that de-escalation on the fly follows no strategy, and the same conflict can be interrupted a dozen times without ever being addressed.
Harmony|Spontaneous.ask: What have you interrupted repeatedly and never addressed?

Harmony|Strong Practical Skills.recognize: You take on the thing two people are fighting over and simply do it yourself, which ends the argument immediately and permanently. The cost is that you have quietly acquired a great deal of work this way, and neither of them ever learned to sort it out.
Harmony|Strong Practical Skills.ask: What did you take on to end an argument?

Harmony|Strong Sense of Duty.recognize: You treat keeping the group together as something you owe rather than something you offer, so you do it on days you have nothing left. The gap is that a duty nobody assigned cannot be handed back, and you have been carrying this one for longer than anyone realizes.
Harmony|Strong Sense of Duty.ask: When did this become your job?

Harmony|Strong-willed.recognize: You will hold firm that a conflict is going to get worked out, and your unwillingness to let people walk away is often what forces a resolution nobody thought possible. The cost is that insisting on agreement is itself a demand, and someone may comply with it rather than mean it.
Harmony|Strong-willed.ask: Who complied with you instead of agreeing?

Harmony|Supportive.recognize: You get behind whoever is struggling in a dispute, which keeps anyone from being crushed and is why weaker voices survive around you. The gap is that supporting whoever is losing is not the same as being fair, and you have propped up positions that deserved to lose.
Harmony|Supportive.ask: Which weak position did you keep alive?

Harmony|Very Loyal.recognize: You will not let a conflict damage a relationship you have committed to, and people in your life have the security of never wondering whether an argument will end things. The cost is that some relationships need the possibility of ending in order to change.
Harmony|Very Loyal.ask: Which relationship has never had to change?

Harmony|Very Responsible.recognize: You take ownership early in a conflict, which lowers the temperature faster than anything else because it gives the other person nothing to fight. The gap is that early ownership can be a technique rather than a reckoning, and you have taken blame in order to end a conversation.
Harmony|Very Responsible.ask: What blame did you accept to make something stop?

Includer|Altruistic.recognize: You bring people in and then actually look after them once they are in, so nobody you invited ends up standing at the edge of the room alone. The cost is that both instincts run on the same reserve, and the circle keeps growing while your capacity to tend it does not.
Includer|Altruistic.ask: Who did you bring in and then lose track of?

Includer|Analytical.recognize: You can see exactly who is being left out and explain the mechanism that keeps doing it, which turns a vague unfairness into something a group can fix. The gap is that mapping exclusion is not the same as ending it, and you may be the only one who has read your own analysis.
Includer|Analytical.ask: What did you diagnose and never act on?

Includer|Bold.recognize: You will say out loud that someone has been left out, in the room, while it is happening, which almost nobody is willing to do. The cost is that naming it publicly can make the excluded person the subject rather than the guest, and they did not ask for that.
Includer|Bold.ask: Who did you speak up for without asking them first?

Includer|Calm and Practical.recognize: You bring people in without ceremony, so joining your group feels like nothing special happened, which is exactly what makes it easy. The gap is that a low-key approach can read as low-priority, and someone who has been on the outside a long time may need the invitation to be unmistakable.
Includer|Calm and Practical.ask: Who missed an invitation because you made it casual?

Includer|Charismatic.recognize: You pull people toward you and then hand them around the room rather than keeping them, which is why your gatherings do not orbit a single person. The cost is that the pull is still yours, and a group assembled by your appeal can dissolve the moment you stop hosting.
Includer|Charismatic.ask: What would this group be without you in it?

Includer|Charming.recognize: You make joining feel effortless, so a newcomer relaxes before they have worked out where they stand. The gap is that comfort is not the same as belonging, and someone can sit relaxed in your room for a year without anyone actually knowing them.
Includer|Charming.ask: Who is comfortable here but not known?

Includer|Clear Communication.recognize: You state without hedging that someone is invited, with no ambiguity about whether they were meant to be there, which removes the guessing that keeps people out. The cost is that a clear invitation covers the door and not the room, and nobody has told them what happens once they are inside.
Includer|Clear Communication.ask: What does nobody explain to new people here?

Includer|Creative.recognize: You invent the format that lets a quiet person contribute, changing how a meeting runs rather than asking them to change. The gap is that an inventive structure is still your structure, and you may be building doors for people you have not asked what they need.
Includer|Creative.ask: What did you build for someone without asking them?

Includer|Curious.recognize: You ask new people actual questions, so they arrive and immediately have somewhere to put themselves. The cost is that interest can outpace intimacy, and a person can be asked a great deal in their first hour and very little after their first month.
Includer|Curious.ask: Who have you stopped asking about?

Includer|Decisive Action.recognize: You decide someone is in and act on it immediately, which spares them the long ambiguity most people endure at the edge of a group. The gap is that a quick inclusion is still your call, and you may be admitting people into something that was not yours to open.
Includer|Decisive Action.ask: Whose group did you invite someone into?

Includer|Dedicated.recognize: You keep pursuing the person who has not responded, going back a fourth and fifth time when everyone else has stopped trying. The cost is that a repeated invitation can become pressure, and someone may be declining on purpose rather than being overlooked.
Includer|Dedicated.ask: Who has been saying no quietly?

Includer|Determined.recognize: You will not accept that a person cannot be brought in, and your stubbornness on this has changed the shape of groups you have been part of. The gap is that determination about someone's inclusion can override their own preference, and not everyone wants what you are certain they need.
Includer|Determined.ask: Who did you include against their wishes?

Includer|Diligent and Observant.recognize: You notice the person who has not spoken in forty minutes and you do something about it before the meeting ends. The cost is that constant scanning is tiring and it never switches off, and you have never simply been in a room.
Includer|Diligent and Observant.ask: When were you last in a room without counting who was left out?

Includer|Direct.recognize: You tell a group flatly that they are leaving someone out, which is uncomfortable and usually correct. The gap is that a correction that direct makes the group defensive, and defensiveness rarely produces the openness you were asking for.
Includer|Direct.ask: Which group closed up after you challenged it?

Includer|Direct and Authentic.recognize: You talk about your own experience of being on the outside, and that admission is often what makes a room safe for someone else to say it. The cost is that your story sets the terms, and a person excluded for entirely other reasons may not see themselves in it.
Includer|Direct and Authentic.ask: Whose exclusion looks nothing like yours?

Includer|Direct and Honest.recognize: You will tell someone unprompted that they are being kept at arm's length by a group they thought they were in. The gap is that information like that cannot be returned, and they may have been happier not being certain.
Includer|Direct and Honest.ask: What did you tell someone that they could not unhear?

Includer|Disciplined.recognize: You build inclusion into the process, with rotations and standing invitations that do not depend on anyone remembering. The cost is that a system produces participation rather than warmth, and a person can be brought in by procedure and still feel like a line item.
Includer|Disciplined.ask: Who is included on paper only?

Includer|Easygoing.recognize: You have no gatekeeping in you at all, so people drift into your circle without any test being applied. The gap is that a group anyone can enter is a group nobody had to be chosen for, and being chosen is part of what makes people stay.
Includer|Easygoing.ask: Who here has never been told they matter to this?

Includer|Efficient Organizer.recognize: You find the fastest way to get a new person functional, cutting the ceremony and handing them something useful to do. The cost is that ceremony is how humans mark that someone has arrived, and you may have made a person productive before you made them a member.
Includer|Efficient Organizer.ask: Who is useful here but not attached?

Includer|Empathetic.recognize: You feel the person on the edge of the room before you can see why, and you are moving toward them before anyone else has noticed anything. The gap is that not everyone standing alone is lonely, and your rescue can interrupt a solitude they chose.
Includer|Empathetic.ask: Who wanted to be left alone?

Includer|Energetic.recognize: You put serious effort into making sure nobody is stranded, and a room you are working has noticeably fewer people staring at their phone. The cost is that this labor is invisible and constant, and you have never once been thanked for a thing that did not happen.
Includer|Energetic.ask: Who else does this work here?

Includer|Enjoy Creating Order.recognize: You set the seating and the groupings so that nobody ends up marooned, and it works because you thought about it beforehand. The gap is that placing people near each other is not connection, and two of them can sit together for a year without either one choosing it.
Includer|Enjoy Creating Order.ask: Which pairing have you engineered that never took?

Includer|Enthusiastic.recognize: You are visibly delighted when someone new shows up, and that delight is often the first time they have felt wanted somewhere. The cost is that a big reception sets an expectation, and the ordinary Tuesday version of your group may be a letdown.
Includer|Enthusiastic.ask: Who found the second visit disappointing?

Includer|Excellent Brainstormers.recognize: You can think of a dozen ways to get a reluctant person involved, and one of them usually fits. The gap is that offering twelve entry points to someone who is nervous can feel like being surrounded rather than invited.
Includer|Excellent Brainstormers.ask: What is the single easiest way in for them?

Includer|Excellent Communicators.recognize: You can present two strangers to each other in a way that gives them somewhere to start, so the conversation survives after you walk away. The cost is that your fluency is doing the work, and neither of them has had to develop the skill of entering a room.
Includer|Excellent Communicators.ask: Who relies on you to start every conversation?

Includer|Excellent Organizers.recognize: You build the arrangements that make a large group navigable, so a newcomer is not left to work out the map alone. The gap is that an organized group has an official way in, and the people who do not fit that route may never find another.
Includer|Excellent Organizers.ask: Who does not fit the official way in?

Includer|Excellent People Skills.recognize: You can talk to anyone, which means the person nobody else knows how to approach has you. The cost is that this makes you the designated handler, and the group never has to develop the ability to do it themselves.
Includer|Excellent People Skills.ask: Who has the group outsourced to you?

Includer|Future Focused.recognize: You see who is drifting toward the exit months before they leave, and you intervene while there is still something to hold. The gap is that acting on a forecast means acting on someone who has decided nothing yet, and being pursued over a departure you were not planning is strange.
Includer|Future Focused.ask: Whose exit did you predict wrongly?

Includer|Generous.recognize: You give away access, your table and your contacts and your hours, without asking what someone brings first. The cost is that unlimited access has no natural limit and you have never set one, and by now more people have a claim on you than you can honor.
Includer|Generous.ask: How many claims on you are outstanding?

Includer|Good Practical Skills.recognize: You bring someone in by handing them a job, which is the fastest route to belonging for people who hate small talk. The gap is that a role is a place to stand, not a relationship, and a person can be needed here for years without being known.
Includer|Good Practical Skills.ask: When did you last talk to them about something other than the task?

Includer|Good at Connecting with Others.recognize: You bring people in and you put them in front of each other, the same instinct arriving twice, so almost nobody in your orbit stays a stranger. What is missing is any threshold. Nothing in you asks whether this particular room is right for this particular person.
Includer|Good at Connecting with Others.ask: Who did you bring somewhere they did not belong?

Includer|Good-Natured and Positive.recognize: You make a group feel like an easy place to be, so people who were braced for awkwardness relax into it. The gap is that good humor can skate over a serious exclusion, and someone being quietly frozen out may hear your good humor as the group agreeing with itself.
Includer|Good-Natured and Positive.ask: What exclusion have you smoothed over?

Includer|Grounded.recognize: You stay steady in a group that is fracturing, and your unwillingness to pick a faction is often what keeps a door open for the people caught between them. The cost is that neutrality reads as absence to someone who needed you to say their name.
Includer|Grounded.ask: Who needed you to take their side?

Includer|Hands-on and Observant.recognize: You see someone standing alone and you are across the room before you have thought about it. The gap is that instant response is response to what is visible, and the person who has been slowly withdrawing for six months never triggers it.
Includer|Hands-on and Observant.ask: Who has been fading here for months?

Includer|Handy and Resourceful.recognize: You find a way to get someone in with whatever is available, inventing a role or a reason when none existed. The cost is that a place made up on the spot depends on you, and it disappears the week you stop maintaining it.
Includer|Handy and Resourceful.ask: Whose place here exists only because you keep making it?

Includer|Hardworking.recognize: You do the unglamorous work of remembering names and following up, which is why people feel held by your group rather than processed by it. The gap is that nobody assigned this, so nobody notices it is a job, least of all the person doing it.
Includer|Hardworking.ask: What would nobody pick up in your absence?

Includer|Honest.recognize: You will say that you do not know someone well rather than pretending, which is why the relationships you do claim are trusted. The cost is that honesty about distance can confirm what a person feared, and they may not have been ready to hear where they stand.
Includer|Honest.ask: Who found out from you that they were on the outside?

Includer|Honest and Direct.recognize: You tell a group directly who is missing and what it costs them, without dressing it up as a suggestion. The gap is that stating it that way puts people on the defensive, and a defensive group closes ranks rather than opening them.
Includer|Honest and Direct.ask: When did your challenge make a group tighter?

Includer|Idealistic.recognize: You hold a picture of a room where nobody is on the outside, and that picture is what keeps you doing this after everyone else has accepted the seating. The cost is that no actual group will match it, and you carry a permanent low-grade sense of falling short.
Includer|Idealistic.ask: What level of belonging would satisfy you?

Includer|Imaginative.recognize: You can imagine what the room looks like from the doorway, which is why you notice things that regulars have stopped seeing. The gap is that imagining someone's experience is not asking about it, and you have been solving for a discomfort you invented.
Includer|Imaginative.ask: What did you assume about how it feels to be new here?

Includer|Independent.recognize: You bring people in without needing the group's permission or approval, which is why you have included people the group would have hesitated over. The cost is that inclusion you perform alone is inclusion the group never agreed to, and the person may end up belonging to you rather than to it.
Includer|Independent.ask: Who belongs to you rather than to this group?

Includer|Informed.recognize: You know who has not been contacted, who missed the last three, and who has never been asked, and you carry that list without anyone assigning it. The gap is that a list is not a relationship, and being counted accurately is not the same as being wanted.
Includer|Informed.ask: Who is on your list and nowhere else?

Includer|Insightful.recognize: You see why a particular person keeps ending up outside, usually something they have never said, and you can address the cause rather than the symptom. The cost is that arriving at their reason before they have named it means you are working with a version of them you constructed.
Includer|Insightful.ask: What did you conclude about them without checking?

Includer|Kind and Encouraging.recognize: You tell the person on the edge that they belong here, and you say it in a way that they believe. The gap is that reassurance can substitute for actual change, and someone can be told they are wanted by you while the group behaves otherwise.
Includer|Kind and Encouraging.ask: Whose experience does your reassurance contradict?

Includer|Knowledgeable.recognize: You remember who is connected to whom and what everyone has already been asked, so nobody gets approached twice or forgotten once. The cost is that holding the whole picture makes you the router, and information about people stops moving when you are not in the room.
Includer|Knowledgeable.ask: What does this group not have because you hold it?

Includer|Loyal, Patient, and Reliable.recognize: You keep the door open for someone for years, long after they stopped using it, and more than one person has come back because it was still there. The gap is that an open door has a cost you absorb quietly, and you have held space for people who were never coming back.
Includer|Loyal, Patient, and Reliable.ask: Which door should you finally close?

Includer|Observant.recognize: You see who is not being spoken to before anyone else registers it, and you have quietly fixed dozens of these without comment. The cost is that quiet fixing leaves the group's actual habits untouched, and they will produce the same problem next week.
Includer|Observant.ask: What keeps regenerating because you keep covering it?

Includer|Open-Minded.recognize: You bring people in and you take them as they come, the same instinct arriving twice, so there is no version of a person your group cannot accommodate. What is absent is any standard for entry. Nothing in you asks what this group is actually for.

Includer|Organized and Effective.recognize: You have a reliable way of getting new people integrated, and it works often enough that you can absorb a lot of them at once. The gap is that a process assumes a typical newcomer, and the atypical one gets run through it anyway.
Includer|Organized and Effective.ask: Who did your process not fit?

Includer|Original.recognize: You are drawn to the person who does not match the group, and you bring them in precisely because they do not. The cost is that being included as the exception is its own kind of outside, and they may know exactly why they were invited.
Includer|Original.ask: Who was invited for not fitting in?

Includer|Passionate.recognize: You care about this with an intensity that makes other people uncomfortable, and that intensity is why things actually change when you are involved. The gap is that heat about someone else's exclusion can take over their situation, and it stops being about them.

Includer|Perceptive.recognize: You pick up the small signal that someone has been shut out, a glance or a pause that nobody else registered. The cost is that a signal that faint cannot be confirmed, and you have acted on exclusions that were never happening.
Includer|Perceptive.ask: Which slight existed only in your reading of it?

Includer|Positive and Enthusiastic.recognize: You bring energy to including people, so being drawn into your group feels like good news rather than charity. The gap is that upbeat framing makes it hard to say no, and a person can end up committed to something they never wanted.
Includer|Positive and Enthusiastic.ask: Who could not turn you down?

Includer|Principled.recognize: You treat leaving people out as a moral failure rather than an oversight, and that conviction is why you keep raising it when it would be easier not to. The cost is that framing it as wrongdoing makes a group defensive rather than curious, and a defensive group does not change.
Includer|Principled.ask: Who stopped listening once you made it a moral question?

Includer|Proactive Initiative.recognize: You reach out first, every time, without waiting to see whether someone will make the effort themselves. The gap is that going first always means the relationship has never been tested, and you do not know whether anyone would come toward you.
Includer|Proactive Initiative.ask: Has anybody here ever pursued you?

Includer|Quick Thinkers.recognize: You can pull a stranded person into a conversation in one sentence delivered at the right second, which is a skill most people do not have. The cost is that a fast intervention is a guess about what they needed, and sometimes the guess is wrong in a way you never find out about.
Includer|Quick Thinkers.ask: Which of your rescues went badly and never got mentioned?

Includer|Rational.recognize: You can make the case for why a group is worse off without a particular person, which moves people who are unmoved by fairness alone. The gap is that arguing for someone's value reduces them to their usefulness, and they may hear the argument you made on their behalf.
Includer|Rational.ask: Who was defended in terms they would not have chosen?

Includer|Rational and Practical.recognize: You get people involved by finding what they can actually contribute, which respects them more than a symbolic invitation would. The cost is that a person with nothing obvious to offer has no route in, and those are usually the ones most on the outside.
Includer|Rational and Practical.ask: Who has nothing to contribute here?

Includer|Receptive.recognize: You bring people in and you take in whatever they bring, the same openness twice, so nobody has ever felt they had to qualify to be near you. What is missing is any filter at all. Nothing in you notices when someone is taking more from this group than they put into it.
Includer|Receptive.ask: Who is taking more here than they give?

Includer|Reliable.recognize: You are the person who actually follows up with the newcomer, and you have never once said you would and not done it. The gap is that this is now expected of you and nobody else has learned to do it, so the group's hospitality is one person deep.
Includer|Reliable.ask: How deep is this group's hospitality without you?

Includer|Research-Oriented.recognize: You find out whether people actually feel included rather than assuming it, asking the question everyone else is afraid of the answer to. The cost is that finding out takes time, and the person who told you they felt outside is still waiting to see whether anything changes.
Includer|Research-Oriented.ask: Who told you and is still waiting?

Includer|Results Oriented.recognize: You measure this by whether people actually stayed, which keeps your inclusion honest rather than performative. The gap is that some people you brought in will leave anyway, and their time here mattered even though it did not last.
Includer|Results Oriented.ask: Who left that you still count as a failure?

Includer|Sensitive and Warm.recognize: You make a person feel personally wanted rather than generally invited, and that difference is why they come back. The cost is that this is what you offer and it does not scale, and there is a limit to how many people can receive it from you.
Includer|Sensitive and Warm.ask: How many people can you actually hold this way?

Includer|Sensitive to Others.recognize: You change how you approach each person so that nobody is brought in a way that would embarrass them. The gap is that endless tailoring means the invitation gets quieter each time, and eventually it is too faint to hear.
Includer|Sensitive to Others.ask: Which invitation did you make so gently it was missed?

Includer|Sociable.recognize: You move around a room making sure nobody is stuck, and you enjoy it, which is why it does not read as duty. The cost is that circulating means nobody gets more than four minutes, and the person who needed a long conversation got the same as everyone else.
Includer|Sociable.ask: Who needed a real conversation and got a lap of the room?

Includer|Spontaneous.recognize: You invite people on the spot, without checking whether it is convenient or whether anyone else agreed, and a lot of good things have started that way. The gap is that invitations made this way are unevenly distributed, and the people who get them are the ones who happened to be in front of you.
Includer|Spontaneous.ask: Who is never in front of you when you decide these things?

Includer|Strong Practical Skills.recognize: You take care of the logistics that keep people from falling out, the ride and the reminder and the spare chair, and none of it gets noticed. The cost is that removing every obstacle means nobody has to want this very much, and effortless participation is easy to drop.
Includer|Strong Practical Skills.ask: What has anyone here had to work for?

Includer|Strong Sense of Duty.recognize: You treat making sure nobody is left out as something you owe rather than something you offer, which is why you do it on days you have nothing left. The gap is that a duty you assigned yourself cannot be handed back, and nobody knows to relieve you.
Includer|Strong Sense of Duty.ask: Who could you tell that you are tired?

Includer|Strong-willed.recognize: You will hold a group to including someone even when the group has decided otherwise, and you have won that argument more than once. The cost is that a person brought in by force of your will knows exactly how they got in.
Includer|Strong-willed.ask: Who knows they were an argument you won?

Includer|Supportive.recognize: You get behind the person with the least standing in the room, which is why the quietest people find they have a voice around you. The gap is that borrowed standing is still borrowed, and the moment you are not present it returns to where it was.
Includer|Supportive.ask: Whose standing here depends entirely on you?

Includer|Very Loyal.recognize: You do not drop people, so someone who has fallen out of favor with everyone else still has you, and they know it. The cost is that loyalty to everyone means loyalty is not a signal, and the people closest to you may not be sure they are.
Includer|Very Loyal.ask: Who is not sure where they rank with you?

Includer|Very Responsible.recognize: You take it personally when someone slips out of a group you are part of, treating it as something you failed to do. The gap is that people leave for reasons that have nothing to do with you, and carrying those departures is a way to wear yourself out on things you never controlled.
Includer|Very Responsible.ask: Whose departure are you still holding as yours?

Individualization|Altruistic.recognize: You see exactly what this particular person needs rather than what people generally need, and then you give them that. The cost is that individual attention does not scale and neither do you, and a group of thirty means thirty separate acts of noticing.
Individualization|Altruistic.ask: Who gets the generic version of you?

Individualization|Analytical.recognize: You can describe precisely how one person operates differently from another, with evidence rather than impression, which makes your read on people unusually reliable. The gap is that a detailed model of someone is still a model, and you may be updating it far less often than they change.
Individualization|Analytical.ask: When did you last revise your read on someone?

Individualization|Bold.recognize: You will tell a person what makes them unlike anyone else in the room, directly, at a moment they were not expecting it. The cost is that being singled out is not always a gift, and someone who has spent years trying to blend may not thank you for the accuracy.
Individualization|Bold.ask: Who did you single out who wanted to blend?

Individualization|Calm and Practical.recognize: You notice what makes each person particular and you act on it without fuss, so people get treated correctly without anyone announcing that a special effort was made. The gap is that unannounced care is uncounted care, and nobody in your world knows how much of what works is you.
Individualization|Calm and Practical.ask: What do people assume just happens by itself?

Individualization|Charismatic.recognize: You draw people in and then treat each of them as a specific person rather than an audience, which is why your appeal survives close contact. The cost is that this level of attention is a promise, and the number of people who now expect it from you has outgrown the hours.
Individualization|Charismatic.ask: Who is expecting attention you cannot deliver?

Individualization|Charming.recognize: You make each person feel that you noticed something particular about them, quickly, which almost nobody else manages. The gap is that a fast read delivered well is very hard to tell apart from flattery, and you may not always be sure yourself.
Individualization|Charming.ask: Which of your observations was performance?

Individualization|Clear Communication.recognize: You can put into words what makes someone particular, in a sentence they will remember for years. The cost is that a well-phrased description becomes a label, and a person can spend a decade living up to something you said once.
Individualization|Clear Communication.ask: Who is still quoting you about themselves?

Individualization|Creative.recognize: You find the form that fits this one person, inventing the role or the approach rather than fitting them to an existing slot. The gap is that a bespoke arrangement is hard for anyone else to run, and it ends when your attention moves.
Individualization|Creative.ask: What arrangement of yours would not survive you?

Individualization|Curious.recognize: You want to know what makes this person work, specifically, and that interest is why people tell you things they have not told anyone. The cost is that curiosity is satisfied by comprehension, and once you have the shape of a person the pull toward them can fade.
Individualization|Curious.ask: Who did you stop pursuing once you had them worked out?

Individualization|Decisive Action.recognize: You size up a person quickly and act on what you see, putting them where they will thrive without a long process. The gap is that a fast placement is a first read, and someone put in the wrong slot early may never get reassessed.
Individualization|Decisive Action.ask: Who is in a role you assigned them years ago?

Individualization|Dedicated.recognize: You keep studying a person long after you have the basics, which is why your read on the people close to you is unusually complete. The cost is that this attention is not evenly distributed, and the people outside your close circle get almost none of it.
Individualization|Dedicated.ask: Who gets none of this from you?

Individualization|Determined.recognize: You will not accept a generic explanation for someone's behavior, and you keep digging until you have the actual reason. The gap is that insisting on a specific answer can pressure a person into producing one, and they may hand you a story that fits rather than one that is true.
Individualization|Determined.ask: Who told you what you were looking for?

Individualization|Diligent and Observant.recognize: You notice what makes each person particular and you notice the small things generally, the same eye pointed twice, so very little about anybody escapes you. What is missing is any threshold for significance. Nothing in you decides which of these observations is worth acting on.
Individualization|Diligent and Observant.ask: Which of these details actually matters?

Individualization|Direct.recognize: You tell a person plainly what you see as their particular strength and their particular limit, which is more useful than most feedback they get. The cost is that your calibration is your own, and a specific observation delivered without cushioning can define someone before they have argued with it.
Individualization|Direct.ask: Who accepted your assessment without questioning it?

Individualization|Direct and Authentic.recognize: You talk about your own particular makeup openly, which gives other people permission to stop presenting a standard version of themselves. The cost is that your openness sets a pace, and someone more private may feel behind before the conversation has started.
Individualization|Direct and Authentic.ask: Who is not ready to be as open as you are?

Individualization|Direct and Honest.recognize: You will tell someone what you have noticed about them without being asked, because you think an accurate read is worth more than comfort. The gap is that an unrequested description of a person is a claim about them, and they may not agree you have standing to make it.

Individualization|Disciplined.recognize: You have a practice for learning people, notes and questions and follow-ups that happen whether or not you feel like it. The cost is that a system for knowing people can turn a relationship into an account you service, and the person may sense the difference.
Individualization|Disciplined.ask: Who might feel managed rather than known?

Individualization|Easygoing.recognize: You take each person exactly as they are with no agenda about who they ought to be, which is why people settle into their actual selves around you. The gap is that acceptance without expectation is comfortable and inert, and someone can be perfectly understood by you and not move an inch.
Individualization|Easygoing.ask: Who have you understood without ever challenging?

Individualization|Efficient Organizer.recognize: You work out fast what each person is best at and route work accordingly, which is why teams you assemble outperform their parts. The cost is that people become their best function, and the parts of them that are not productive get no assignment at all.
Individualization|Efficient Organizer.ask: What part of them does your system have no use for?

Individualization|Empathetic.recognize: You feel the particular texture of what this person carries, not what someone in their situation generally carries, which is why your comfort actually lands. The gap is that this level of attention is expensive, and you can only afford it for a few people at a time.
Individualization|Empathetic.ask: Who is currently outside the few?

Individualization|Energetic.recognize: You put serious work into learning what makes each person tick, and the sheer labor of it is why your reads are accurate rather than lucky. The cost is that this is a per-person cost that never drops, and a growing circle means a growing bill.
Individualization|Energetic.ask: What is this costing you per person?

Individualization|Enjoy Creating Order.recognize: You sort people accurately into what they are good at, and things run better because everyone is where they belong. The gap is that a person filed correctly is still filed, and the categories you use are yours rather than theirs.
Individualization|Enjoy Creating Order.ask: Which of your categories would they reject?

Individualization|Enthusiastic.recognize: You get visibly excited about what makes a person particular, and for many of them nobody has ever been excited about that before. The cost is that your enthusiasm attaches to what you found interesting, and the parts of them you did not find interesting go unmentioned.
Individualization|Enthusiastic.ask: What about them have you never remarked on?

Individualization|Excellent Brainstormer.recognize: You can think of many ways one specific person might be used well, which is why nobody in your orbit gets stuck in a single track. The gap is that a person offered many roles is a person who has not been given one, and choosing is what they needed help with.
Individualization|Excellent Brainstormer.ask: Which one would you pick for them?

Individualization|Excellent Communicator.recognize: You can explain one person to another in a way that dissolves a misunderstanding neither could name. The cost is that you become the translator, and two people can work together for years without ever learning to read each other directly.
Individualization|Excellent Communicator.ask: Which two people still need you in the middle?

Individualization|Excellent Organizers.recognize: You build arrangements that account for how each person actually operates rather than how the org chart assumes they do. The gap is that a setup tuned to specific people breaks when those people leave, and you have made things nobody else can inherit.
Individualization|Excellent Organizers.ask: What would break if two people left?

Individualization|Excellent People Skill.recognize: You adapt to each person so precisely that almost everyone finds you easy, which is why you can work with people others find impossible. The cost is that adapting is automatic now, and there may be no room in which anyone has met the unadapted version.
Individualization|Excellent People Skill.ask: Who has met you without adjustment?

Individualization|Future Focused.recognize: You see what a specific person could become, not what people like them typically become, and you aim your attention there. The gap is that a forecast about one person is a heavy thing for them to carry, and they did not agree to your projection.
Individualization|Future Focused.ask: What future have you assigned someone?

Individualization|Generous.recognize: You give each person exactly what would help them rather than what is easy to give, which takes far more from you than a standard gesture would. The cost is that tailored giving has no natural cap, and you have never worked out what yours is.

Individualization|Good Practical Skills.recognize: You match the task to the person with real accuracy, so people spend their time on work that suits them. The gap is that a good fit is comfortable, and someone can spend five years doing what they are already good at and learn nothing.
Individualization|Good Practical Skills.ask: Who has been comfortable in the same role too long?

Individualization|Good at Connecting wit.recognize: You know exactly which two people should meet and why, and your matches work at a rate that is not luck. The cost is that being right about people is not the same as being asked, and you have made connections that neither party wanted.
Individualization|Good at Connecting wit.ask: Which of your matches did neither of them want?

Individualization|Good-Natured and Posit.recognize: You notice what is particular about a person and you tend to notice the good version of it, which is why people feel generously seen by you. The gap is that a generous read is still a read, and the difficult thing about them is also true and also worth naming.
Individualization|Good-Natured and Posit.ask: What is the hard truth about them you have never said?

Individualization|Grounded.recognize: You keep a stable read on each person, so they are not re-evaluated every time they have a bad week. The cost is that stability can become a fixed opinion, and someone who has actually changed may still be met by the version of them you settled on.
Individualization|Grounded.ask: Who has changed since you last looked?

Individualization|Hands-on and Observant.recognize: You learn people by watching them work rather than by asking, which is why your read is based on what they do rather than what they claim. The gap is that observable behavior is a fraction of a person, and what you cannot see from across the room stays invisible.
Individualization|Hands-on and Observant.ask: What do you know about them that is not from watching?

Individualization|Handy and Resourceful.recognize: You find a way to use what a person happens to have, even when it does not match anything anyone needed. The cost is that a fit assembled on the spot is fragile, and the role you invented for someone can vanish the moment circumstances shift.
Individualization|Handy and Resourceful.ask: Whose role here was invented and never made permanent?

Individualization|Hardworking.recognize: You put in the hours to actually know people rather than relying on a quick impression, and that labor is why you are so rarely wrong about someone. The gap is that this work is invisible and unpaid, and it sits on top of everything you were actually assigned.
Individualization|Hardworking.ask: How many hours a week does knowing people take you?

Individualization|Honest.recognize: You will say what you actually think a person is like rather than the polite version, which is why your assessments are worth asking for. The cost is that an honest read is still one person's read, and yours arrives with enough confidence to be mistaken for fact.
Individualization|Honest.ask: Which of your assessments went unchallenged?

Individualization|Honest and Direct.recognize: You say what makes someone particular without hedging it, and people who are tired of vague feedback find that a relief. The gap is that a firm description leaves nowhere to stand for someone who disagrees with it.
Individualization|Honest and Direct.ask: Who disagreed with your read and never said so?

Individualization|Idealistic.recognize: You see the best particular version of a person, the one they would be at their finest, and you address that version. The cost is that they live as the ordinary version, and being spoken to as someone better can feel like not being seen at all.
Individualization|Idealistic.ask: Who is tired of being your best version of them?

Individualization|Imaginative.recognize: You can imagine how a specific person experiences a situation, in detail, which is why your accommodations are so precisely right. The gap is that an imagined interior is your construction, and you have never checked most of it against them.
Individualization|Imaginative.ask: How much of your version of them has been confirmed?

Individualization|Independent.recognize: You form your own view of a person and do not tune it to match the room's, which is why you have been right about people everyone else misread. The cost is that an unshared view is also an unchecked one, and you have been confidently wrong in private.
Individualization|Independent.ask: Whose read on someone should you have listened to?

Individualization|Informed.recognize: You follow what is going on with each person specifically, so you know who is struggling and who is thriving without asking. The gap is that accumulating detail about people is not the same as relationship with them, and a person can be well documented and rarely spoken to.
Individualization|Informed.ask: Whose file is thick and whose visits are rare?

Individualization|Insightful.recognize: You see what is particular about a person and you see straight to what is underneath, the same instinct twice, so you arrive at the core of someone very fast. What is absent is any pause. Nothing in you waits to find out whether they wanted to be understood that quickly.
Individualization|Insightful.ask: Who was not ready to be seen that clearly?

Individualization|Kind and Encouraging.recognize: You praise the specific thing rather than offering general encouragement, which is why what you say is believed when other people's praise is not. The gap is that specific praise teaches a person which parts of themselves you value, and they will show you more of those.
Individualization|Kind and Encouraging.ask: What are they hiding because you never praised it?

Individualization|Knowledgeable.recognize: You remember the particulars of every person you have worked with, what they are good at and what they avoid, going back years. The cost is that a large collection of detail about people can become a collection of fixed impressions, and the oldest entries are the least likely to be updated.
Individualization|Knowledgeable.ask: Which of your impressions is a decade old?

Individualization|Loyal, Patient, and Re.recognize: You give a person the time it takes to actually be understood, months if necessary, rather than settling for a first impression. The gap is that patience of that kind is finite in practice, and the people who got it were the ones who happened to be nearby.
Individualization|Loyal, Patient, and Re.ask: Who never got that much time from you?

Individualization|Observant.recognize: You register what makes each person particular and you register everything else too, the same attention twice, so you carry an enormous amount of detail about the people around you. What is missing is any way of putting it down. Nothing in you stops gathering.
Individualization|Observant.ask: Where does all of this detail go?

Individualization|Open-Minded.recognize: You resist the categories people get sorted into, holding each person as their own case, which is why you see people others have written off. The cost is that rejecting categories entirely means starting from nothing every time, and some patterns about people are worth trusting.
Individualization|Open-Minded.ask: Which reliable generalization do you keep discarding?

Individualization|Organized and Effectiv.recognize: You have a working way of learning what each person needs, applied consistently, which is why nothing about anyone falls through. The gap is that a repeatable approach produces comparable results, and comparison is exactly what individual attention was supposed to avoid.
Individualization|Organized and Effectiv.ask: Who are you comparing that you promised not to?

Individualization|Original.recognize: You see what sets each person apart and you are drawn to what sets anyone apart, the same instinct doubled, so ordinary people become interesting the moment you look. What is absent is any interest in the typical. Nothing in you finds the person who is exactly like everybody else worth studying.
Individualization|Original.ask: Who here have you found boring?

Individualization|Passionate.recognize: You care intensely about people being understood correctly, and you will spend real energy correcting someone's mischaracterization of a person who is not in the room. The cost is that intensity about accuracy can make you a difficult person to be wrong around.
Individualization|Passionate.ask: Who is careful about how they describe people to you?

Individualization|Perceptive.recognize: You see what makes each person particular and you pick up what people are not saying, the same instrument twice, so you assemble a version of someone very quickly and from very little. What is missing is any check. Nothing in you asks whether the person you assembled exists.
Individualization|Perceptive.ask: Which of your certainties about someone came from them?

Individualization|Positive and Enthusias.recognize: You bring energy to noticing what is particular about people, and being singled out by you feels like good news rather than scrutiny. The gap is that upbeat attention is still attention, and someone who wanted to be unremarkable has been made visible.
Individualization|Positive and Enthusias.ask: Who did you make visible against their preference?

Individualization|Principled.recognize: You treat seeing people accurately as a duty rather than a talent, which is why you keep doing it with people you dislike. The cost is that accuracy as a duty can turn into judgment as a duty, and a person you have assessed fairly may still feel sentenced.
Individualization|Principled.ask: Who felt judged by an assessment you thought was fair?

Individualization|Proactive Initiative.recognize: You work out what a person needs and provide it before they ask, often before they have named it themselves. The gap is that anticipating someone accurately takes away the moment where they would have asked, and asking is how people learn what they need.
Individualization|Proactive Initiative.ask: Who never has to name what they want around you?

Individualization|Quick Thinkers.recognize: You form an accurate read on a person in minutes, which is a genuine skill and not a guess. The cost is that a read that fast is a read from very little, and your confidence in it does not scale down to match.
Individualization|Quick Thinkers.ask: Whose file did you close in the first ten minutes?

Individualization|Rational.recognize: You test your impressions of people against what they actually do, which is why you are wrong about people less often than most. The gap is that a person is not fully accounted for by their behavior, and the parts that do not show up in the record get left out.
Individualization|Rational.ask: What is true of them that never shows up in their behavior?

Individualization|Rational and Practical.recognize: You focus on what each person can actually do here, which keeps your read grounded rather than abstract. The cost is that a person is more than their application, and someone whose particular gift has no place in this context may as well not have it.
Individualization|Rational and Practical.ask: Whose best quality has no place here?

Individualization|Receptive.recognize: You let each person define themselves to you rather than deciding in advance, which is why people feel accurately met. The gap is that a person's own account is partial, and the thing they cannot see about themselves is exactly what your attention was for.
Individualization|Receptive.ask: What can they not see that you can?

Individualization|Reliable.recognize: You treat each person consistently according to what you have learned about them, so nobody has to guess which version of you they will get. The cost is that consistency toward a person is consistency toward your model of them, and the model is older than they are.
Individualization|Reliable.ask: How old is your model of them?

Individualization|Research-Oriented.recognize: You gather real information about a person before concluding anything, asking others and checking over time rather than trusting a first impression. The gap is that thoroughness takes months, and someone needed to be understood by you last week.
Individualization|Research-Oriented.ask: Who needed to be understood before you were ready?

Individualization|Results Oriented.recognize: You use what you have learned about each person to get better work out of a situation, which keeps your attention to them honest rather than merely appreciative. The cost is that attention justified by production has to keep producing, and a person whose output drops may quietly stop receiving it.
Individualization|Results Oriented.ask: Who stopped getting your attention when their work dipped?

Individualization|Sensitive and Warm.recognize: You notice what is particular about a person and you respond to it tenderly, so being understood by you does not feel like being examined. The gap is that tenderness around an accurate observation makes it much easier to accept, and someone may accept a description of themselves that is wrong.
Individualization|Sensitive and Warm.ask: Who agreed with your read because you were kind about it?

Individualization|Sensitive to Others.recognize: You see what makes each person particular and you shape yourself to fit it, the same responsiveness twice, so almost nobody experiences friction with you. What is missing is a constant. Nothing in you stays the same across two people.
Individualization|Sensitive to Others.ask: Is there a you that does not depend on who is present?

Individualization|Sociable.recognize: You learn people by spending time among them, in volume, which is why your sample is larger than anyone's. The cost is that breadth and depth compete, and knowing something particular about four hundred people is not the same as knowing four.
Individualization|Sociable.ask: How many of those four hundred would notice you were gone?

Individualization|Spontaneous.recognize: You respond to what a person needs in the moment rather than according to a plan, which is why your attention feels alive rather than scheduled. The gap is that attention given this way goes to whoever is present, and the people rarely in front of you are rarely thought about.
Individualization|Spontaneous.ask: Who have you not thought about in months?

Individualization|Strong Practical Skill.recognize: You take what you notice about a person and do something concrete with it, arranging the thing that actually helps rather than commenting on it. The cost is that acting on your read means acting before they have confirmed it, and you can be very helpful in a direction they did not want.
Individualization|Strong Practical Skill.ask: What help did you provide that missed?

Individualization|Strong Sense of Duty.recognize: You treat understanding each person as part of what you owe them, which is why you do it for people you have no natural interest in. The gap is that a duty like this expands with every new person, and nobody has ever told you where it ends.
Individualization|Strong Sense of Duty.ask: How many people do you owe this to now?

Individualization|Strong-willed.recognize: You hold your read on a person against the group's opinion, and you have been the only one right about someone more than once. The cost is that the same firmness applies to a wrong read, and a person you have characterized has a long way to go to change it.
Individualization|Strong-willed.ask: Whose reputation with you is out of date?

Individualization|Supportive.recognize: You get behind what is particular about a person rather than what is generally valued, which is why people develop unusual strengths around you. The gap is that supporting someone's distinctiveness can commit them to it, and they may want to be ordinary in a way you are not offering.
Individualization|Supportive.ask: Who might want permission to be ordinary?

Individualization|Very Loyal.recognize: You speak up for a person's particular way of operating when others call it a problem, and they may never learn how often you have done it. The cost is that loyalty to how someone is can protect a genuine flaw, and the criticism you deflected was occasionally correct.
Individualization|Very Loyal.ask: Which criticism of them was right?

Individualization|Very Responsible.recognize: You take it as your job to make sure each person is placed where they can actually work, and you feel it personally when someone is in the wrong seat. The gap is that people's fit is not entirely yours to control, and you are carrying misplacements that were never your decision.
Individualization|Very Responsible.ask: Whose bad fit are you carrying as your fault?

Positivity|Altruistic.recognize: You lift people and you put them first, so your good mood is not something they have to work around; it is aimed at them. The cost is that both run on the same fuel and you refill neither, and the person who is cheerful for everyone has nowhere to be otherwise.
Positivity|Altruistic.ask: Where do you get to be in a bad mood?

Positivity|Analytical.recognize: You keep people's spirits up and you can also explain why a thing is going wrong, which is a rarer pairing than it sounds. The gap is that hope and diagnosis pull against each other in a single sentence, and people usually only hear one of them.
Positivity|Analytical.ask: Which do people hear from you, the hope or the problem?

Positivity|Bold.recognize: You will be openly optimistic in a room that has decided to be grim, which takes more courage than pessimism ever does. The cost is that cheerfulness against the mood of a room reads as not having grasped the situation.
Positivity|Bold.ask: Who thinks you do not understand how bad this is?

Positivity|Calm and Practical.recognize: You raise the mood without raising the volume, so people around you feel better without quite knowing why. The gap is that a quiet lift is easy to miss, and someone in serious trouble may need you to be obviously on their side.
Positivity|Calm and Practical.ask: Who needed you to be obvious about it?

Positivity|Charismatic.recognize: You pull people toward you and you are good news at the same time, which is why rooms reorganize themselves around you within minutes. The cost is that people come for the feeling, and a person can spend a year near you without either of you knowing the other.
Positivity|Charismatic.ask: Who comes to you for the mood rather than for you?

Positivity|Charming.recognize: You put people at rest and you lift them, so almost nobody resists you, and a hard week feels shorter after ten minutes. The gap is that both instincts smooth a surface, and nothing in you is built to sit in something ugly.
