Positivity|Charming.ask: What was the last thing you refused to make lighter?

Positivity|Clear Communication.recognize: You can say the encouraging thing in words that do not sound like a slogan, which is why people believe you. The cost is that a clean hopeful sentence is very portable, and it gets repeated in situations where it is no longer true.
Positivity|Clear Communication.ask: Which of your lines is being used where it does not apply?

Positivity|Creative.recognize: You find an unexpected way to lift a group, an idea or a gesture nobody saw coming, and it works because it was not the standard move. The gap is that novelty carries the lift, and the same trick will not work twice on the same people.
Positivity|Creative.ask: What worked once that you keep reaching for?

Positivity|Curious.recognize: You are interested in people and glad to see them, which is a combination that makes strangers relax fast. The cost is that both are pleasant and neither is weighty, and a person may not realize they are allowed to bring you something heavy.
Positivity|Curious.ask: Who does not know they can bring you bad news?

Positivity|Decisive Action.recognize: You decide the mood of a situation and then set it, rather than waiting to see what the room does. The gap is that setting the mood is a decision made for other people, and someone who needed the room to be heavy has been overruled.
Positivity|Decisive Action.ask: Who needed the room to stay heavy?

Positivity|Dedicated.recognize: You keep showing up cheerful for people long past the point where it costs you nothing, which is why your encouragement means something. The cost is that being the bright one is a commitment with no end date, and nobody has offered to take a shift.
Positivity|Dedicated.ask: Is there a substitute for this role?

Positivity|Determined.recognize: You will not let a group give up on itself, and your insistence on the possible has carried teams through things that should have finished them. The gap is that insisting on hope is still insisting, and a person who has honestly assessed the situation may feel steamrolled by it.
Positivity|Determined.ask: Who did the math and got overruled by your optimism?

Positivity|Diligent and Observant.recognize: You notice the small thing worth celebrating that everybody else walked past, and naming it changes the temperature of a whole day. The cost is that constant scanning for the good means you are also filtering, and the small bad signs get less of your notice.
Positivity|Diligent and Observant.ask: What small bad sign have you been filtering out?

Positivity|Direct.recognize: You will say the encouraging thing flatly, without decoration, which is why it does not sound like flattery. The gap is that a direct manner plus a positive message is a strong combination to argue with, and people may agree with you out loud and disagree privately.
Positivity|Direct.ask: Who agreed with you and did not mean it?

Positivity|Direct and Authentic.recognize: You are openly hopeful and you do not hide the work it takes, which is what separates you from someone performing optimism. The cost is that admitting the work invites people to check whether today is a hard one, and some days you would rather not be asked.
Positivity|Direct and Authentic.ask: What do you do on days you cannot manage it?

Positivity|Direct and Honest.recognize: You offer an honest encouragement, one that acknowledges the bad parts, which is why yours is trusted where general cheer is not. The gap is that honest hope is still hope, and you are the one deciding how much bad news the encouragement can carry.
Positivity|Direct and Honest.ask: What did you leave out of your last encouragement?

Positivity|Disciplined.recognize: You have made a practice of finding something good, done daily whether or not you feel it, and that habit is why it survives hard seasons. The cost is that a practiced response can outlive its honesty, and you may be producing the sentence rather than meaning it.
Positivity|Disciplined.ask: Was this morning's version felt or performed?

Positivity|Easygoing.recognize: You are positive and you are unbothered, the same disposition twice, so almost nothing that happens here registers as a crisis. What is absent is any urgency. Nothing in you produces the alarm a group occasionally needs.
Positivity|Easygoing.ask: What would you actually call a crisis?

Positivity|Efficient Organizer.recognize: You lift a group quickly, with a word or two rather than a whole intervention, and then get back to the work. The gap is that a fast lift is a lift that skipped the part where somebody explains what is wrong.
Positivity|Efficient Organizer.ask: Who never got to explain what was wrong?

Positivity|Empathetic.recognize: You feel exactly how low a person is and you meet that with warmth pitched to their level rather than yours. The cost is that feeling it and countering it happen at once, and you may be lifting them partly to get yourself out of the low place.
Positivity|Empathetic.ask: Were you lifting them or getting yourself out?

Positivity|Energetic.recognize: You brighten a room and you fill it with force, the same current arriving twice, so a group's mood moves the moment you walk in. What is missing is any low setting. Nothing in you can enter a room quietly.
Positivity|Energetic.ask: What happens to a room when you do not come?

Positivity|Enjoy Creating Order.recognize: You build the small rituals that give a group something to look forward to, and those markers are why the year has shape rather than being a blur. The cost is that a ritual keeps running after the feeling has left it, and people can attend a celebration nobody is enjoying.
Positivity|Enjoy Creating Order.ask: Which tradition here has stopped meaning anything?

Positivity|Enthusiastic.recognize: You lift people and you arrive keen about everything, the same warmth doubled, so your presence raises the expectation of any occasion. What is absent is any restraint. Nothing in you can let an ordinary thing be ordinary.
Positivity|Enthusiastic.ask: What here should be allowed to stay ordinary?

Positivity|Excellent Brainstormers.recognize: You can produce a dozen reasons a situation might turn out fine, and at least three of them are usually sound. The gap is that abundance makes each one lighter, and a person in trouble wanted one reason they could hold.
Positivity|Excellent Brainstormers.ask: What is the one reason that is actually true?

Positivity|Excellent Communicators.recognize: You can put hope into words that people carry out of the room, which is a form of leadership and not a soft skill. The cost is that fluency makes the hopeful case sound stronger than the facts support, and you are persuasive before you are right.
Positivity|Excellent Communicators.ask: What have you talked people into believing?

Positivity|Excellent Organizers.recognize: You build the systems that keep a group's morale from depending on any one day, so a bad week does not sink anybody. The gap is that a well-run group can carry people who have quietly stopped caring, and attendance is not enthusiasm.
Positivity|Excellent Organizers.ask: Who is showing up here without caring?

Positivity|Excellent People Skills.recognize: You work out what would lift a particular person and deliver exactly that, which is why your encouragement lands where general praise slides off. The cost is that this is also a technique, and you can execute it perfectly on a day you feel nothing.
Positivity|Excellent People Skills.ask: When did you encourage someone while feeling nothing?

Positivity|Future Focused.recognize: You are hopeful about what is coming, specifically rather than vaguely, which is why your optimism holds up under questioning. The gap is that a good future is not an answer to a bad present, and the person in front of you is in the present.
Positivity|Future Focused.ask: What is bad right now that you keep answering with later?

Positivity|Generous.recognize: You give away encouragement freely, to people who will never return it and people you will not see again. The cost is that free and unlimited are different things, and you have run out in private more than once this year.
Positivity|Generous.ask: What is left in reserve tonight?

Positivity|Good Practical Skills.recognize: You lift people by fixing something for them, so your encouragement arrives as a repaired thing rather than a phrase. The gap is that a solved problem is not the same as a heard person, and some of them wanted to be listened to.
Positivity|Good Practical Skills.ask: Who wanted listening and got a repair?

Positivity|Good at Connecting with Other.recognize: You put people together with visible delight, so both of them start the conversation already flattered. The cost is that your enthusiasm does the vouching, and you have connected people you did not actually know well.
Positivity|Good at Connecting with Other.ask: Who did you vouch for on very little?

Positivity|Good-Natured and Positive.recognize: You lift the mood and you are good-natured about everything, the same disposition arriving twice, so there is no version of you that a room finds difficult. What is missing is any weight at all. Nothing in you can make a group take something seriously.
Positivity|Good-Natured and Positive.ask: What have you never been able to make anyone take seriously?

Positivity|Grounded.recognize: You stay hopeful without floating, so your optimism has substance and people can rest on it. The cost is that steady good spirits are easy to take for granted, and nobody has ever asked whether you are all right.
Positivity|Grounded.ask: Who checks on the person doing the cheering?

Positivity|Hands-on and Observant.recognize: You lift the mood with something concrete and on the spot, a gesture in the moment rather than a speech later. The gap is that an instant response addresses the visible mood, and the person who has been low for six months does not present as low today.
Positivity|Hands-on and Observant.ask: Who has been low for months without showing it?

Positivity|Handy and Resourceful.recognize: You can find something to be glad about using whatever the situation gives you, however thin the material. The cost is that the skill works even when it should not, and you can produce a bright reading of a situation that genuinely has none.
Positivity|Handy and Resourceful.ask: Which situation are you determined to see well?

Positivity|Hardworking.recognize: You do the work of keeping other people's spirits up, and it is work, whatever it looks like from outside. The gap is that nobody counts it as labor, including you, so it never appears on the list of what you carry.
Positivity|Hardworking.ask: What is on your list that nobody counts?

Positivity|Honest.recognize: You will be positive without lying about it, which is why people can tell the difference between your encouragement and a platitude. The cost is that honest optimism sometimes has nothing to work with, and you have gone quiet in moments where people wanted you to speak.
Positivity|Honest.ask: Where did you go quiet because you could not say something true?

Positivity|Honest and Direct.recognize: You put the hopeful case plainly and you do not pad it, which is why it holds up when people test it. The gap is that a plain positive claim invites a plain negative one, and you have started arguments while trying to lift a room.
Positivity|Honest and Direct.ask: Which argument began with your encouragement?

Positivity|Idealistic.recognize: You believe things could be genuinely good, not merely tolerable, and that belief is why you keep working on situations others have accepted. The cost is that the distance between what could be and what is stays constant, and you have carried a private sadness for years.
Positivity|Idealistic.ask: What sadness have you never mentioned?

Positivity|Imaginative.recognize: You can imagine the good version of how this turns out in enough detail that other people can see it too. The gap is that a vivid future is not a plan, and the next actual step remains unassigned.
Positivity|Imaginative.ask: Who is doing the first thing, and by when?

Positivity|Independent.recognize: You keep your own spirits up without needing the room to supply them, which is why you can be the only cheerful person present. The cost is that morale you generate yourself is never checked against anything, and you can be relentlessly upbeat about a situation everyone else has correctly given up on.
Positivity|Independent.ask: What are you the last person still hopeful about?

Positivity|Informed.recognize: You keep hold of what is going well across a lot of situations, and you can produce a concrete example when a group needs one. The gap is that a curated set of good examples is still curated, and the ones you do not mention are also data.

Positivity|Insightful.recognize: You see quickly what would actually encourage a particular person, which is usually not the obvious thing. The cost is that arriving at it fast means you deliver it before they have finished saying what is wrong.

Positivity|Kind and Encouraging.recognize: You lift people and you build them up, the same instinct arriving twice, so nobody leaves a conversation with you feeling worse. What is absent is any capacity to disappoint. Nothing in you can tell a person something they will not enjoy.
Positivity|Kind and Encouraging.ask: What have you never told anyone here?

Positivity|Knowledgeable.recognize: You can point to the precedent where this went well, which turns a vague hope into something with a case behind it. The cost is that a precedent is chosen, and you have reached for the encouraging example rather than the representative one.
Positivity|Knowledgeable.ask: Which example did you pick because it helped?

Positivity|Loyal, Patient, and Reliable.recognize: You keep being the encouraging presence for years, so people know exactly what they will get from you and that it will still be there. The gap is that a fixed role becomes an expectation, and there is now no acceptable way for you to arrive discouraged.
Positivity|Loyal, Patient, and Reliable.ask: How would people react if you arrived discouraged?

Positivity|Observant.recognize: You spot the person whose mood has slipped before they have said anything, and you address it early. The cost is that you are reading surfaces, and a person who has learned to present well can be in serious trouble and never trigger your notice.
Positivity|Observant.ask: Who presents well and is not fine?

Positivity|Open-Minded.recognize: You stay hopeful about people and situations that others have written off, which is why second chances happen around you. The gap is that keeping every case alive is its own problem, and some things genuinely are finished.
Positivity|Open-Minded.ask: What is finished that you will not let go?

Positivity|Organized and Effective.recognize: You build morale into how the work runs rather than leaving it to chance, so a group's spirits do not depend on anyone's mood that morning. The cost is that manufactured morale is detectable, and people can tell when good feeling is on the agenda.
Positivity|Organized and Effective.ask: What here feels scheduled rather than felt?

Positivity|Original.recognize: You find the encouraging angle nobody had thought of, which is why your encouragement does not sound like everyone else's. The gap is that an unusual reading is still a reading, and being inventive about why this is fine is a skill that can serve avoidance.
Positivity|Original.ask: What are you being inventive about avoiding?

Positivity|Passionate.recognize: You care intensely about people not losing heart, and you will spend yourself keeping a group's spirits up long past the point of reasonable effort. The cost is that intensity attached to mood is exhausting to maintain, and you have crashed privately after carrying a room.
Positivity|Passionate.ask: What happens to you after you carry a room?

Positivity|Perceptive.recognize: You pick up the exact moment a person's spirits drop, often before they notice it themselves, and you move. The gap is that a signal that fine can be misjudged, and you have cheered up people who were simply thinking.
Positivity|Perceptive.ask: Who did you cheer up who was just concentrating?

Positivity|Positive and Enthusiastic.recognize: You lift the room and you bring enthusiasm into it, the same instinct arriving twice, so there is no gap at all between how you feel and what the group catches. What is missing is any counterweight. Nothing in you registers that a mood might need to be left alone.
Positivity|Positive and Enthusiastic.ask: Which mood should you have left alone?

Positivity|Principled.recognize: You treat keeping people's spirits up as something owed rather than optional, and you do it for people who have not earned it. The cost is that a duty to encourage can collide with a duty to be honest, and you have chosen encouragement more often than you would admit.
Positivity|Principled.ask: Where have you chosen encouragement over honesty?

Positivity|Proactive Initiative.recognize: You are the first to say something hopeful, before anyone else has decided what the mood is going to be, and that timing is why you so often set it. The gap is that setting the mood first means nobody else got a turn, and the room's actual feeling never surfaced.
Positivity|Proactive Initiative.ask: What was the room actually feeling?

Positivity|Quick Thinkers.recognize: You can turn a moment around in one line delivered at the right second, which is a skill and not a personality trait. The cost is that a fast turn is a turn away, and the thing being turned away from is still there.
Positivity|Quick Thinkers.ask: What keeps getting turned away from?

Positivity|Rational.recognize: You can make the actual case for optimism, with grounds that survive scrutiny, which is why your hopefulness is hard to dismiss. The gap is that a sound argument for hope does not produce hope, and the person you convinced still feels exactly as bad.
Positivity|Rational.ask: Who was convinced by you and felt no better?

Positivity|Rational and Practical.recognize: You lift people by pointing at what can be done, which helps more than being told to feel better. The cost is that a next step is not always available, and when there is nothing to do you have less to offer than you are used to.
Positivity|Rational and Practical.ask: What do you say when there is nothing to do?

Positivity|Receptive.recognize: You take in what people bring and you send back something better, which is why they keep bringing things. The gap is that both instincts are accommodating, and you have absorbed a great deal without ever handing any of it on.
Positivity|Receptive.ask: Where does what you absorb go?

Positivity|Reliable.recognize: You are consistently the good weather in someone's week, and you have never once failed to be. The cost is that reliability turns into expectation, and the day you cannot manage it will register as a change rather than a rest.
Positivity|Reliable.ask: What would it cost you to have an off day?

Positivity|Research-Oriented.recognize: You check whether the hopeful reading is actually supported before you offer it, which is why nobody has caught you being wrong. The gap is that checking takes time and a low moment is short, and you have been careful while somebody needed you to be quick.
Positivity|Research-Oriented.ask: Who needed speed and got care?

Positivity|Results Oriented.recognize: You aim your encouragement at getting something done, so it functions rather than merely feeling nice. The cost is that encouragement tied to production stops when production does, and the person who most needed it is usually the one delivering least.
Positivity|Results Oriented.ask: Who are you not encouraging because they are struggling?

Positivity|Sensitive and Warm.recognize: You lift people and you do it tenderly, so being encouraged by you does not feel like being managed. The gap is that both instincts are gentle, and there is no version of you that a person would find bracing.
Positivity|Sensitive and Warm.ask: Who needed bracing rather than comfort?

Positivity|Sensitive to Others.recognize: You calibrate the lift to what each person can accept, so nobody gets an enthusiasm that would embarrass them. The cost is that constant calibration reduces the message, and the encouragement can end up too small to be felt.
Positivity|Sensitive to Others.ask: Which encouragement did you make too small?

Positivity|Sociable.recognize: You raise the mood of a lot of people, moving through a room and leaving everyone slightly better. The gap is that a slight lift for forty people and a serious one for two are different jobs, and you have been doing the first while somebody needed the second.

Positivity|Spontaneous.recognize: You lift a moment with whatever occurs to you, unplanned, which is why it lands as sincere rather than staged. The cost is that unplanned means undistributed, and the people who get your good moments are the ones who were standing there.

Positivity|Strong Practical Skills.recognize: You lift people by taking something off them, so the encouragement arrives as relief rather than words. The gap is that competence delivered as care means people bring you tasks rather than feelings, and you may not have heard anything real in months.
Positivity|Strong Practical Skills.ask: When did someone last bring you a feeling rather than a task?

Positivity|Strong Sense of Duty.recognize: You treat the mood of the group as your responsibility, which is why you keep lifting it on days you are the one who needs lifting. The cost is that a duty you assigned yourself has no relief system, and there is no one you have told.

Positivity|Strong-willed.recognize: You will insist that things can be good, against the room and against the evidence, and more than once you have been right. The gap is that the same firmness applies when you are wrong, and a group can be talked past a warning it should have heeded.
Positivity|Strong-willed.ask: Which warning did you talk a group past?

Positivity|Supportive.recognize: You get behind people and you lift them, the same instinct twice, so nobody around you is ever unsupported or discouraged. What is missing is any pressure. Nothing in you supplies the discomfort that would make someone move.
Positivity|Supportive.ask: Who has never felt any pressure from you?

Positivity|Very Loyal.recognize: You stay positive about your people specifically, speaking up for their prospects when others have doubts. The cost is that loyalty plus optimism is a strong shield, and the accurate criticism of someone you care about may never reach them through you.
Positivity|Very Loyal.ask: What accurate criticism have you blocked?

Positivity|Very Responsible.recognize: You take the group's mood as something you are responsible for, and a flat week feels like something you failed to prevent. The gap is that other people's spirits are not yours to control, and you are carrying moods that had nothing to do with you.
Positivity|Very Responsible.ask: Which flat week did you file as your failure?

Relator|Altruistic.recognize: You go deep with people and you spend yourself on them, so the few you are close to get an extraordinary amount of you. The cost is that both instincts point at the same small group, and there is nothing left over for anyone standing outside it.
Relator|Altruistic.ask: Who is standing outside your circle?

Relator|Analytical.recognize: You are close to your people and you can also say precisely how each relationship works, which is why you rarely misjudge someone near you. The gap is that examining a friendship is a way of standing slightly outside it, and you may be doing that in every room you are in.
Relator|Analytical.ask: Where has your commentary replaced your presence?

Relator|Bold.recognize: You will go straight past small talk to the serious question, with someone you have just met, which most people would not risk. The cost is that intensity offered early can be more than a person wanted, and some of them retreat rather than say so.
Relator|Bold.ask: Who backed away after you went too far in too fast?

Relator|Calm and Practical.recognize: You build close relationships without drama, so the people near you have a steady thing rather than an intense one. The gap is that quiet closeness is easy to mistake for mild interest, and someone may not realize how much they matter to you.
Relator|Calm and Practical.ask: Have you ever told them plainly?

Relator|Charismatic.recognize: You draw a lot of people and you actually want only a few, which is a strange combination to live with. The cost is that the many who come toward you experience a warmth that will not go further, and most of them cannot tell where the line is.
Relator|Charismatic.ask: Where is the line, and who has never been shown it?

Relator|Charming.recognize: You are easy to like and hard to know, both at once, which is why people are often surprised how little they have on you. The gap is that a pleasant surface is a very effective place to hide, and you may be using it deliberately.
Relator|Charming.ask: What does the likeable version of you keep people from?

Relator|Clear Communication.recognize: You say directly what someone means to you, in words that do not hedge, which is rarer than it sounds and lands hard. The cost is that saying a bond out loud makes it official, and the other person may not have been ready to agree to it.
Relator|Clear Communication.ask: Who did you name a friendship to before they had?

Relator|Creative.recognize: You build closeness in your own way, with the shared project or the private language that becomes the thing holding you together. The gap is that a relationship built on something invented is hard for anyone else to join, and your closest ties tend to be pairs.
Relator|Creative.ask: Which of your friendships has room for a third person?

Relator|Curious.recognize: You want the whole of a person, not a summary, and that appetite is why people tell you things they have never said. The cost is that going that far in takes months, so you can only do it a few times, and everyone else gets the surface.
Relator|Curious.ask: Who has only ever had the surface of you?

Relator|Decisive Action.recognize: You decide someone is one of yours and then behave like it, without the long ambiguous stretch most friendships involve. The gap is that deciding fast is still deciding, and you have been fully invested in people you barely knew.
Relator|Decisive Action.ask: Whose character did you vouch for on a month's evidence?

Relator|Dedicated.recognize: You go deep and you do not let go, the same instinct arriving twice, so the people you have chosen have something almost nobody gets. What is missing is any exit. Nothing in you can end a relationship, even one that has clearly finished.
Relator|Dedicated.ask: Which relationship of yours has clearly finished?

Relator|Determined.recognize: You will keep working at a relationship through long stretches where it gives you nothing back, and more than one of your closest friendships survived only because of that. The gap is that persistence with a person can override what they are telling you, and not every distance is a problem to be solved.
Relator|Determined.ask: Whose distance have you been treating as a problem?

Relator|Diligent and Observant.recognize: You notice the small changes in the people close to you, the tone that is slightly off, and you ask about it. The cost is that this scrutiny only applies to the few, and someone just outside that circle could fall apart without your registering it.
Relator|Diligent and Observant.ask: Who came apart while you were not looking?

Relator|Direct.recognize: You say the hard thing to the people closest to you, because you think that is what closeness is for. The gap is that your directness is calibrated to a relationship that can take it, and you sometimes forget which conversations are inside that circle.
Relator|Direct.ask: Who got the inner-circle version of you without being in it?

Relator|Direct and Authentic.recognize: You show people who you actually are rather than a managed version, but only after they have earned it, which is why your openness means something. The cost is that earning it takes a long time and you have never said what the requirements are.
Relator|Direct and Authentic.ask: What would someone have to do to get in?

Relator|Direct and Honest.recognize: You will tell a close friend something painful because the relationship is strong enough to hold it, and usually it is. The gap is that your confidence in the relationship is your own assessment, and they may be less sure of it than you are.
Relator|Direct and Honest.ask: Which friendship is less solid than you assume?

Relator|Disciplined.recognize: You look after your close relationships deliberately, with standing calls and remembered dates, which is why they survive distance and years. The cost is that a tended relationship can become a tended duty, and you may be keeping something running out of habit rather than desire.
Relator|Disciplined.ask: Which of these do you keep up out of duty?

Relator|Easygoing.recognize: You are close to people without making demands of them, which is why your friendships are restful in a way most are not. The gap is that no demands means no pull, and a person can drift out of your life without either of you doing anything about it.
Relator|Easygoing.ask: Who drifted away while you both let it happen?

Relator|Efficient Organizer.recognize: You get past the preliminaries fast and into the conversation that matters, which is why an hour with you is worth three with someone else. The cost is that preliminaries are how some people warm up, and you have skipped the on-ramp a slower person needed.
Relator|Efficient Organizer.ask: Who needed the small talk you cut?

Relator|Empathetic.recognize: You are close enough to your people to feel what they feel without being told, which is why they do not have to explain themselves to you. The gap is that not having to explain means they never practice it, and you may be the only person on earth who can follow them.
Relator|Empathetic.ask: Who can they talk to when you are not there?

Relator|Energetic.recognize: You put serious energy into a small number of relationships rather than spreading it, so the people you have chosen get a version of you nobody else sees. The cost is that concentrated work is still finite, and you have very little left for anyone new.
Relator|Energetic.ask: How long has this circle been closed?

Relator|Enjoy Creating Order.recognize: You build routine into your close relationships, the standing dinner or the annual trip, so closeness has a container and does not depend on anyone remembering. The gap is that a container can carry a relationship that has quietly emptied out, and attendance is not intimacy.
Relator|Enjoy Creating Order.ask: Which of these routines is empty now?

Relator|Enthusiastic.recognize: You are openly delighted by the people you are close to, and they know it, which is not something most people ever get. The cost is that your delight is concentrated, and the difference between how you treat your few and everyone else is visible to everyone else.
Relator|Enthusiastic.ask: Who can see they are not one of your few?

Relator|Excellent Brainstormers.recognize: You can think of many ways to be useful to someone you care about, and you produce them faster than they can use them. The gap is that all of it goes to the same few people, and the volume of ideas is really a volume of care with nowhere else to go.
Relator|Excellent Brainstormers.ask: Where else could that care go?

Relator|Excellent Communicators.recognize: You can talk about a relationship itself, its state and its difficulties, which most people cannot do at all. The cost is that having the words makes you the one who starts every hard conversation, and the other person never develops the ability.
Relator|Excellent Communicators.ask: Who has never opened a difficult conversation with you?

Relator|Excellent Organizers.recognize: You keep the logistics of your close relationships running, the visits and the calls that would otherwise not happen across distance. The gap is that if you stopped, you would find out how many of these are mutual, and you have never wanted to run that test.
Relator|Excellent Organizers.ask: Which of these would survive if you stopped arranging it?

Relator|Excellent People Skills.recognize: You can be close to people who are difficult for everyone else, because you have the patience to get past the version they show first. The cost is that this makes you the designated person for someone hard, and the relationship may be more of a job than you admit.
Relator|Excellent People Skills.ask: Which of your close relationships is actually work?

Relator|Future Focused.recognize: You invest in relationships for the long run, treating a new friendship as something that will matter in twenty years. The gap is that a person is not a position you hold, and treating a relationship as an investment can make the present visit feel like a deposit.
Relator|Future Focused.ask: When did you last enjoy someone without thinking ahead?

Relator|Generous.recognize: You give a great deal to the people close to you, time and money and access, without any accounting. The cost is that generosity concentrated on a few can look like favoritism to everyone else, and usually it is.
Relator|Generous.ask: Who has noticed what your people get?

Relator|Good Practical Skills.recognize: You show closeness by doing things, the airport run and the repaired fence, and your friends know exactly what you mean by it. The gap is that not everyone hears a task as affection, and someone may be waiting for words you have never once said.
Relator|Good Practical Skills.ask: Who is waiting for you to say it?

Relator|Good at Connecting with Others.recognize: You know a lot of people and you are close to almost none of them, and you can tell the difference precisely. The cost is that everyone else uses one word for both, and people in your wide circle may think they are in the small one.
Relator|Good at Connecting with Others.ask: Who would be hurt to learn where they actually sit?

Relator|Good-Natured and Positive.recognize: You are warm with everyone and close with a few, and the warmth is real enough that the line between them is invisible. The gap is that an invisible line still exists, and someone can spend years believing they are getting nearer when nothing has moved.
Relator|Good-Natured and Positive.ask: Who thinks they are getting nearer?

Relator|Grounded.recognize: You are a fixed point for the people close to you, which is why they can go through anything and still know where you will be. The cost is that being the stable one is a role, and nobody has considered that you might need somewhere to stand too.

Relator|Hands-on and Observant.recognize: You show up in person when it matters, which is why your presence in a crisis is what people remember about you. The gap is that showing up is a response to an event, and the slow ordinary erosion of a friendship does not produce one.
Relator|Hands-on and Observant.ask: Which friendship has been eroding without an event?

Relator|Handy and Resourceful.recognize: You find ways to stay close across distance and circumstance, inventing whatever a relationship needs to survive a hard year. The cost is that you are the one doing the inventing, and a relationship kept alive by one person is a question neither of you wants to ask.
Relator|Handy and Resourceful.ask: Which of these are you keeping alive alone?

Relator|Hardworking.recognize: You put in the hours a serious friendship takes, which is why yours are unusually strong and unusually few. The gap is that the hours have to come from somewhere, and where they came from is the wider set of people who would have liked to know you.
Relator|Hardworking.ask: Who gave up trying to get time with you?

Relator|Honest.recognize: You are honest with your close people to a degree you are not with anyone else, which is part of what makes those relationships what they are. The cost is that the rest of your life gets a filtered version, and the distance between the two is wider than you probably realize.
Relator|Honest.ask: How different are you with your close people?

Relator|Honest and Direct.recognize: You tell the people close to you exactly where things stand between you, which almost nobody does. The gap is that a position said out loud is hard to move from, and you have defined a relationship in a moment that then held for years.
Relator|Honest and Direct.ask: Which relationship got defined in a bad week?

Relator|Idealistic.recognize: You hold a high picture of what a friendship can be, and the ones you have built come closer to it than most people ever get. The cost is that the bar is invisible and nobody was told, so people fail a test they did not know they were taking.
Relator|Idealistic.ask: What test are people failing without knowing?

Relator|Imaginative.recognize: You can imagine the whole interior of someone you are close to, and you are often right, which is why they feel known. The gap is that the version in your head is partly your own construction, and after years it may have drifted from the person.
Relator|Imaginative.ask: How much of them is remembered rather than current?

Relator|Independent.recognize: You need very few people and you are honest about that, which spares everyone the pretense. The cost is that self-sufficiency plus a small circle is a short distance from being alone, and you would probably not notice the moment you crossed it.
Relator|Independent.ask: How would you know if you had crossed it?

Relator|Informed.recognize: You hold the details of your people's lives, the ongoing situations and the names of everyone involved, going back years. The gap is that having a life catalogued is not the same as being in it, and you may be better informed about someone than you are present to them.
Relator|Informed.ask: How long since you were in the same room?

Relator|Insightful.recognize: You see into the people close to you, arriving at what is going on well before they have put it into words. The cost is that being seen that clearly is not always a comfort, and someone may occasionally want to be with you and not be understood.
Relator|Insightful.ask: Who wants a break from being understood by you?

Relator|Kind and Encouraging.recognize: You are gentle with the people you are close to, and they get something from you that is specific and impossible to dismiss. The gap is that closeness plus gentleness makes the hard sentence very hard, and there is something you have been not saying for a long time.
Relator|Kind and Encouraging.ask: What have you been not saying?

Relator|Knowledgeable.recognize: You have your people's history and their patterns and what they do under pressure, all of it. The cost is that being that familiar with someone can freeze them, and you may be the last person to notice that they have changed.
Relator|Knowledgeable.ask: How have they changed while you were not updating?

Relator|Loyal, Patient, and Reliable.recognize: You go deep and you remain, the same instinct arriving twice, so the people you have chosen have never once had to wonder about you. What is missing is any threshold. Nothing in you can decide that a relationship has cost too much.
Relator|Loyal, Patient, and Reliable.ask: What would a relationship have to cost before you left?

Relator|Observant.recognize: You follow the people close to you carefully and notice what others miss about them, which is why your read is accurate. The cost is that attention aimed at a few is attention withdrawn from everyone else, and you may be missing a great deal about people just outside.
Relator|Observant.ask: Who just outside your circle is struggling?

Relator|Open-Minded.recognize: You let the people close to you change without holding them to who they were, which is why your oldest friendships have survived people becoming different. The gap is that accepting every change means never objecting to one, and a friend heading somewhere bad has heard nothing from you.

Relator|Organized and Effective.recognize: You have a working way of keeping close relationships alive across busy years, and it is why yours survived when other people's did not. The cost is that a system for closeness is still a system, and the people in it may be able to tell they are being managed well.
Relator|Organized and Effective.ask: Who might be able to tell?

Relator|Original.recognize: You form relationships that do not look like anyone else's, with their own shape and their own rules, and they work. The gap is that unusual arrangements are hard to explain, and the people in them may not have the same account of what this is that you do.
Relator|Original.ask: Would they describe this relationship the way you do?

Relator|Passionate.recognize: You care about your few people with an intensity that would be too much spread wide, which is exactly why you do not spread it. The cost is that intensity concentrated has nowhere to go when one of those ends, and you have taken years to recover from a loss others would call ordinary.
Relator|Passionate.ask: Which loss are you still recovering from?

Relator|Perceptive.recognize: You pick up what your close people are not saying, so a shift in one of them registers with you before it registers with them. The gap is that this only works on people you have studied for years, and you are far less accurate about everyone else than you assume.

Relator|Positive and Enthusiastic.recognize: You bring energy into your close relationships, so being one of your people is genuinely fun rather than only serious. The cost is that upbeat is the default setting, and someone may not be sure whether your friendship can hold something bleak.
Relator|Positive and Enthusiastic.ask: Who is not sure you can take their bad news?

Relator|Principled.recognize: You hold your close relationships to a code, honesty and follow-through, and you do not make exceptions for people you love. The gap is that a friend who breaks it has very few routes back, and you have ended relationships over a single breach.
Relator|Principled.ask: Which relationship ended over one thing?

Relator|Proactive Initiative.recognize: You reach out first and you keep reaching, so your relationships do not depend on the other person's initiative. The cost is that going first always means you have never found out who would come toward you, and you may be carrying more of these than you think.
Relator|Proactive Initiative.ask: Which of these has ever been returned?

Relator|Quick Thinkers.recognize: You can get to something serious with a person quickly, faster than the usual timetable, which is why some of your closest relationships began abruptly. The gap is that arriving that fast means arriving past the part where you would have found out who they are.
Relator|Quick Thinkers.ask: Which fast friendship turned out badly?

Relator|Rational.recognize: You think clearly about your relationships, which is why you are rarely blindsided by one and rarely deceived about where you stand. The cost is that analysis applied to intimacy can hold it at arm's length, and someone close may feel evaluated.

Relator|Rational and Practical.recognize: You keep your relationships grounded in what people actually do rather than what they say, which is why your trust is well placed. The gap is that a relationship judged by conduct alone leaves out what a person intended, and someone trying and failing gets the same reading as someone not trying.

Relator|Receptive.recognize: You take in whatever your close people bring and you never make them regret bringing it, which is why they bring everything. The cost is that absorbing is your position in these relationships, and there may be nobody whose job it is to do that for you.
Relator|Receptive.ask: Who takes what you are carrying?

Relator|Reliable.recognize: You are the person your close people can count on absolutely, and you have never once not been. The gap is that absolute reliability makes it very hard to have a bad year, and you would rather struggle privately than be less than what they expect.
Relator|Reliable.ask: What have you gone through privately?

Relator|Research-Oriented.recognize: You take your time before deciding someone is close, watching how they behave over months rather than trusting an early impression. The cost is that the long assessment is invisible to them, and a person may have concluded you were not interested while you were still deciding.
Relator|Research-Oriented.ask: Who gave up while you were still deciding?

Relator|Results Oriented.recognize: You bring the same seriousness to a relationship that you bring to work, which is why yours actually go somewhere rather than idling. The gap is that a friendship is not a project with an end point, and someone may feel there is a bar they are being held to.
Relator|Results Oriented.ask: What are they being measured against?

Relator|Sensitive and Warm.recognize: You are tender with your close people in a way the rest of the world never sees, which is why they would describe you very differently than colleagues would. The cost is that the two versions have to be kept apart, and the labor of running both is invisible even to you.
Relator|Sensitive and Warm.ask: How much work is the other version?

Relator|Sensitive to Others.recognize: You move carefully around the people closest to you, because you know exactly where each of them is fragile. The gap is that knowing where someone is fragile means never going there, and the fragile place may be the thing they most need addressed.
Relator|Sensitive to Others.ask: What fragile thing have you been going around for years?

Relator|Sociable.recognize: You enjoy being among people generally and you need closeness specifically, and the two do not substitute for each other however much of the first you get. The cost is that a full social calendar can disguise the absence of the second, and you can be surrounded and still short of what you need.
Relator|Sociable.ask: How many of last week's conversations went below the surface?

Relator|Spontaneous.recognize: You go deep in unplanned moments, the late conversation that was not on anyone's schedule, which is where most of your real relationships were formed. The gap is that these moments require unstructured time, and a full calendar quietly removes the conditions your closest relationships need.
Relator|Spontaneous.ask: When is your next unscheduled evening?

Relator|Strong Practical Skills.recognize: You are the person your close people call when something has gone wrong, because you will actually turn up and sort it out. The cost is that being useful is how you show up, and a friend who needs nothing practical may not know how to reach you.
Relator|Strong Practical Skills.ask: Who has nothing broken for you to fix?

Relator|Strong Sense of Duty.recognize: You treat your close relationships as things you owe rather than things you enjoy when convenient. The gap is that a debt like that cannot be renegotiated, and you are still fully committed to relationships that stopped being good for you.
Relator|Strong Sense of Duty.ask: Which one would you not choose again today?

Relator|Strong-willed.recognize: You decide who your people are and nothing moves you off it, including their own behavior and everyone else's opinion. The cost is that the same firmness applies to a relationship that has turned harmful, and you will hold on well past the point anyone could argue for.
Relator|Strong-willed.ask: Has anyone ever been released by you?

Relator|Supportive.recognize: You are the one holding your close people up, reliably and without being asked, which is why they have got through things they should not have. The gap is that help flowing one direction for years builds a relationship neither of you can easily rebalance now.
Relator|Supportive.ask: Which of these has never flowed both ways?

Relator|Very Loyal.recognize: You go deep and you never leave, the same instinct arriving twice, so the people you have chosen are chosen permanently. What is missing is any condition. Nothing in you can name a thing a person could do that would end it.
Relator|Very Loyal.ask: What could someone do that would end it?

Relator|Very Responsible.recognize: You take your close relationships as something you are responsible for, so when one is not going well you treat it as yours to fix. The gap is that a relationship has two people in it, and you have been repairing things alone that were never yours alone.
Relator|Very Responsible.ask: What have you been repairing by yourself?

wordBank.note: Each item carries a three-word bank: its original essence word plus two synonyms. A card prints six words, three from each side. essence/action/shadow are unchanged -- bank is additive. Asserted by scripts/verify_word_bank.js.
